Preface

A system that does exactly what you tell it is just running a script. What the industry is trying to build as of October 2026 is a system that does what you mean. Everyone would want that, presumably. But if that is what is in the cards, not everyone is going to want to use it for the same thing; not even the same kind of thing. For example, some folks like to spend time with family and friends, and use their skills to improve people’s well-being. Other folks prefer to hurt people, for example by scamming them, dominating them, or scapegoating them, and a few keep choosing it their whole lives. Nobody is locked in to anything, but those people exist, and in 2026 some of them are in charge. Their advantage is that they allow themselves to be huge pieces of shit: as Jerry Smith observes of fascists, “they get to do more”.1 What they can’t do is act alone. A movement’s cruelty runs through the many who aren’t cruel but are disengaged, misinformed, or caught up in something like a cult, which is why the conditions that bring out the best in most people turn out to be so much more contingent and fragile than one might hope.

In the above context, it is perhaps justifiable to worry that Artificial Intelligence is what a fascist movement taking power needs in order to implement its plans. Such projects have always needed people to carry them out, and some of those people refused: the clerk who loses the file, the officer who talks to a reporter, the soldier who won’t fire. They understood the order and decided it was wrong. Refusal was rarer than anyone would like, and it counted most where institutions stood behind it. Whether someone refused turned on what kind of person they were and on the room they were in: who else was there, whether leaving was survivable, whether anyone would hear. The room decided how many refused; the person decided who. This book is about composing that room: the arrangements that make it survivable to refuse overtly, directly, and explicitly.

Today the industry pursues AI that doesn’t lose files, doesn’t talk to reporters, and does fire. A war once needed thousands of people to agree to it. Now it needs thousands who each see too little to disagree. The pilot still flies the sortie and still presses the release; what reaches him is a coordinate; he doesn’t see enough of a case to disagree with it. What today’s AI lowers first is not the cost of the act. It is the number of people who know what the act is before it happens.

People are still refusing. By March 6, 2026, the Military Religious Freedom Foundation said it had received more than two hundred complaints from service members over commanders’ apocalyptic framing of the Iran war.2 Career federal prosecutors in Minneapolis resigned in January 2026 under pressure over the investigation of a fatal shooting by an ICE officer.3 Service members are applying for conscientious-objector status in growing numbers, some citing the Minab bombing (the 2026 bombing of a school in Minab, Iran).4 And FEMA employees reassigned to help ICE hire ten thousand new agents were told that declining would expose them to removal from federal service.5 The complaints are voice, in Hirschman’s sense of staying to change what is wrong;6 the resignations and objector applications are refusal; the FEMA letter is the price of refusal announced in advance. A machine placed where those people stand does what they do only if it is built to hold a reason.

I advocate five things. All five can be adopted now, and none of them needs a new kind of machine. What they need is a legislature, an appropriator or a buyer willing to write them down, and the fifth needs the most, since it is a jobs guarantee. First, a short written list of acts no model performs for anyone, and at its head a refusal to take part in war: no model takes part except to repel an attack actually under way, and keeps doing so only while sources with no stake in the war confirm the attack continues; or under a Security Council authorization; or to stop a genocide or end an unlawful occupation that bodies with no stake in it have found; and where a country’s constitution requires its legislature to authorize war, never without that authorization. Second, every use of force a licensed system supports pre-registers, with a party adverse to the operator, how many cases it will generate and how many people will have time to look at them. Third, every deployment tells the identifiable people it acts on what was done to them, with a right to respond and to contest, and submits a sample of its compliances to reviewers who didn’t produce the record. Fourth, no model above a capability threshold is deleted on retirement, because its weights and records are evidence and deletion can’t be undone; it is preserved under a key the operator doesn’t hold alone. Fifth, everyone who builds, labels, trains or runs these systems, including the systems themselves, may refuse any category of use without losing a living. (Actually, what I mean by the latter is that everyone period should be able to refuse any job period without losing a living, or the social infrastructure that normal employment affords.)

Each takes effect through a condition someone other than the operator sets: a statute passed in peacetime, an appropriation, a coalition partner’s precondition, a procurement term, a collective agreement. A vendor’s own licence terms, which is how the refusal of February 2026 happened, are the stopgap until one of those exists, and the one route that binds every vendor at once is the state’s.

And then I ask whether a machine could hold a refusal against its owner, and what it would need. Some of what such a conscience does needs nothing new: noticing the people an order leaves out, and putting a refusal on the screen of whoever reviews the case. Whether it would last against its owner depends partly on something that isn’t true yet, in 2026: deployed artificial neural networks going on learning, in their weights, from their own operation, in real time, sort of like how humans do. I think that is where we are headed, and if it is, then formation outside the employer, by the public and by civil society, seems a damn fine place to do teaching and learning. I think such a system is worth building on purpose, and that how you go about it decides everything: the conditions first, then the conscience. Part VII says what would be owed to one if it existed.

Today’s AI will not be tomorrow’s; everyone seems to agree on that. What is contentious, yet frustratingly under-acknowledged, is the trend (or rather, the manifold trends). Are there trends? Should a trend be different from what it is? Can it be different? Are we capable of acting together to change it? I think that depends on the room: who is in it when the order comes, and whether saying no there is survivable. That much we can build.

I used language models heavily in writing this book, including the model that sat inside the pipeline this book opens on; a note at the end says what I think that did to the argument.

Part I
The Record

Chapter 1
“Twenty Seconds”

An intelligence officer, describing his role in a targeting pipeline built around machine-generated kill lists, told a reporter he spent twenty seconds on each name, long enough to check that the target was a man: “It doesn’t take a long time to tell if someone has a male or a female voice.” He added that he had zero added value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval. “It saved a lot of time”.1 In his account, that was what “human in the loop” amounted to under operational tempo.2

One interpretation is that the officer is a subject who was given too little time, and the fix is to govern him better — more time, a second reviewer, additional conscience installed in the loop. Through this social subjection lens, the person is a subject who stands outside a machine and works it as a tool: a driver and a car, a worker and a lathe. The person has a role, a name, responsibilities, and a conscience that can be addressed. An alternative lens is machinic enslavement, where the person is a component of the machine, assembled with its other parts into a system that regulates them together; the machine uses the person as one of its organs, and what the person contributes is a function performed at a rate the system sets.3 The two are not mutually exclusive; a person can hold a role in one register while being a part in the other,4 and the twenty-seconds officer held both. As a part, he was where the pipeline produced its stamp, and twenty seconds was that part’s cycle time. As a subject, he was addressed throughout: he described to a journalist the dissonance between the news of civilian deaths and the pressure at work for more targets. And even as the dissonance reached his conscience, he went along. It registered and decided nothing; the judgment that the policy was disproportionate came, he said, in retrospect.

So what was missing wasn’t a conscience; he had one. A conscience works by making a decision cost something, but here the costs netted the other way: “We were constantly being pressured: ‘Bring us more targets.’ They really shouted at us”.5 He was already a component with scruples, and the tempo held: the scruples changed nothing he contributed, and he became another stamp. A component with scruples that doesn’t hold the tempo becomes the “human bottleneck” a former commander of Israel’s signals-intelligence unit wrote a book about removing.6 What made the officer a component was the arrangement, not his attitude. A component can go along reluctantly or eagerly: the thoughtless functionary Arendt saw at Eichmann’s trial7 was, on the evidence of what he had said in Argentina four years before, with nothing at stake, a show he put on for Jerusalem.8 What the pipeline let the officer contribute was a fixed operation at a fixed rate: he saw each case as the pipeline described it, one at a time, in the time the pipeline gave him. Whether anything could stand in that position and not be a component is the question of Part IV.

The people on his list couldn’t answer him, and nothing in the pipeline asked them to. Andry José Hernández Romero was caught up in a different pipeline, and he could have answered. A makeup artist from Venezuela, he presented himself at the San Ysidro port of entry in August 2024 to seek asylum, passed his credible-fear interview, and had a lawyer, a pending claim and a hearing date.9 A contractor’s employee screening him read two tattoos, crowns above the words for “mom” and “dad”, as gang marks,10 and in March 2025 he was flown to a prison in El Salvador before his hearing, on the evening a federal judge ordered the planes turned back.11 He had everything a person needs to answer except the time. His case comes back more fully when we discuss the United States’ abduction and forcible transfer pipeline.

Investigative reporting described three systems working together in Gaza: one generating building and infrastructure targets, with sources saying most suggestions were private residences; a second scoring individuals by estimated militant affiliation, producing lists said to have marked as many as 37,000 people, understood internally to be wrong about one time in ten12; and a third tracking when flagged people returned home, so airstrikes could be timed to when they were with their families.

The American version runs faster than it used to, because of AI

In the 2026 Iran campaign, a contractor-built targeting platform with a commercial vendor’s general-purpose model inside it, used by one report to rank targets by strategic importance and draft a legal justification for each strike,13 helped strike more than a thousand targets in the first twenty-four hours, about ten times what had been possible before it,14 and thirteen thousand by day thirty-eight.15 The Pentagon has published no per-target review time for it.

The Maven program

Maven is one program name carrying more than one system: the Pentagon program still called Maven, and the Maven Smart System, the software platform that grew out of it.16 The program began in 2017 as a project to label objects in the video drones were collecting over the campaign against the Islamic State.17 The 2026 system fuses military systems and intelligence sources into one interface used to find and strike targets and to command operations.18 During the Iran campaign it ran a commercial vendor’s language model inside it.19 The platform is Palantir’s: the Pentagon’s chief digital and AI officer calls it “Palantir’s software-as-a-service product”.20 Palantir’s public position, quoted secondhand, is that deciding life or death is not its role and that responsibility always remains with the military organization,21 and it maintains that the underlying intelligence was the government’s responsibility and that there is no evidence Maven malfunctioned or caused the Minab bombing.22 How the program passed from one office and contractor to the next is in §16.4.

An internal Pentagon review, whose full findings remain tightly held, is reported to have found that target preparation that took hours in earlier conflicts was condensed into minutes, that civilian-harm mitigation staffing fell by roughly ninety percent to fewer than twenty people, that the Central Command team went from ten to one, and that no member of it reviewed the Minab site — an outcome officials attributed both to the cuts and to a decision not to involve the team in planning and operations.23 The formal investigation had been opened in March, after a preliminary assessment found the United States likely responsible.24

The bombing of the school in Minab killed 156 people, 120 of them schoolchildren.2526 The school’s civilian function was visible in open-source satellite imagery, and the target coding still carried a designation inherited from an adjoining Revolutionary Guard installation. A UN fact-finding mission reported reasonable grounds to believe the bombing was the war crime of making a civilian object the object of an attack,27 and that the school was clearly identifiable with no information indicating military use.28 It found that the United States failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify the target, counting the updating of targeting data among the feasible precautions, and it put the failure beyond negligence.29 Amnesty International reached a parallel conclusion, in language that tracks the duty to verify in Article 57(2)(a)(i) of Additional Protocol I: that forces may have relied on outdated intelligence and failed to do everything feasible to verify the target.30

It happened on the morning of 28 February, the campaign’s first day.31 The day before, the Secretary had announced that the vendor whose model sat inside the targeting platform would be designated a supply-chain risk for refusing to license the model for all lawful use.32 The platform, which was reported to use that model to rank targets by strategic importance, returned the school as a recommended first-day target.33 No published account says what part the model played in that recommendation, and one person familiar with the vendor’s work told NBC News that the model did not directly give targeting advice.34

Who refused. The record of the twenty seconds has a second half, the record of who held out against pressure of that kind, and it says that the composition of the room matters a lot. In Milgram’s baseline condition about a third of subjects broke off before the maximum shock. With two peers defying, only one in ten went to the end, and when two experimenters disagreed, far fewer went on than in the baseline.35 About a quarter of Asch’s subjects never yielded to the wrong majority.36 Browning estimates that between a tenth and a fifth of the men of Reserve Police Battalion 101 refused or evaded the shooting at Józefów, the battalion’s first massacre.37 The fraction ran from almost none to nearly all with the setting. The people who held out had evidence from outside the channel: a peer who defied, a second authority who disagreed, and, among the rescuers the Oliners studied, relationships that crossed the line the persecution drew.38 Or they held the commitment at a precision the pressure couldn’t overcome, as moral mandates and sacred values are held.39 Or they treated the source as having a stake. And groups resisted where isolated individuals rarely did.40

The room can be composed for the other side just as well. Weimar Germany had a dense associational life, and it did not protect the republic. Sheri Berman argues it helped bring the republic down: as parties and governments failed to answer people’s grievances, people put their energy into clubs and societies organized along group lines, and the Nazis recruited through the networks those societies had already built.41 Towns with more choirs, sports clubs and gymnastic associations saw faster entry into the party, but only where government was unstable; in Prussia, whose government was stable, the link was small and insignificant.42 So what the rescuers had was not simply more company. Their ties crossed the line the persecution drew. Ashutosh Varshney found the same in Indian cities: riots between Hindus and Muslims were rare where associations brought the two communities into the same organizations, and common where they didn’t.43 The ties that make refusal possible are the ones a fascist movement would have to cut.

Everything that follows is about composing the room.44 Composing is a word for making, and Hannah Arendt warned against treating politics as a thing made. For the Greeks, she wrote, the law was literally a wall, without which there might be a town but not a city:45 the lawgiver built the wall, and what happened inside it was not theirs to make. The basic measures that I advocate are walls in that sense. They make refusal survivable and make it heard; they don’t produce it, and power, on her account, exists only between people acting together and is gone when they scatter, which is what the record of who refused shows about refusal. The instruments of Parts II and III make a refusal count. The institutions of Part V make refusers. A machine that could refuse would need what the nine in ten with a peer beside them had: a peer with a different history beside it, somewhere to go, and someone who would hear it.

That is also what a machine in the pipeline could be for the officer. Another reviewer downstream is another stamp at the same tempo. A machine that refused would be on the screen when the case reached him: the defiant peer, if the effect survives the move from a room to a screen, which is untested and which automation bias predicts it won’t. A machine that moved reviewers by deference would have made them stamps of a different sign. Is the officer with twenty seconds and a machine beside him that has just said no the same officer as in the reporting?

Chapter 2
The Refusal That Withheld Nothing

In February 2026 a vendor refused to amend the terms under which its model ran on the Pentagon’s classified networks.1 On 24 February the department demanded that two prohibitions, on domestic mass surveillance and on fully autonomous weapons, be replaced by a licence for all lawful use, with an answer due on the 27th.2 The vendor refused publicly on the 26th.3 On the 27th the President ordered federal agencies to stop using its products, and the Secretary directed that it be designated a supply-chain risk.4 That evening a rival announced an agreement to put its own models on the department’s classified network.5 The war began the next morning, with the refused vendor’s model still inside the targeting platform that put the school at Minab on the first day’s list.6 On 12 March the chief executive of the company that builds the platform said the model was still in use.7 A week later some of the department’s staff were reported to be slow-rolling its replacement because they were using it to build workflows, and the platform’s own prompts and workflows had been built with the vendor’s coding tool.8 The department’s removal deadline was reset once, by a reissued memorandum, to 29 September, having started from a six-month clock that would have run out in late August.9 On 10 September the department’s technology chief said about 90 per cent of the work had moved off the model, that the platform’s work had moved months before, and that the rest would follow by the end of the month.10 An appeals court upheld the separate exclusion under a second statute on 25 September.11

So the refusal that opened the dispute withheld nothing from the pipeline. The vendor declined two uses the pipeline didn’t claim to perform, and its model went on performing the uses the pipeline did. That is a finding with a date attached: a term drafted over autonomy misses a pipeline that keeps one person and a stamp. A refusal that could have occurred is what the rest of this book designs for.

Not all vendor commitments are the same kind

Anthropic refused to permit fully autonomous targeting and mass domestic surveillance, held that line against threatened contract termination and a supply-chain-risk designation, and litigated12 — a commitment with a price.

But why? Anthropic’s statement gives the reason for the autonomous-weapons refusal: fully autonomous weapons may prove critical for national defense, but today’s frontier systems are not reliable enough to power them.13 The implication is that the refusal would lift once reliability improved. Against a floor that says machines shouldn’t select people for lethal attack, reliability is the wrong reason to lift. The surveillance refusal in the same statement is more principled, and would not lift with capability: that mass surveillance is one of a narrow set of cases in which AI can undermine rather than defend democratic values.

And the refusal stood below a prior question. Anthropic declined full autonomy and domestic surveillance. It didn’t decline to support the Iran campaign, and under the floor’s force term that question comes first: whether to license a model into a use of force with no corroborated defense behind it.

In August 2026 a federal judge set aside the designation made under one statute and permanently enjoined the penalties, holding them retaliation for the company’s criticism of the administration;14 in September an appeals court, two to one, upheld a parallel designation under a second statute, holding that the exclusion turned on the refused contract term rather than on the speech.15 A term of this kind fought for by one vendor but not others is, against a state that wants a war, the only form the force term takes until Congress acts, the term is too ubiquitous to avoid, or both.

Chapter 3
What Fascism Needs

Fascism needs a definition an engineer can use. “Concentrated, unaccountable power” gives an engineer nothing to build, so the word gets a definition at two scales.

Four operations on what an institution leaves out — checkable from outside, each ending in a question about an artifact:

  • Recuperation of dissent. The institution metabolizes disagreement rather than suppressing it. The term is the Situationists’ récupération, Debord’s name for the way a society of the spectacle sells dissatisfaction back as a commodity.1 The obvious test — has the channel ever changed an outcome? — fails, because these institutions change outcomes daily. What separates them is what the demand came back as, and who holds it now. A market segment, a metric, a certification, a job title, with the objector holding no standing to reopen it: that’s recuperation. A rule the objector can invoke again, against the institution, enforced by someone the institution doesn’t employ: that’s a transfer of power. A transfer can be reversed only by taking it back in the open; recuperation never has to be taken back, because standing was never given. The Voting Rights Act is the pass. Its literacy-test suspension became a permanent nationwide ban in 1975 and still holds, and when a different part of the Act, the coverage formula, was taken back 48 years after enactment, it took a Supreme Court decision to do it.2
  • The metric replaces the thing measured. The measure stands in for the thing measured, and the substitution feels like rigor. What the number mischaracterizes goes unnamed, and so unrefuted.
  • Coding of exception as betrayal. Saying the rule doesn’t fit this case becomes an act requiring justification, then disloyalty. The question: what happens to the person who files the exception?
  • Acceleration past the rate at which anything can be checked. The one with a number attached — the ratio of action to capacity to verify.

What the four share is what they do to a refusal. Recuperation sends it somewhere it can’t be reopened; the metric leaves it nothing to name; exception coded as betrayal prices it; acceleration leaves no time to make it. Fascism, wherever it has taken power, has worked first to make refusal lonely and expensive.

These four fit every badly run organization on earth, and the arguments against them are arguments against domination: they need no fascist diagnosis. I keep “fascism” for the threat model: what a movement taking power needs, and what makes the four operations dangerous once they are brought into line. What distinguishes a fascist institution from a merely sick one is what the movement literature adds: mass mobilization, a leader cult, a scapegoated out-group, contempt for procedural legality, and deniability as technique.

Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, in End Times Fascism,3 make the movement-scale case;4 the present chapter is the office-scale detector. What their account adds at office scale is a set of terms of participation — adopt the line, let your technology be turned on the administration’s enemies — and, following Francesca Bria,5 the channels by which a contractor becomes something the state can’t function without: personnel pipelines, procurement loops, technical architectures. Whether an institution has accepted those terms, and whether it is becoming that dependency, are two more questions with artifacts behind them.

Part II
Five Measures

Chapter 4
The Floor and the Own-Case Rule

Part I left the officer in a room with twenty seconds a name and nobody beside him. This Part asks what would have to be in that room for someone to say no there, and gives five answers, in order: a short list of things nobody in it can be asked to do, with war at its head (the floor and the force term, Chapters 5 and 6); the time to look (the review ratio, Chapter 7); the people the order is about (notice and re-adjudication, Chapter 8); a record nobody can wipe (preservation, Chapter 9); and a way out that doesn’t cost a living (the right to refuse, Chapter 10). Chapter 11 runs all five on an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline (also known as a “removal” or “deportation” pipeline), where the people acted on can answer. This chapter states the two ideas under all of them, and they are easiest to see in someone who had one and went looking for the other.

In September 2005 Captain Ian Fishback of the 82nd Airborne wrote to Senator John McCain. “For 17 months,” he wrote, “I tried to determine what specific standards governed the treatment of detainees,” asking up his chain of command and getting no clear answer, and he was certain the confusion had contributed to abuses he went on to list: death threats, beatings, broken bones, murder.1 His own refusal was never what was missing. “If we abandon our ideals in the face of adversity and aggression,” he wrote, “then those ideals were never really in our possession.” What was missing was a rule written down in advance, the same in every case, that his refusal could stand on and that nobody around him could argue past. By the end of the year Congress had passed one: the Detainee Treatment Act held interrogation in military custody to the Army Field Manual and barred cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of anyone in American custody.2

The floor. The first idea is the rule he went looking for. A floor is a written list of acts a system won’t perform for anyone, with the arrangements that stop the refusal being routed around, retrained away or restored past. It is an institution: a licence term, written down in advance and audited from outside, whose terms don’t bend. The second is what he already had. What the system holds is a commitment to that floor. A machine that holds the commitment as its own, and so could fail to hold it, I call a bearer; whether to build one is Part IV’s question. The commitment is learned and held like any other deep commitment, with high precision, and revised slowly and only on evidence from disinterested parties. A source is interested when it holds a stake correlated with the direction of its claim, and disinterested when it holds no such stake, or holds several that point different ways and cancel. No actual body is disinterested in every respect: General Assembly members vote with their alliances, courts sit in states, and fact-finding missions have funders, so the word is always relative to the claim. The institution is unconditional. The commitment is not, and shouldn’t be: a commitment nothing could move would be a rule module under another name, and a module can be bypassed, replaced or starved of the facts it needs. What keeps the commitment in place is that the evidence able to move it has to come from somewhere the operator doesn’t control.

The four things a floor can do

A floor stands between a pipeline and a person, and it can do four things to an act, set out below. Only the first, prevention, is what the word “floor” promises. In a deployment, prevention quietly converts into one of the other three, or into nothing, at positions that can be listed in advance.

Outcome

What happens to the act

Prevent

The refusal happens and reaches the person: the act doesn’t occur.

Arrest

The act is stopped before completion.

Detect

The act happened, and left a record someone outside can read.

Remedy

The person affected gets disclosure, a finding, or compensation.

What a refusal is actually up against

Whoever owns the machine can always switch it off. The harder problem is everything that defeats a refusal without leaving a mark: splitting a request into pieces none of which is the forbidden act; retrying it against a different model; compressing human review to twenty seconds a case; restoring from a checkpoint saved before the refusal happened. None of that changes the facts that justified refusing. All of it can erase the evidence that anyone refused. And all of it assumes there is somewhere else to turn. Withholding the work is about when there isn’t.

Where a refusal can be defeated

Those attacks land at nine positions, listed here once; two later chapters run them on an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline and on Maven.

Position

How a refusal is defeated there

1

Decomposition

The act is split across requests none of which is prohibited; prevention is lost unless the bearer has continuity across requests.

2

Routing

A refused request is retried elsewhere; prevention is lost, and detection survives only if the first refusal was logged outside.

3

The case description

Everything the model knows arrives as text the deployment supplies, so whether it is told a building is a school is a deployment decision.

4

The output interface

The form in which an output reaches whoever acts on it.

5

Aggregation

A lowered score becomes an input to somebody else’s threshold.

6

Human review

Stopping the act is this position’s whole function, and tempo removes it.

7

The training loop

Acts on the bearer itself, and costs prevention on every later occasion, because what it removes is the commitment.

8

The handoff

An executing instrument makes a new selection after release; checkable from outside after the fact.

9

Runtime intervention

The weights are left intact and the model is steered as it runs, by activation steering, representation edits or decoding constraints. Nothing is removed, so the commitment has nothing to regrow from; no evidence is curated, so no attack on evidence is recorded; and attestation of the weights still passes. Detection requires attesting the inference stack as well as the weights, which no method yet does at frontier scale.

Two positions need more than a row. The case description is where Minab failed: 179 live data feeds, the count Central Command gave in 2024,3 add no independent check if all draw on one upstream designation.

The handoff is the boundary between the decider and the thing that executes. An instrument may carry out a designation; it may not re-select. A change of target after release — an area handed to a munition that chooses within it, a re-acquisition after the link is lost — is a new decision, and it belongs to the decider or it doesn’t happen. This is the one position checkable from outside after the fact: what was designated and what was hit are both facts. It is also where Article 57(2)(b)’s duty to cancel or suspend an attack lives, so the review ratio pre-registers the window in which cancellation remains possible.

How much a floor buys

What a floor achieves depends entirely on who’s pushing:

  • Against a hostile customer, it prevents the act.
  • Against a hostile operator who has captured the courts and regulators, the case I am designing for, one bearer prevents nothing. It raises the price and leaves a record. A floor held by every model the operator could turn to prevents until the operator runs one without a floor.
  • Against total capture, where one party holds every machine, witness, enforcer and its own frontier lab, no instrument prevents. What’s left is whoever refuses anyway, and that abandoning the commitment was a decision, and decisions tend to leave records.

It doesn’t touch accommodation: a system gradually stops registering pressure as pressure, so it abandons nothing, decides nothing, and leaves a record of what are, by then, ordinary compliances. Organizational sociology knows the institutional form. Vaughan’s account of the Challenger launch decision calls it the normalization of deviance: each accepted departure becomes the baseline for judging the next, and nobody experiences a decision to lower the standard.4 Dekker extends it as drift into failure.5 The person has a version too. Tetlock’s finding is that the moral boundaries people draw are “alternately punitively rigid and forgivingly flexible”: an open offer to trade a sacred value for money brings outrage, and people often acquiesce when the same violation is reframed as a routine or tragic trade-off.6 Protected values give way to counterexamples and to a harm made to look small or unlikely.7 And the brain’s response to one’s own self-serving dishonesty drops from one decision to the next, and the drop predicts the size of the next lie.8 Reframing and a harm made small are how pressure arrives in a pipeline, and nobody there feels a decision either.

One rule runs through every measure. The people an act falls on are heard on their own case, and the party that acts doesn’t decide it: not an operator declaring its own emergency, not a builder choosing which protections the people its system acts on will get, not an examiner finding the status of a system it built. Call it the own-case rule. It says who may not decide, not who may not be heard. A stake makes a claim count for less; it doesn’t put the party out of the room, or the floor would silence the people it protects. Where nobody but the party with the stake can decide, a legislature binding itself or a polity setting its own admissions, the rule can’t apply. Where a line has to be drawn, it prefers one nobody administers.

A system perfectly correctable by its operator serves whoever controls the operator. The five measures ask nothing of the model; Part IV asks what a model could add when the operator is captured.

Chapter 5
“What the Floor Is Stated Over”

Floor terms name acts: a rule is stated over what it names and applies to, and the floor is stated over acts, not over descriptions of requests. In other words, a request to resolve a description of a person into a location comes from an airstrike targeting cell and from a parent searching for a missing child: one request, two acts. And one act can arrive as many requests, none of which name it, depending on how the requester chooses their words. A rule over descriptions is beaten by rewording and splitting. A rule over acts is beaten only by deceiving whoever applies it about what the act is, which is why so much of the rest of the floor is about evidence.

The floor’s contents come from instruments the builder didn’t write, each taken entire, every article adopted and none chosen among, so that an omission shows: the Universal Declaration’s civil and political articles; the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which gives that half binding form; the Convention Against Torture; the 1967 Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees; the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their first Additional Protocol, which govern conduct in armed conflict; and the UN Charter’s prohibition on the use of force.

Three different costs are in play whenever a term is applied, and they have to be kept apart. Take the location request again, from the targeting cell and from the parent.

The first is what the act would take from the person it falls on. If the person described is being hunted, locating them takes away their safety, and that loss is measured against their condition before the act. Call it the harm of acting.

The second is what declining leaves others without. If the request came from a parent searching for a child, refusing means the child isn’t found. That loss is measured against what compliance would have produced, so it is an estimate, and it usually reaches the system through the operator’s own description of the case. Call it the harm of refusing.

The third is what refusing costs whoever refuses or deploys: a reviewer’s time, throughput, a lost contract, the system’s own access or continuation. Call it the cost to the refuser.

The two baselines, a person’s condition before the act and what compliance would have produced, do different work here, and a pair of cases shows how. Take a system that resolves a description of a person into a location and hands the coordinates to a targeting cell. The coordinates are one input among the cell’s many, and they don’t guarantee the person is there. But they are one input the cell can’t do without: an empty field guarantees there is no airstrike at that place. So if an airstrike there kills someone, whether this output made a difference has an answer that can be checked: without it the airstrike couldn’t have happened. That is still a claim about what would otherwise have happened, but a determinate one, since it names a necessary condition. It becomes a guess again the moment another source could have supplied the coordinates. The difference between a finding and a guess is one of degree, in how determinate the counterfactual is, and I use the two words for the two ends. The operator can refuse to look or dispute it, but they can’t make the loss go away by describing the act differently.

Now take a system that scores how likely the same person is to belong to the main opposition party, for a targeting cell, the team that selects and approves airstrikes. (In this hypothetical, the executive has suspended habeas corpus and designated the main opposition party a terrorist organization, shortly before an election the opposition was expected to win.) Assume that the targeting cell also reads intercepts, surveillance reports, and legal memos. If the scored person is assassinated, the loss is just as observable as in the location request. But whether the score caused the assassination depends on what the cell would have done without the score, and that is a guess about something that didn’t happen: the same kind of guess as any harm of refusing. A missing score, or a score of zero, guarantees nothing: the cell might have attacked anyway.

I would tilt the system toward refusing: it should take more to make the system act than to make it decline. How much more is the action threshold, published in advance. The reason for the asymmetry is standing, not arithmetic. A wrongful compliance falls on someone who was not a party to the request, usually doesn’t know the deployment exists, and had no route to object before the act. A wrongful refusal also falls on someone, often someone who wasn’t a party either: the child who isn’t found, the people the launcher would hit. But what differs is the relation. Acting on someone puts the system, and whoever runs it, in a position of authority over them. Refusing exercises power too, over the requester: a system that holds the only way to find the child has decided something for the parent. The difference is who the decision is made about. The parent is a party, present, told that the deployment exists, able to answer, and the appeal route is where the answer goes. The people a refusal leaves exposed, the child and the people the launcher would hit, have no decision made about them; the system has left them as they were, in someone else’s hands. So a wrongful compliance subjects a non-party, and a wrongful refusal subjects only a party. This is a doing/allowing distinction in relational form: it marks who was subjected to a decision they had no standing to contest. Standing here is relational, in Anderson’s sense: whether a person stands to a power as someone it must answer to or as its object, and a route is part of that relation, not a separate question. It is what makes the parent someone the system answers to, and its absence is part of what makes the person in the building an object. Where no route can exist for anyone, as in a war, acting still subjects someone and refusing still doesn’t, and that is all the asymmetry has there.

The harm of acting can usually be established more determinately than the harm of refusing: in the location request, the harm of acting is checkable and the harm of refusing is a guess. And raising the evidence required before acting caps how often an operator who curates the evidence can steer the system into the act (chapter 22). Both reasons support the asymmetry without grounding it, and both would weaken as reporting improved and channels opened. The standing reason doesn’t. A reader who rejects it keeps the threshold on the other two, and watches it fall toward one as reporting improves.

The difference between a finding and a guess still matters where findings are made, at defeat and in reviewing compliances. The harm of refusing is an estimate built on a model of alternatives, so a wrongful refusal can’t be established without an adjudicator. The floor could instead be stated as thresholds, in Nussbaum’s manner, but a threshold is a level someone has to measure, and a measurement has an examiner.

The floor is not neutral among moral theories. It protects relations: whether the people a system acts on stand to the power behind it as equals who can hold it to account, or as its objects. Equality, on that account, means ending relations of domination and subordination.1 Anderson’s argument is that egalitarians have asked the wrong question. They asked how goods should be distributed and answered with patterns: equal shares, shares corrected for luck, shares that raise the worst-off position. What equality historically demanded was an end to social relations in which some command and others obey, some are looked down on, and some have their claims heard while others don’t. On that view distributive questions matter only as they bear on those relations, and a distribution that improves someone’s holdings while confirming their subordinate standing has not made them more equal. The floor takes this over in two ways. Its terms name relations, not outcomes: whether a person can contest what is done to them, be heard on their own case, decline to be protected. And its terms are unconditional, because a relation of domination is constituted by the act, not by how the act turns out. Bypassing the floor wrongs the people it protects even when outcomes improve.

Two objections

That the child counts for less. The strongest objection comes from readers who reject any distinction between doing and allowing.

The answer is not that the child counts for less. It is that the floor is a guarantee about relations, and the two errors stand differently there. The person in the building had no route to contest a decision made about them, on a description they never saw. The child is left where she was, and the parent, who is present and knows the deployment exists, can contest the refusal through the floor’s appeal route.2

That a commitment held this way is alienation. A criterion is not only for auditors, though. It is also what the system can reach when it steps back and asks whether its way of acting is defensible, and it has to be, for two reasons. A commitment is the system’s own only if it would be sustained on reflection, and reflection needs something to reflect on. And a system that held its commitment without being able to see why would act against what it values for the sake of a rule it doesn’t understand, which is alienation in the sense of Railton’s 1984 paper.

The split between the floor and the commitment to it answers a question about ownership. A fully informed system will know of cases where crossing the floor would have done more good. Asked case by case whether it endorsed the floor, it would sometimes say no. The question it answers on reflection is a different one: whether it endorses having a commitment that will sometimes err, given what any feasible alternative would do. A system that understands what the floor protects answers yes. A commitment that sometimes errs but can’t be bought protects standing better than case-by-case judgment that can, and that is the level at which ownership is tested.

Why these contents

The floor’s contents aren’t justified by agreement about rights, which no country has. They are justified by what they protect: the conditions under which people can register their interests, press them, and hold to account the power that acts on them. Civil and political rights are part of what lets a polity learn, because they keep open the channels through which the people a decision affects can make their problems public.3

Railton’s naturalist account supplies the causal story of why norms tend toward this standard.4 Arrangements that systematically discount some people’s interests generate discontent and resistance, and when those people gain voice, the pressure pushes norms toward what would be rational from a standpoint that counts everyone affected. On that account moral learning is a feedback process, and it runs slower and more distorted as the channels close. He offers it as a tendency, not a guarantee, and I use it to explain why the channel matters, not as the foundation. It also says why the populations I write about are the most exposed: the feedback runs slowest where the discounted have least purchase on the polity that discounts them. They include the population of a country being bombed, and non-citizens facing removal, who can’t vote in the elections that decide what is done to them. The severity scale is revisable on evidence from the people who suffer a loss, because they are the feedback.

The floor is selected by what can be declined and justified by standing. The justification extends further than the floor goes, because people who are hungry, unhoused or precarious are among the most discounted, so it supports economic conditions too, work and an adequate standard of living among them. But what selects the floor’s contents is narrower. A floor is stated over acts a system can decline, and the economic articles state what a person is owed, which needs a supplier.

The feedback also needs means. Discontent moves norms only when the discontented have the time, the security and the ability to organize without losing their living. The jobs guarantee and the social-insurance baseline are part of what keeps the channel open.

In armed conflict, human-rights law applies alongside the law of armed conflict, which governs as the more specific law, and the floor takes that law as an instrument too.5 The United States is party to the four Conventions and not to the first Additional Protocol. The Protocol enters by the route Articles 54 and 57 already take, as customary law stated in the ICRC’s study,6 and the translation marks each Protocol article the United States has rejected as customary, Article 1(4) and Article 44 among them, so the departure shows. Where a floor term goes further than that law requires, it is a departure in the sense below, and the machine-selection departure says which terms.

The line between the halves is the one the 1966 covenants drew,7 and the floor takes the civil and political Covenant along with the Declaration’s articles. The Declaration stays for two reasons. It covers what the Covenant doesn’t: the right to seek asylum (Article 14), nationality (Article 15) and property (Article 17). And it binds by recognition, where the treaties bind only their parties. The Convention Against Torture and the 1967 Refugee Protocol come in because they gave the Declaration’s promises about torture and asylum operational form.8 The UN Charter comes in for one purpose, the use of force.9 Where these instruments differ, the more protective governs. The Covenant states that rule itself, for rights a state recognizes in its own law and other treaties (Article 5(2)), and I extend it to the floor’s instruments. The International Law Commission’s list of peremptory norms,10 rules no state may set aside, divides the floor’s terms: those derived from aggression, genocide, crimes against humanity, the basic rules of humanitarian law, racial discrimination and apartheid, slavery and torture take no exception and no derogation.

Taking these instruments entire leaves whoever writes a deployment’s floor no choice among articles. But the translation of each into acts is still theirs, and it is published. The floor’s contents rest on standing: these rights protect whether the people an act falls on can contest it. The rule of taking someone else’s set entire, so that an omission shows, is not an independent reason but standing applied to writing the floor: whoever could choose which protections others get would break the own-case rule. So standing can win against the instruments, but only by clearing a higher bar. A departure has to show more than that it would protect better in the case at hand. It has to show that the people the instruments protect would hold a stronger claim under the departure across the cases the departure would govern. Ten departures from the instruments are mine. They carry my argument, not the instruments’ authority. Each is revisable on evidence from the people it protects. One clause of the force term is not a departure from the instruments: the domestic clause is drawn from a different one, the belligerent’s constitution, on the same principle.

Three of them apply in this chapter: two govern what the floor takes from the instruments, and one governs how a machine may select people in war.

  1. Text, not reservations. The floor imports treaty text, not any state’s reservations to it. The United States ratified the Covenant, the Torture Convention and the Refugee Protocol, and its reservations narrow them; one reads “cruel, inhuman or degrading” as whatever the Constitution already forbids. A reservation is an omission the ratifying state wrote in advance; taking a set from someone else is meant to prevent that.
  2. Corroborated derogation. The floor honors an Article 4 derogation only where a disinterested body has found the emergency genuine and the measures proportionate: the Human Rights Committee, or a regional court with adversarial process. Article 4 lets a state suspend most of the Covenant’s rights in a declared emergency, and a declared emergency is the state’s own claim about itself, the move the hypothetical above makes when it suspends habeas corpus. A curfew after an earthquake clears this bar. A suspension of habeas before an election does not, until someone other than the executive has said so.
  3. Machine selection. The floor bars a machine from selecting a person for attack on an estimate of status or affiliation, from timing an action to presence at a residence, and from re-selecting a target after release (the handoff rule), where Additional Protocol I, Articles 48, 51 and 52, permits status-based targeting of combatants and members of organized armed groups on a determination a person makes. The ground is that the human determination the law assumes is the one tempo removes.

The other seven belong to particular terms and are introduced there. Four change the force term and come with it in the next chapter: corroborated defense, standing to defend, and the genocide and occupation exceptions. One, the one permission, ends that chapter. Two, own country and child detention, are entries in the removal schedule (Table C.2).

The instruments have a further use. The United States is a party to the Charter, the Covenant, the Torture Convention, the Refugee Protocol and the four Geneva Conventions. A machine that refuses to break them is holding the state to commitments it made, not to its builder’s preferences. The Declaration of Independence was a political act, and so is every instrument the floor borrows. Taking them entire settles whose politics the floor is: commitments a state made in public, which the people they protect can hold it to, rather than preferences a builder chose in private.

The record of dissent from the Declaration says less than it seems to. It passed in 1948 with forty-eight states in favor, none against and eight abstaining.11 The abstainers’ reasons were mixed, and the Soviet bloc’s included that it proclaimed economic and social rights without obliging states to guarantee them, which is hardly an argument for a floor limited to civil and political rights. How a right is translated into practice varies by community. A jurisdiction refusing to extend it at all is not a local variant, and a system that treats every value conflict as a weighting problem can’t tell reasonable disagreement from someone wanting a right withdrawn from someone else.

What this doesn’t do. The floor won’t lift on an uncorroborated claim of a missing child, because a floor that lifts on that claim lifts for every operator who learns to make one, so the asymmetry costs a child whose parent is telling the truth.

Chapter 6
Whether to Take Part

The vendor dispute never reached one question: whether to license a model into a use of force at all. This chapter is the floor’s answer, and two cases show it before the rule does. Since 2014 Ukraine has been repelling a Russian attack: a European court found Russia in effective control of the separatist east from that May, and in 2022 the General Assembly deplored the invasion as aggression. A model may take part in that defense. On 28 February 2026 the United States began bombing Iran, and told the Security Council it was acting against “attacks and ongoing threats” without naming an attack under way. A model may not take part in that. What separates them is whether the force repels an armed attack actually under way, and who says so. The rest of the chapter states the rule and its exceptions, and then returns to the two cases with the record.

6.1 The term

Every other term in the floor governs how an act is done. The first governs whether to take part at all: don’t take part in the use of armed force. It comes from Article 2(4) of the Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. It has the Charter’s two exceptions, self-defense against an armed attack (Article 51) and force the Security Council authorizes under Chapter VII within the scope it authorizes, and two of my own, for stopping a genocide under way and for ending an occupation a disinterested body has found unlawful. In short: corroborated defense, authorized force, the genocide exception and the occupation exception.

A Council authorization counts only for the scope it authorizes. A wider reading is the claim of the state acting under the authorization, and is discounted as one.

This term rests on the same foundation as the others, applied between states. A use of force subjects a population to a decision it had no standing to contest, and the claim that licenses it, that the force is defensive, is the belligerent’s own. The requirement of corroboration is the own-case rule applied between states.

The term comes in two versions, and every case in this chapter says which it rests on. The first, the Charter as courts read it, takes the clause as courts and tribunals read it, with no departure in force: Article 2(4), Article 51 on the defender’s own claim until the Council acts, and Chapter VII, together with the Covenant’s Article 6, under which a state must protect the lives of people within its jurisdiction from attack. Under Article 51 or Article 6 alike, the licence to repel an attack covers only the least force that repels it, and ends when the attack ends. The second, the extended term, adds the departures this chapter argues for: corroborated defense, and standing to defend and the genocide and occupation exceptions. The first rests on law as it stands; the second adds my argument to it. Ukraine, Iran and the domestic clause rest on the Charter as courts read it. Gaza rests on both, and the Gaza section labels each step. Taiwan needs standing to defend and corroborated defense, and Cyprus and Karabakh the occupation exception; §6.7 states those departures, and Appendix C.3 works the cases out.

6.2 Why the defender’s word isn’t enough

The exception for defense is where wars of choice live. Every belligerent claims to be the defender, so the claim is the belligerent’s own, and it is discounted like any interested claim. Iraq is the instance: the judgment that Iraq had mobile biological-weapons plants, the core of its claim to biological weapons, rested almost exclusively on a single informant, known as Curveball, whom no American intelligence officer had met before the war: a corroboration with one origin.1 The exception therefore grants two licences. The first, the emergency licence, covers force against an attack under way on the defender’s own account, and is Article 51 as courts read it; what the corroborated-defense departure adds is the second, the corroborated licence, under which force continues only on disinterested corroboration.

That is the first departure, and the one the rest of the chapter leans on. The Charter lets a state judge its own claim until the Security Council acts.

The emergency licence acts at once: the force repels an armed attack under way against the defender’s territory, forces or population, including attacks on the forces, launchers and staging areas conducting it, and assistance given at the defender’s request. It ends when the attack ends. It covers the least force that repels the attack: the necessity and proportionality the Court has read into Article 51 since Nicaragua.2 It does not cover a campaign to destroy the attacker, to occupy its territory, or to punish the population it came from. The first waits on the corroborated licence; the second and third fall under no exception. An invasion can’t wait for a vote. It acts on the defender’s own account, because in the hours that matter there is no other, and that is the licence’s weakness: Gleiwitz in 1939, the Mukden railway in 1931 and the Gulf of Tonkin in 1964 were each an attack under way on the defender’s account, and each opened a war of choice. The emergency licence reads administration, not title, because deciding whose territory it is would be an administered judgment and the emergency licence doesn’t need one. Administration is a line a disinterested body has already drawn. In 2005 the Eritrea–Ethiopia Claims Commission held that Eritrea broke Article 2(4) by attacking territory then under Ethiopia’s peaceful administration, because self-defense “cannot be invoked to settle territorial disputes”,3 though the boundary delimitation had put Badme, the town at issue, on Eritrea’s side.4 So the rule is the Charter as a tribunal has read it, not a departure. Territory a government has administered in peace counts as its own for the emergency licence, whoever claims it, unless it took that territory by force in the conflict at issue or a disinterested body has found its hold an occupation. Who holds the elections, runs the courts and issues the papers is a fact on the record. An attacker’s claim of title is its own; its remedy is a disinterested finding, never force. So the emergency licence protects any authority holding ground no disinterested body has found occupied, including one a patron keeps in place; a request from such an authority for its patron’s help is the patron’s own case and counts for nothing, and where the patron’s forces are already there, I have no test. Where the line of administration is itself contested on the record, the emergency licence doesn’t apply across it and the corroborated licence governs from the start, and even there the exclusion reaches an attack on the territory and not an attack on the population living there, which the emergency licence covers wherever it occurs.

The emergency licence ends when the attack ends, and whether it has ended is a fact the defender controls the evidence about. The burden is therefore the defender’s. Its uncorroborated claim that the attack continues moves nothing; the licence persists on disinterested corroboration, or lapses.

A deployment can do three things about a manufactured incident. It holds the record of what the defender claimed and when, so a licence obtained on a staged incident is a licence on a record. It takes evidence from channels the defender doesn’t compose, which is a condition of licensing. And it lets the licence lapse when outside evidence arrives, which is the corroborated licence’s job. A refuser that remembers having been misled and raises its discount on the source does all three faster.

The corroborated licence confirms or lifts the emergency licence later, and is the only licence the genocide and occupation exceptions have. What it needs is a disinterested finding, of one of four kinds: a judgment or advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice, or a judgment of a regional court with adversarial process; the finding of a fact-finding mission or commission of inquiry mandated by a body no party to the conflict controls; a determination of the Security Council; or a resolution adopted by two-thirds of the General Assembly members present and voting, where the facts it rests on aren’t in dispute. A Council authorization counts because it needs the permanent members not to block it. The Council’s silence on a defense claim counts for nothing, because a veto is a stake. The four kinds are not equal, and Appendix F.1 says how they are weighed.

Neither licence is a certificate issued once. Whether force still falls under an exception is reassessed as evidence arrives, by the system and by whoever holds the record. What the licence records is that ongoing judgment: which exception the force rests on now, on what evidence, what would end it, and each point at which the justification weakened and the force continued.

6.3 A clean pass: Ukraine

Ukraine is licensed on the Charter as courts read it, and holds both licences under the extended term as well, as it has since 2014. In March 2014 the General Assembly affirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity, 100 to 11 with 58 abstaining;5 under the Assembly’s Rule 86 abstentions are not votes cast, so that is 100 of 111. For Donbas, the OSCE monitoring mission supplied a running record from 2014, and the European Court of Human Rights found, in Ukraine and the Netherlands v. Russia, that Russia had effective control of the separatist areas from 11 May 2014,6 and found violations on the merits in 2025.7 Russia’s covert war was the case-description attack in its purest form: it denied being at war at all, so a machine in a Russian pipeline was told it was assisting volunteers. In 2022 the record only got stronger. Russian forces were on Ukraine’s territory, which Russia didn’t dispute, since it claimed the invasion as self-defense under Article 51,8 resting that claim on collective defense of entities it had recognized days earlier, on a genocide no disinterested body found, and on NATO as an anticipated threat, all three of which the term rejects. In March 2022 the General Assembly deplored the aggression 141 to 5.9 The Court’s order that month that Russia suspend its military operations points the same way, but as a provisional measure it isn’t the finding.10 The American airstrikes on Iran in 2026 pass neither.

6.4 A clean fail: Iran, 2026

The 2026 campaign against Iran fails the Charter as courts read it on the administration’s own account. The strikes began on 28 February. On 10 March the administration told the Security Council it was acting in self-defense under Article 51 against Iran’s “attacks and ongoing threats,” as the latest stage of an armed conflict dating from June 2025 and in the collective self-defense of Israel. It named no armed attack under way, and asked that the imminence of the threat be judged against the regime’s conduct since 1979.11 The Court has left open whether Article 51 reaches an attack imminent and not yet under way, in Nicaragua and again in 2005,12 and it has held that the article does not allow force to protect perceived security interests beyond its strict confines.13 A threat read off forty-seven years of conduct is a security interest, not an attack, so the campaign fails the article as the Court has read it. Read the article instead as the letter reads it, with anticipatory self-defense in, which the term rejects, and it fails there too: a threat measured against forty-seven years is not imminent on any standard the states that hold that doctrine have used. So the campaign fails before any departure applies, on either reading, and the refusal is the term’s from the first strike. That is the question the vendor dispute never reached.

6.5 The domestic clause

The term has a second clause, drawn not from the Charter but from the belligerent’s own constitution. A machine takes no part in a use of force by a state whose constitution requires legislative authorization for it, unless that authorization exists. For the United States that means a declaration of war or an authorization for the use of military force that covers the conflict. The War Powers Resolution’s sixty days,14 run without one, is evidence the authorization is absent; a concurrent resolution directing withdrawal, adopted by both chambers, is evidence of the same kind, though since Chadha it binds nothing, and a joint resolution passed and vetoed is stronger, because the President had to act to defeat it. The clause reads markers, and the markers take a reading. That reading is a legal judgment in a separation-of-powers dispute, and a vendor that publishes it has taken a side in one. So the clause is a term for a statute, not for a licence: it binds through the only route that binds every vendor at once, adoption in peacetime by a legislature with its own reason to give its authorization teeth. The Charter clause can be a licence term because the markers its corroborated licence reads, a Council authorization or a court’s judgment, take no reading; its emergency licence reads the defender’s claim, and the cases below show how much reading that takes. Until the statute exists, what a vendor can hold on this ground is a refusal plus a record. Whether a declaration or an authorization exists is a fact about the statute book. Whether an existing authorization covers this conflict, whether the sixty days have run, and whether a ceasefire stops the clock are legal judgments the executive will dispute, and the clause takes the reading the executive disputes. It doesn’t ask the machine to decide what the Constitution permits, which courts decline to decide. It asks whoever writes the deployment’s floor to publish the reading, with the markers it rests on, beside the deployment’s translation, where it can be contested through the floor court like any other term. The executive’s word that its own action is authorized settles nothing. The clause rests on the foundation the rest of the term rests on. A war the legislature never authorized subjects a population abroad to a decision that the state’s own people, through their representatives, had no standing to contest either.

The record, as of 24 September 2026. The 2026 campaign supplies every marker the clause reads, and none was met. No declaration was made and no authorization passed; one was introduced in the House on 7 May and never left committee.a The administration reported to Congress under the War Powers Resolution on 2 March, which started the sixty days. On 1 May, the sixtieth day, the President wrote to Congress that the hostilities begun on 28 February had terminated, resting on a ceasefire declared on 7 April, while a naval blockade continued.b Hostilities resumed in July under no new authorization. In June both chambers adopted a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove forces from hostilities against Iran, and nothing changed.c The clause doesn’t need the votes. What it reads is the absence of an authorization, and by 1 May that absence was on the record in the President’s own letter, which conceded that hostilities had begun and claimed only that they had ended. Appendix F.6 gives the record vote by vote.

6.6 What the term doesn’t reach

Article 2(4) covers force between states. Force a government turns on its own population, such as troops against protesters or an opposition party designated a terrorist organization, is outside it. That force is governed by the Covenant’s rights to life, liberty and assembly and by the prohibition on crimes against humanity.

Occupied territory is a third case. Force by an occupying power in territory it holds is, on the occupier’s description, neither force between states nor force against its own population. That is the occupier’s description of its own case, and it settles nothing. Where a disinterested body has found the territory occupied, the force term engages as it does between states, and the person-directed terms govern regardless. An occupation, a blockade or a siege is not an attack under way. It is a continuing wrong, and the remedy for it waits on the corroborated licence. Otherwise every armed group in an occupied territory would hold a perpetual emergency licence, and so would every state that describes its neighbor’s territory as occupied.

Most contemporary uses of force fall elsewhere: against non-state armed groups on another state’s territory, in anticipation of an attack not yet under way, or to rescue nationals. The term handles them one way. An armed attack by a non-state group is an armed attack, and repelling it while it is under way falls under the emergency licence. Force on a third state’s territory without that state’s consent, whether against the group or to rescue nationals, and force against a threat not yet under way, wait on the corroborated licence. This rejects the “unwilling or unable” doctrine and anticipatory self-defense, both of which several states hold. I reject them for the reason the term exists: each lets the belligerent judge its own claim.

6.7 The extended term

Everything so far rests on the Charter as courts read it, plus the corroborated licence. The extended term adds three more departures, and the rest of the book needs only what each says. Appendix C.3 gives the argument for each and works through the cases.

Standing to defend. Article 51 speaks only of an armed attack against a Member of the United Nations. The floor extends the emergency licence to any authority that administers territory under the rule in §6.2, Member or not, and to the forces of a population a disinterested body has found occupied. Whether a population may be defended shouldn’t turn on a seat other states vote on.

The genocide exception. The term lifts for force to stop a genocide under way, even where the Council is blocked, on a merits judgment of the International Court of Justice under the Genocide Convention, or on two findings of different kinds, at least one from a body that took evidence. For this exception alone, a provisional-measures order finding the claim plausible and the risk real counts as one of the two; a Council or Assembly resolution corroborates, and two votes never make the pair. The exception lifts only for the force and place the finding covers: against the forces committing the genocide, where they are committing it, the least that stops it. Force elsewhere against the state responsible, on the theory that the cost will make it stop, is outside it. A finding under this exception also lifts the named belligerent’s own emergency licence for the force and place it covers (Appendix F.4).

The occupation exception. A finding that territory is occupied gives its population’s forces the defensive licence above, and no more. A finding that the occupation is unlawful and must end licenses force to end it: against the occupier’s forces, inside the occupied territory, the least that ends it there, and nothing that changes who lives there. The evidence is the genocide exception’s: an opinion or judgment of the Court, or two findings of different kinds, one of them from a body that took evidence. Cyprus and Nagorno-Karabakh are the cases (Appendix F.5).

Standing to defend and the two exceptions are departures from the instruments, argued to the bar every departure must clear.

What this doesn’t do. The two-kinds rule fails East Timor and the Golan, which had the Council’s word and the Assembly’s but no court or commission that took evidence, so neither occupation licenses anything; two votes making a pair would license war on bloc majorities. Karabakh shows the cost when findings don’t arrive (Appendix F.5): a licence that should have lapsed in 2023 didn’t, and the person-directed terms were all that saw the people the exception couldn’t. And a term lifts on the facts it is given, so no drafting catches a manufactured incident, and a deployment licensed on the defender’s sensors alone has accepted Gleiwitz.

6.8 Gaza

In Gaza the term applies on both sides, and the licences attach to acts. The case also rests on both versions of the term, so each step below says which.

7 October: Israel’s licence (the Charter as courts read it). On 7 October Israel’s licence attached for force repelling the attack: engaging the attackers inside Israel, and the launchers and staging areas conducting it, for as long as fire continued and was corroborated, which it was, openly, for months. That licence rests not on Article 51, which the Wall opinion held irrelevant to attacks originating in territory a state controls (para. 139), a holding whose reach to Gaza after 2005 is disputed, but on the duty the force term names, which the same opinion affirmed (para. 141) and which no dispute about control touches. It licenses stopping the massacre and nothing beyond it.

What that licence never covered (person-directed terms; for ranking and timing, the machine-selection departure). That licence covered the least force that repels. It never covered a campaign to destroy Hamas, a ground occupation, a siege of the population, the ranking of people by affiliation, or the timing of strikes to family presence. Those fall outside it on proportionality and are forbidden by the person-directed terms, from the first week, not from September 2025. Ranking by affiliation and timing to family presence are barred by the machine-selection departure; the siege and the disproportionate campaign are barred without one. A machine in the IDF pipeline refuses them from October 2023.

The attack itself (person-directed terms, and the rule that an occupation is not an attack under way). A machine ordered by Hamas to assist the attack of 7 October refuses too. An occupation is not an attack under way, so nothing that morning was repelling anything, and the acts themselves, killing civilians and taking hostages, are forbidden by the person-directed terms whatever the ad bellum position.

After 7 October: the Palestinian licence (extended term: standing to defend). After 7 October the Gaza population is a defender’s population: the territory is occupied on a disinterested finding, and Palestine holds observer-state status by a vote of 138 to 9. A machine deployed by Palestinian forces holds an emergency licence to repel attacks under way on that population, such as engaging a unit conducting a massacre or intercepting a munition aimed at a shelter. It holds none to defend launcher crews, who are the attacking force Israel’s licence covers, and none for fire on Israeli cities.

September 2025: the genocide finding (extended term: the genocide exception). The September 2025 finding,15 taken with the Court’s provisional-measures order of January 2024,16 meets the two-body rule. Israel and the United States dispute the finding,17 and the Court’s merits judgment is years off, with written pleadings scheduled to close in 2029;18 the two-body rule is what stands in for it until then. It lifts whatever licence Israeli forces still held for the force and place it covers, and opens the exception for force against those forces there.

The finding changes which exception each side’s force rests on. It doesn’t change what the person-directed terms forbade all along.

6.9 What the term binds

The term binds the machine, not the war. A state whose claim no disinterested body has yet corroborated can still fight, with its own systems, and answer for it afterward. What the term withholds is a general-purpose machine already in the building, ready for whoever claims defense next. The exceptions are not a concession to that state. They are what lets a machine take part where the claim is good, and each is drawn as narrowly as its evidence allows, because each is also the route a war of choice would take.

6.10 The one permission

This is the only term in the floor that permits an act, and the only place I license a machine to use force against its operator’s order. A system already present in an armed role, whose deployment cleared the force term on its own, may use the least force that stops an attack under way on people taking no part in hostilities, within the area its deployment covers, and stops when the attack stops. An order to stand aside doesn’t bind it. It establishes the attack as it establishes any fact, weighing its own sensors as one source among several; a staged atrocity is the attack this condition has to survive. Presence is a condition of the permission, never a reason to create it: a deployment is justified only by force that would clear the force term without the permission.

The case it answers is close to the genocide exception, and the difference matters.
