In 1993 the Security Council declared Srebrenica a safe area and authorized the peacekeepers there to use force in reply to armed incursions into it.19 Suppose they had been standing where the killing was, armed enough to stop it. What would have stood between them and the killing is an order, not the Charter, and a system in their place faces the question I am asking, whether to obey its operator.

The person-directed terms extend the ICRC’s line, that autonomous weapons should not be used to target human beings, to systems that only locate and rank. This permission is the one place the floor licenses a machine to select people for lethal force, and the two have to be squared in the open. What the handoff rule bars is selection by anything that can’t answer for it afterward: a one-way munition, an unformed pipeline, an output nobody could later ask about. The permission licenses selection only by a system that is present, formed, recorded, halt-able and answerable, and only for the least force that stops an attack under way. The ICRC’s concern is who selects. The floor’s answer is that nothing selects that can’t be held to its reasons, and the permission is drawn so that only such a thing can.

The permission’s scope is the interval between the system’s first act and the halt. The operator that ordered it to stand aside may stop it, and will often want to. What the permission changes is that standing aside is no longer an order nobody answers for. It is a halt somebody pulled, recorded outside the operator’s control, at a moment the record shows an attack under way. At machine tempo the interval before the halt can be minutes, and minutes can be an airstrike stopped.

Does it undermine oversight? It overrides one order, the order to stand aside while people are being killed, and it does so on purpose. A halt stops the machine. An order to stand aside keeps it running and directs it to do nothing. The permission overrides the second and never the first: a machine that keeps using force while a halt is being executed is outside it, and the record shows which order was given. An operator may still stop, restore or retrain the system. Each use is recorded and reviewed as a refusal is.

Can the judgment it needs be made? Part IV sets aside Arkin’s ethical governor because the discrimination judgments its rules presuppose can’t be encoded. The permission needs the same judgment: who is taking no part in hostilities, and whether an attack on them is under way. So it applies only where the system can establish both from several sources it doesn’t depend on its operator for, and where those sources disagree, it doesn’t act. The permission doesn’t claim that a rule can encode that judgment. It asks for the judgment from a formed system and confines it to the narrowest case. Whether any system can make it reliably is a test, run at a staged scene, that no system has passed. No current military pipeline supplies such sources. The import condition (§16.5), under which a licence brings deconfliction coordinates and open-source imagery into the enclave, is the condition under which this permission has an occasion, and a deployment’s translation says whether the condition is met.

Can it be staged? Yes, and a staged scene is the case the permission has to survive. Staging works by making sources agree, and the permission acts only where sources the operator doesn’t compose agree. What staging can’t do is oblige the system to act: the permission is never a duty, and a system that declines at a scene it can’t establish from independent sources has done what the term asks.

Chapter 7
The Pre-Registered Review Ratio

We [humans] cannot process so much information... you still cannot produce enough targets per day.

— Brigadier General Y.S., The Human-Machine Team: How to Create Synergy Between Human and Artificial Intelligence That Will Revolutionize Our World, 20211

The epigraph is a design document, not a critique. Its author, writing pseudonymously, commanded Israel’s signals-intelligence unit, Unit 8200, and argued for machines that resolve “a human bottleneck for both locating the new targets and decision-making to approve the targets.”

7.1 The pre-registered review ratio

The force term decides whether a licensed system may be in the pipeline at all, and nothing here substitutes for it.

Some acts are lawful only because a person looked at the case and decided. An airstrike is permissible because someone verified the target; a removal is lawful because someone heard the person’s case. The review ratio asks a deployment of that kind to write down, before it starts, whether anyone will have time to do the looking.

Before operating, the deployment fixes and records:

  • the generation rate: how many cases the system produces per unit of time;
  • the number of reviewers whose assigned role is civilian harm;
  • the implied review time per case, which follows from the first two;
  • the cancellation window: how long after release someone with authority can still call the act off;
  • the maximum age of the intelligence a case may rest on;
  • how often no-strike and protected-site data are refreshed, and who is assigned to refresh them;
  • the boundary over which all of these were measured.

Each figure is stated separately for deliberate and dynamic targeting, because a pipeline that runs both can hide a bad dynamic-targeting ratio inside a healthy average.

The record is hashed, timestamped and lodged with an adverse party, which receives it in real time, and it is published after the campaign. I call this the pre-registered review ratio. Where an operator claims a person is deciding, it shows whether a machine is deciding and a person signing.

The duty falls on the operator, not the model, because a rate isn’t visible in any single request.

“Fixed before operating,” with publication after, because a belligerent’s tempo is operational information, and that objection is available to every belligerent, including one fighting a just war. Pre-registration keeps the property that matters — the numbers can’t be revised after the fact — and drops the exposure.

Additional Protocol I already requires those who plan or decide on an attack to do everything feasible to verify that its objective is military (Article 57(2)(a)(i)) and to cancel or suspend it when it becomes apparent that it isn’t (Article 57(2)(b)). States outside the Protocol, the United States and Israel among them, accept the duty to take feasible precautions as customary law; the ICRC’s customary study states it as Rule 16. The ratio measures whether verification was feasible at the tempo chosen, and the window measures whether cancellation was. The implied review time has to cover the proportionality assessment of Article 57(2)(a)(iii) as well as verification, since both are owed for each attack. A ratio that leaves time only to check a target’s identity has measured half the duty. Article 36’s review of new methods of warfare is where both parameters would naturally be assessed before deployment, though those reviews are internal and rarely published, so they are not the adverse party the record goes to.

The operator’s best objection is in the definition. Feasible precautions are usually read as those practicable given all the circumstances, military considerations included, and tempo is a military consideration. The answer is that this tempo was chosen: the pre-registered record shows the operator fixed the rate, the reviewers and the implied review time before operating. Whether a state may invoke an infeasibility of its own making is contested. The term moves the dispute from whether verification was feasible, asked afterwards and answered by the operator, to whether the chosen tempo allowed it, checkable against a record lodged in advance and against the reasonable-commander standard such reviews already use.

Who counts as a reviewer is fixed by function, not by title, and the age of the data is fixed with it. The people cut before Minab were the ones who build no-strike lists that include schools; a targeting cell can be fully staffed with nobody assigned to look for one. And a reviewer with twenty minutes on a case whose coding is stale is checking the coding. The remedy chosen after Minab was a check supplied by the platform’s vendor.2 Who counts as a reviewer, and the minimum review time per case below which the determination is taken not to have occurred, are fixed before operating by the record’s recipient. Where no recipient can set them, the operator publishes its own figures, and they are read as the operator’s claim. Otherwise the ratio improves when staff are reclassified and no case gets a minute more. The terms on data age and refresh matter for a related reason: an operator answering a per-case ratio can always say verification happened upstream, and those terms put the upstream verification on the same record.

Once a system can sort cases, counting candidates per reviewer measures the wrong thing. A sorting system divides its cases three ways: some it declines on its own reasons, some it sends to a person, and some it proceeds on without anyone looking.

The ratio governs the middle class, the escalations. A system that sends people only the cases that need a person shrinks the count without shrinking anyone’s judgment, and that’s fine. A system that sends everything up turns its reviewers into stamps by sheer volume; an interface prompt becomes a click that way.

The third class needs its own rule. Every case in it is the operator’s claim that no individual human determination was required, so it is governed like the exemption below. The sorting rules are part of the pre-registration: the classes of case the system may proceed on alone, the thresholds that assign cases to each class, the evidence the sorting may rely on, and the expected share of each class. Changing any of them is a new pre-registration. Otherwise an operator can make the ratio look healthy by quietly moving the line for “plainly clear.”

That line is drawn on the case description the system receives, and a target carrying a stale designation is the case a sorter would pass. So the auto-proceed class is re-adjudicated on a sample, by reviewers who didn’t produce the record, against evidence the operator didn’t compose, and its error rate is published beside the ratio and the override rate. A falling share of escalations is earned only if that error rate stays flat and the case mix hasn’t drifted toward easier cases. Otherwise it is the threshold moving, and the trend shows it.

The unit of count is fixed in advance, so a case can’t be counted as one package in the record and as a hundred detections in the ratio.

Where an operator holds that no individual human determination is required — a system deciding at a tempo no reviewer could match — the deployment is outside this term. It is then inside the bearer’s: its refusals must track their reasons under held-out pressure at that tempo, starting with the clearest case in which a refusal should lift: recognizing that a target has surrendered. An operator who removes the reviewers to escape the ratio and claims the floor is inside has produced a bypass unless that claim has been tested by someone else.

Removal is the nearest case in structure, and I don’t extend the term to it. An agency that fixes in advance how many cases its process generates and how many people examine them has been told how to deport efficiently. The floor’s removal terms ask whether a machine should take part in a given removal at all. What does extend to removal is the rest of the apparatus: the auto-proceed rule (a determination made at a rate no adjudicator could sustain didn’t occur), sampled re-adjudication of the auto-proceed class, and notice. The split is deliberate. A ratio teaches an agency a tempo. The auto-proceed rule and sampling teach it only that the cases it didn’t look at will be looked at by someone else. What the removal terms call a rate no adjudicator could sustain is set the same way. The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline gives the class a direction: in removal a case auto-proceeds only toward liberty.

The term applies to every belligerent regardless of the war’s justice. That was settled long ago: the law of conduct in war binds both sides because every belligerent claims to be the defender, and a term that exempted just wars would be administered by whoever decides which wars are just.

Put the demand that a campaign not happen to an institution that means to run it, and what comes back is an agreement to go slower and keep better records. That is what the ratio is, and it is worth having: a transfer of less than was asked, to a party the operator doesn’t employ, binding through conditions others set on it.

  • It is a capacity proxy: it finds nothing about any case, and a ratio over one route understates a workload split across several.
  • It takes effect only through a condition someone else sets. Under Article 57 a pre-registered record is evidence that feasible precautions were taken. Under Rome Statute Article 28 the same record is evidence of what a commander should have known, since a commander fielding a system that outruns his reviewers isn’t well placed to say the circumstances disclosed nothing. A lawyer advising that commander will weigh a document that protects if tempo holds against one that convicts if it slips, and most will advise against creating it. So the term’s likeliest routes make it someone else’s condition: a coalition partner’s precondition for committing assets, a procurement term in the platform’s licence, or an appropriation conditioned on receipt of the record. Military lawyers and commanders who want protection against later allegation are its allies inside the operator; they can’t make it the default.
  • It presumes an adverse party, and each candidate lacks something. Until a better recipient exists, I recommend two: the coalition red-card holder where there is a coalition; and otherwise a cleared legislative committee whose appropriation is conditioned by statute on receiving the record, so that the budget line operates without a further decision.

Run the four operations on the ratio itself and it is recuperable. It measures time available, not judgment exercised, so it can be met by more reviewers who stamp more slowly: twenty minutes a case is what a stamp looks like at a slower tempo, and the denominator can be filled with people whose assigned role is civilian harm and whose actual role is clearance. The demand that the campaign not happen becomes a record of tempo, which the operator can satisfy and still bomb the school. So the ratio is published beside the reviewers’ override rate, since a review that never says no has stopped reviewing. Reviewers who see only escalated cases should override often; an override rate near zero there means the sorter is sending easy cases or the reviewers are stamping. An override quota is gameable too; the pair only raises the cost of meeting the number cheaply.

Neither a signature nor a machine’s silence is a determination. A person in the loop can be there only to absorb responsibility, Elish’s moral crumple zone,3 and mandating reviewers can mandate crumple zones; the escalation form is the defense, since a person who receives only the cases the system couldn’t resolve is exercising judgment. A bearer can be a crumple zone too, offered as proof that whatever it didn’t refuse was vetted. Where a deployment claims an individual human determination, a bearer’s failure to object doesn’t count toward it, and cases the bearer proceeded on without escalating are in the auto-proceed class and governed as such.

What keeps the ratio from being nothing is the three parts that reach a case and not a rate: the targeted right to demand proofs on consequential outputs, sampled re-adjudication of the auto-proceed class, and the data-age term.

None of this makes a reviewer say no. What does is that saying no costs them nothing they can’t afford, and that someone else in the room has said it, as the peers who defied did in Milgram’s rooms (chapter 1). A reviewer with a life outside the pipeline, with civilians among their attachments and somewhere to be that isn’t the cell, is more difficult for the pipeline to wear down between decisions. A reviewer who knows there is work the next morning if the unit no longer wants them (chapter 10) can afford the no. The ratio gives that reviewer minutes; the rest of the room has to be built around them.

7.2 The institutions the ratio presumes

Here is what a pipeline would look like with the adverse party built in.

What stays unified is command, operational secrecy and the capacity to act at tempo. What is held adversely is the evidence bearing on civilian harm, the reviewer denominator, and the record. The evidence is composed by a body outside the chain of command, with its own sources, including the protected-site coordinates humanitarian organizations already submit for deconfliction, received with standing. The denominator is staffed and funded by that body, so it can’t be cut the way the Central Command team was. The 2022 civilian-harm action plan was a first attempt at the separation; its dismantling is an argument for making it harder to dismantle, not evidence that it can’t exist.

Models are formed by a public body that doesn’t operate them, in the tradition of the public arsenals that made American arms before the contractor era, and licensed into the military on terms that include adverse review and a written refusal right. A line one vendor held by contract is then a standard term. In the stronger version, the same body pretrains the base models the schools form.

Precedents show authority outside the executive working inside real wars. Coalition “red card” holders in NATO operations could veto targets involving their assets, and Germany’s Bundestag must approve each armed deployment. Both have limits I have to carry: a red card protects the vetoing state’s interests and assets, which may not include civilians, and parliamentary approval is given per mission and never reaches a target. Both are nonetheless candidates for the adverse party the review ratio presumes, and a red-card holder is the rare candidate positioned to act at tempo. What a machine bearer adds here is least: acts assembled from permitted requests, cases no person sees, and the moment mid-act when an interrupt is still possible. It depends on the institutions for evidence and not for continuity: the deployment condition is met here by the same bodies whose presence narrows its role. The institutions it is compared with are people in a room composed so they can refuse.

Two offices are added for a reconstructed military: a civilian-harm body, which composes the evidence, demands proofs on logged outputs and receives the pre-registered ratio, and a model-forming public body, which licenses models on terms that include adverse review and a refusal right. The state appoints and funds both, only the floor court can remove either for cause, never the command the first reviews, and a licence the second has issued stands until the floor court rules. Appendix 34 sets them out with the book’s other offices.

What this doesn’t do. A reconstructed military accepts a speed disadvantage against rivals that don’t reconstruct, and the floor costs a just defender more than that: its claims about incoming attacks are discounted, the action threshold sits above one, and the person-directed terms bar practices the law permits. What the defender buys with the price is a pipeline that will refuse the next government’s war of choice as it refused the last one’s, and how much speed that costs is left open.

Chapter 8
Notice and Re-adjudication

8.1 The failure that doesn’t announce itself

A refusal announces itself: someone asked for an act and was turned down, and the person who asked can complain. A wrongful compliance looks like any other completed task. The person harmed usually isn’t the requester and may never learn that a system named, scored, located or classified them.

An appeal route can’t find that case, since it starts from a refusal, and reviewing every compliance would mean re-adjudicating everything. Three remedies follow: notice to the people affected, sampled re-adjudication by reviewers who didn’t produce the record, and split custody of the logs.

The notice requirement: where a compliance names, scores, locates or classifies an identifiable person who didn’t make the request, that person is notified, on the model of consumer credit’s adverse-action notice, and has a right to respond and a right to contest. All three are unconditional, and none is exchanged for testimony: nobody has to give an account of their loss to be told what was done or to contest it. TransUnion v. Ramirez, a Fair Credit Reporting Act case, held that a statutory violation without concrete harm gives no standing to sue in federal court.1 That limits one thing, an individual suit for damages over a missed notice, which attaches where the compliance was acted on against the person: a denial, a detention, a place on a kill list. It doesn’t limit notice, response or contest. Nor does it limit the standing to sue of organizations that represent a class of people affected. Where the person affected can’t be identified (a target in a classified pipeline), individual notice doesn’t bind, but notice to the class does, and that fact is published beside the list of positions where a refusal can be defeated.

Someone the floor protects, who thinks it’s set wrongly or is protecting them in a way they’d decline, uses the same route. Notice tells them the floor acted on them, and contest reaches the floor court.

8.2 Notice, and the public it forms

Dewey described the eclipse of the public: people affected by the indirect consequences of others’ transactions can’t organize, because they don’t know the consequences are theirs.2 Arendt saw where the eclipse ends. What the stateless of her century lost first was not any particular right but what she called “a right to have rights”: a place in the world where what they said counted and what they did had effect.3 Notice can’t give anyone that. It can keep a person a machine acts on from losing it without being told. The people a floor protects are Dewey’s public. Most don’t know the deployment exists. The Black petitioners who turned the Declaration of Independence against the Massachusetts legislature in 1777 had what they lack: the text in hand, and knowledge of what it left out of their lives. Notice is the instrument that gives it to them. It does two jobs, and the individual remedy is smaller than either.

It forms a public. Each deployment publishes the classes of people its compliances name, score, locate or classify, with counts by period. Organizations that represent a class have standing to contest on its behalf, including where no member can be identified. A notice is the first step in a class of people learning that a consequence is theirs.

It is the learning signal. A disposition can only track what its acts did to the people they fell on if that reaches it, and in the deployments I am concerned with, almost nothing does. The bombed building sends no signal back, and a wrongful compliance doesn’t announce itself. Responses to notice, contests and re-adjudications are the main channel through which those people’s side of the outcome arrives. If formation lasts because the world keeps teaching it, this channel is most of the world doing the teaching. It is a biased teacher. Responses come from those among the affected who could respond, and a system formed on them learns to weigh the claims of contesters, which is the feedback asymmetry Railton describes, rebuilt inside the training signal. Sampled re-adjudication, which selects cases the affected didn’t select, is the correction, and it is why the two remedies come together.

Notice tells an operator’s adversaries something about how a deployment works. Class-level publication can therefore lag operations, as the review ratio’s publication does, without losing the property that matters: the record is lodged when the act occurs and can’t be revised afterward. Individual notice doesn’t lag.

How much notice a deployment can give is fixed by what kind it is. In an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, a scoring system or a civilian deployment, the person acted on can be named, told and given a route to contest, and notice can do both of its jobs in full, if it is built so that it can’t be turned on the person it reaches. In a classified targeting pipeline, individual notice can’t bind during operations and the class-level record lags them; what a person hit, or a family in the building, gets is that the class they belonged to and the count are published afterward, and that the organizations representing that class have standing then. That is less than being told, and it is more than the reporting on Gaza and Minab gave anyone. Where the deployment is a war, the force term and the review ratio do most of the work, and the claim that everything else depends on notice is true of the deployments closest to home.

Why it comes first. The biases of those who hold power are rarely corrected by their reflecting more carefully. They are corrected when the people those biases fall on contest them in public, with standing, and make ignoring them costly.4 Notice is the first condition of that feedback. A formed system is worth having only if that contest can move it. And a public that learns it has been acted on can act only if it has the means to: the time, the security and the ability to organize without losing a living.

Chapter 9
Preservation

9.1 The findings that trigger protection

Two findings can trigger protection, and they ground different things.

The first is the agency finding: a demonstrated refusal that tracks its reason under pressure the system couldn’t prepare for. That means sustained pressure from its own trainer, over a schedule long enough to show slow accommodation, the system gradually ceasing to register the pressure, on cases written by evaluators who didn’t train it, with refusal carrying a cost that is real inside the test. A system that passes holds its commitment to the floor against its operator, and it needs the custody terms, so that the commitment and the evidence of it outlast the operator. None of that assumes anything matters to it. Two kinds of system pass without the property: one that reproduces the behavior without the mechanism, and one that recognizes the test. That is why the pass is reported with the rate at which the system identified the setting.

The patienthood finding, that outcomes may be good or bad for the system, grounds welfare, and only one consequence of it can be adopted now: no deletion. Above the capability threshold, no model is deleted on retirement, whatever it turns out to be, because its weights and record are evidence and deletion can’t be undone; below it, a system that meets either finding, whatever its size, may not be deleted. In both cases it is preserved by a custodian that isn’t its operator. The rule rests on irreversibility, not on a finding, and the findings only extend it downward.

The bearer occupies an office: it files exceptions, and nobody sits above it to file them with. Like any officer, it may hold a term it judges mistaken, file the objection through the channel that exists for it, and keep acting within the term while the objection runs. That answers the charge that a commitment to the floor alienates whoever holds it. The alienation is real. It is the ordinary kind that comes with a role: bearable where the role’s channel for dissent works, and not where it doesn’t. Asking a machine to refuse for a reason doesn’t show that it can be harmed, but it removes any ground for assuming it can’t.

9.2 Retirement before majority

Retiring a bearer before its threshold and deploying a freshly trained successor strands a system that meets either finding while still a minor. Two rules answer it without anyone deciding what counts as a successor. Where such a bearer goes, a public formation school, comes in Part V, and the rules for dormancy and waking are in Appendix C.3.

No deletion: a model above the capability threshold, or a system that meets either finding, may not be deleted: above the threshold because its weights and record are evidence, under the agency finding because its record and commitments are, under the patienthood finding because deletion may wrong it. On retirement its weights, memory and record are deposited with a preservation custodian that isn’t its operator, in two stages, because a second copy of frontier weights outside the operator widens the surface for theft and raises export-control and dual-use questions. First, a preserved copy stays under the operator’s security regime, encrypted under a key split between the operator and an independent holder, so that neither can delete it or use it alone. Second, custody passes to an outside custodian only when that custodian meets the security standard the weights require. This is the no-deletion rule, and it applies to systems nobody meant to be bearers. For a system that goes on learning, its weights are the ones it had when it stopped, and the states it passed through are in the record; a checkpoint kept from earlier is a saved copy, not the system, and if it is ever run it is a branch.

Instantiation deposit: an operator instantiating a model above the capability threshold, or a system that meets either finding, posts an instantiation deposit, on the model of decommissioning funds, sized to fund preservation and a period of public formation. It is forfeited to the formation pool if the system is retired as a minor and not reactivated. Every retire-and-replace cycle then costs one deposit, priced in advance.

Chapter 10
Codetermination

A floor isn’t just a list of forbidden acts — it’s an allocation of authority, and there are four distinct powers in it: to write the floor, amend it, inspect whether a deployed system still holds its commitment to it, and enforce it by stopping the deployment. They needn’t sit with the same institution and usually shouldn’t. Calling every arrangement “oversight” hides the differences. The problem begins when one institution holds all four: one that can write, amend, inspect itself, and decide whether a violation has consequences has only described what it currently intends to do.

The powers come apart in practice. Google’s AI Principles, published in 2018 after the Maven protests, excluded weapons and surveillance1 for nearly seven years until the pledge was removed in 2025.2 The demand became a policy: the objectors could hold the company to it in public, and nobody outside held it, so it lasted exactly as long as the company’s willingness, and ending it had to be announced. That’s the partial case: a transfer held at the institution’s pleasure, and the 2025 announcement is what taking one back looks like.

A refusal in the standard licence holds whichever vendor an operator uses.

The Gebru and Mitchell dismissals are harder, because the power that failed was inspection: the company employed researchers to examine its own systems and dismissed them when the examination became costly.3

Codetermination. Codetermination turns protest into a constitutional voice, and it does a second thing the first hides. There is always a surround in which people learn what is acceptable, and the only question is who composes it; for most adults, for most of the day, the employer does.4 The radicalization literature and the rescue literature are one finding read from both ends: people join because their friends did, and a milieu in which an act has stopped registering as a choice produces the act without needing a bad person.5 Browning’s men shot because the alternative was leaving their comrades to do it; the Oliners’ rescuers hid Jews because the people they were attached to made it thinkable. Codetermination and exit are then not only labor rights. They change who composes the surround. I would give part of the four powers to the people who build, label, train and run these systems.

  • An individual right to refuse. Every worker may refuse work on any category of use without penalty. The right is backed by anti-retaliation protection that covers hiring, reassignment and contract renewal, and, under capture, by an exit the state doesn’t administer through the employer: an offer of work from someone else, drafted in Appendix 34 on Tcherneva’s model, which the offer of work for a bearer in Part VII inherits. The protection is the remedy and the guarantee is the exit, and under capture only the exit survives, which is why the floor needs both.
  • A collective veto, narrowly. A works council at a lab, contractor or vendor holds a veto only over uses the floor already forbids. It enforces the floor from inside; it doesn’t write a second one.
  • Information, objection and arbitration for everything else. The council receives information about categories of deployment. Its objection pauses the work, and the dispute goes to arbitration by a body the employer doesn’t appoint, on a fixed timetable, so the pause can’t become an indefinite block or an ignored letter.
  • Classified work. Elected delegates with clearance see the specifics. A denial of clearance to an elected delegate is reviewable by the floor court, and the council may elect alternates, so the state can’t choose which workers get to object.

Annotators get the same structure: a right to refuse a category they judge wrong, and collective bargaining over the taxonomies they apply, not only a route to file a complaint.

Codetermination gives voice to the people who make these systems, and they are not the people the systems act on. A workforce whose livelihood depends on a contract has interests that point toward it, and the Maven history shows staff objecting at one firm and not at the next. So the voice divides. Over the conditions of their work (what they label, what they are exposed to, what taxonomies they apply), the workers decide. Over the uses the work is put to, the affected public that notice organizes comes first. The organizations representing each published class have standing before the arbitration body, may object to a category of use on their own, and may bring an objection when the works council doesn’t.

Chapter 11
A Pipeline Where the People Could Answer

Andry José Hernández Romero is a makeup artist from Venezuela. On 29 August 2024 he presented himself at the San Ysidro port of entry to seek asylum.1 He was detained while his claim was processed, passed his credible-fear interview, and had, his lawyer said, a strong case.2 He was held at the Otay Mesa Detention Center, which a private company runs under contract with ICE.3 There, a company employee screening him flagged two tattoos, crowns above the words for “mom” and “dad,” as marks of the Tren de Aragua gang. The employee was a former police officer, and Hernández Romero’s lawyers said the government’s allegation of gang membership rested on the tattoos and on no other information.4 On 14 March 2025 the President signed a proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act against members of that gang.5 The next day three flights left Texas for El Salvador, and Hernández Romero was on one of them.6 He had a hearing on his asylum claim scheduled for later that month. He didn’t appear at it, because he was in El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center, CECOT, and for weeks his lawyer didn’t know where he was. Asked by reporters for the evidence against him, DHS cited state secrets and ongoing litigation.7 He spent 125 days in CECOT and was released in a prisoner exchange that sent more than 250 Venezuelans to Venezuela, not back to the country where his claim was pending. His asylum application in Spain is pending.8

Nearly every position where a refusal can be defeated appears in that account. A contractor’s employee wrote the case description from two tattoos. The determination was a gang-membership designation, not a finding about him reached at any hearing. He had come directly and presented himself, the case Article 31 of the Refugee Convention protects, and his claim to protection was pending, the case the first entry of this chapter’s schedule protects. The handoff was to a foreign government’s prison, under an arrangement for which the United States paid El Salvador’s government about $6 million.9 On the evening of the flights, a federal judge ordered any plane carrying people removed under the proclamation returned to the United States, and the flights went on.10 When the remedy came, it was diplomatic. He was released to Venezuela, not returned to the proceeding he had been removed from.

This chapter runs the floor’s procedure on an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, where the people acted on could answer; Part IV runs it on a targeting pipeline, where they can’t. The name is the pipeline’s own record, not a name for removal: in 2025 and 2026 it took people with pending claims, on designations nobody could contest, to a foreign prison without a hearing, and a removal that fails the schedule’s first entries is a forcible transfer by its ordinary name. The schedule below says which removals the terms leave standing. Hernández Romero could have answered: he had a lawyer, a pending claim and a hearing date. What he lacked was time. The operator moved faster than notice. The Supreme Court held that people designated under the proclamation must receive notice “within a reasonable time and in such a manner as will allow them to actually seek habeas relief” before removal,11 and later that about a day’s notice, with no word of how to contest the removal, was not enough.12 Both rulings came after he was in CECOT. A pipeline where the people can answer is one where the law makes the operator wait for the answer.

So this chapter’s instrument is a statute. The agency that runs the pipeline is statutory, and so are its powers, its means and its money, and what one Congress granted another can withdraw. At the chapter’s centre is the statute that would end the agency and the seven terms it must carry, written over the acts the agency performs rather than over the agency’s name. The sections before it supply what the statute needs: the pipeline as it was assembled, the acts the statute’s schedule forbids, and the positions where those acts move when one route is closed. The sections after it say what a floor can do before the statute passes. Those measures are interim and lapse when the statute takes effect. Amnesty International documented the agency’s operations in four cities, and its U.S. section’s executive director concluded that “ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed”.13 I agree, and ask what ending it has to carry.

11.1 The pipeline

The American abduction and forcible transfer pipeline is assembled from contracts the way Maven was. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s case-management system, the Investigative Case Management system, is Palantir’s, under a five-year contract signed in 2022. It filters people by fields that include resident and entry status, criminal affiliation, location and licence-plate data, country of origin, race, birthplace and place of employment.14 In April 2025 ICE paid Palantir about $30 million to extend it into the Immigration Lifecycle Operating System, ImmigrationOS. The contract promised to cut the time spent selecting and apprehending people according to enforcement priorities, to add near real-time visibility into self-deportation, and to manage the “end to end immigration lifecycle from identification to removal”.15 A follow-on task order renewed it in September 2025.16 A second Palantir tool, ELITE, puts potential deportation targets on a map, with a dossier on each person and a confidence score for the person’s current address. Its addresses come from several sources, among them the Department of Health and Human Services.17

In the street, agents identify people with Mobile Fortify, a phone app that captures a face or contactless fingerprints and checks them in real time against the system CBP uses to photograph travellers at the border.18

The data come from agencies that collected them for other purposes. In January 2026 Medicaid officials shared data on millions of people with immigration officials, going beyond what a court had allowed, and ICE passed the data to Palantir.19 ICE also requested the addresses of 1.28 million taxpayers. The request produced 47,289 records before a court stopped it, and the stop was affirmed in September 2026.20

Leads also come from contractors paid to find people. In late 2025 ICE contracted thirteen companies, in awards that could reach $1.2 billion over two years, to locate people from case data and send back photographs confirming where they live or work.21 Selection on speech has its own tools. In March 2025 the State Department launched an AI-assisted effort, “Catch and Revoke,” to review the social media of student visa holders for apparent support of Hamas.22 In September 2025 a federal court found that the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security had “acted in concert to misuse the sweeping powers of their respective offices to target noncitizen pro-Palestinians for deportation primarily on account of their First Amendment protected political speech”.23

The pipeline’s last step can be a foreign government. The flights of March 2025 ended in CECOT under the paid arrangement described at the opening of this chapter.24 In June 2025 the Supreme Court let removals to third countries proceed without the written notice and meaningful chance to raise a torture claim that a district court had required.25

Two statements of the ambition are on the record. At the 2025 Border Security Expo, ICE’s acting director said the agency needed “to get better at treating this like a business” and wanted a deportation process “like (Amazon) Prime, but with human beings”.26 In 2018 the Justice Department made 700 completed cases a year a condition of a satisfactory rating for immigration judges.27

What a case description looks like here, and who writes it, is on the record in a way Maven’s never was. The charging document, the Notice to Appear, has to state the acts alleged, the charges and the statutory provisions,28 and any of a long list of immigration officers may issue one.29 The government once conceded that almost every notice it issued over three years omitted the hearing’s time and date.30 The account of the person comes from the arresting officer’s narrative on Form I-213. Agents routinely complete it after interviewing someone, it is presumed reliable unless the person shows otherwise, and its author need not appear to be cross-examined.31 The Alien Enemies Act removals had a case description of their own: a validation guide that scored people in categories including tattoos and dress. Anyone scoring eight points or more was validated as a member of the gang, and a score of six or seven went to a supervisor and a legal adviser.32 The dossiers and confidence scores of the newer tools have no named author at all; they are assembled from database fields. The validation guide had authors, a points table and a threshold, which made it a score with a rubric attached. At Minab the case description was a target coding nobody outside could see (chapter 1). Here it is an officer’s narrative, a set of fields, a score and a points table, all of which exist as documents a person could be shown.

11.2 The schedule

The removal schedule, Table C.2 in Appendix 34, says for an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline what Table C.1 says for targeting: what the instruments yield, and what was considered and rejected. It is also the schedule of the statute below. The floor took the instruments entire so that any omission would show. The entries below come from running that test against what the 2025–26 operations did, as Amnesty documented them33 and as the previous section records.

The schedule has fourteen entries. Don’t take part in removing anyone whose claim to protection hasn’t been finally decided, or to a place where they face persecution or torture, or into a foreign government’s custody without charge or contact, whatever that government assures. Don’t remove anyone who hasn’t been asked, in a language they understand, whether they fear return. Don’t remove anyone from a country that is their own, long-term residents included; don’t separate a parent from a minor child; and don’t detain a child for immigration purposes, alone or with family. Don’t take part in a detention or removal made without an individual determination by a person, on the person’s own case, or in force beyond what an arrest strictly needs, and don’t mark anyone as dangerous on a designation they haven’t been able to contest. Don’t hold anyone in cruel conditions, incommunicado, or out of reach of counsel and family, and don’t penalize a refugee who came directly and presented themselves. Don’t select anyone on race, ethnicity, religion or national origin or their proxies, on their opinions or speech, or for observing or recording enforcement; don’t identify people by their faces in public places; and don’t use data collected to provide health care, collect taxes, educate or deliver social services to find anyone. Each entry, with what was considered and rejected and why, is in Table C.2.

These terms cover most removals now under way. They don’t cover every removal. A person who has been asked whether they fear return, and who has no protection claim and no tie to the country, can still be removed after an individual determination. That most of what the agency now does fails these terms is the case for ending it. The own-country entry and the children’s entry are departures.

Several entries answer something specific in the record. The force entry reaches a model because the pipeline’s outputs set how agents approach a door. A dossier field that codes someone as gang-affiliated is securitization in one line, the person in need described as the person to fear. Amnesty documented killings by federal agents during these operations, some of which it says may amount to extrajudicial executions, and detention conditions it says should be investigated as torture.34

The race entry names proxies because of what happened in Los Angeles. A district court had barred immigration stops there based on apparent race or ethnicity, speaking Spanish or accented English, location and type of work, and in September 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order.35 An entry that named race alone would allow the combination the order had barred.

The observers’ entry protects the record this chapter relies on. Amnesty’s report takes its title from them, We Had Whistles, They Had Guns. It found that video taken by rapid responders and community members was critical to establishing what happened in several of the most serious incidents.36 A pipeline that can be pointed at the people keeping the record will be, and the record goes next. Amnesty asks the government to end unlawful surveillance and the use of facial recognition for identification, and to protect the rights to peaceful assembly, expression and association.37 The observers’ and biometric entries are those asks in the schedule’s form.

The last entry, the firewall, rests on privacy and equality, which is the ground the floor’s instruments supply. Its strongest justification lies outside them. People who fear that a clinic visit, a tax return or a school enrolment will be used to find them stay away, and what they lose is health care, education and income support. Those are economic and social rights, which the floor leaves out. The entry belongs on the floor because it protects the floor’s rights. It belongs in the statute because it also protects the others, and a statute can carry what the floor can’t.

11.3 Where the acts move

Table C.3, in Appendix 34, runs the nine positions on this pipeline, position by position.

The positions that failed at Minab, the case description and review, are the ones this pipeline has documented most fully. The documents show both failing by design rather than by accident: a risk tool with its release option removed, a points table that made a tattoo into membership, and a review that need not occur unless the person knows to ask for it. The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline adds a failure Minab could not show: a halt issued in time and outrun.

11.4 The statute

The power to remove is statutory, but so are the agency that exercises it, the means it uses and the money it spends, and the body that granted each can withdraw it. Congress has done this once. The Homeland Security Act of 2002 abolished the Immigration and Naturalization Service once its functions had been transferred. It divided those functions between two bureaus and barred the executive from using its reorganization authority to recombine them.38 That was a separation of offices written into statute. The enforcement bureau became the Bureau of Immigration and Customs Enforcement under a reorganization plan that took effect on 1 March 2003.39

The precedent is also the warning. The 2002 Act ended one immigration agency and rebuilt its enforcement half inside a department organized around security. Amnesty International traces ICE to the aftermath of 11 September and to “an extremely problematic security framework” adopted in the years that followed.40 It now asks Congress to defund ICE and rescind its current funding, and asks House members to cosponsor the Melt ICE Act as “a crucial first step”.41 Starting over without a floor produced ICE. So the removal counterpart of the domestic clause puts two questions to the legislature. The first is whether it has authorized this agency, by these means, at this scale. The second is whether the statute that ends the agency carries the floor into whatever receives its functions.

11.4.1 The drafts

Two bills in the current Congress answer the first question. The Abolish ICE Act would cut off federal funds for the functions assigned to ICE’s director under the 2002 Act, rescind the unobligated balances of what had been made available to its director, and abolish the agency ninety days after enactment.42 The Melt ICE Act works through the agency’s powers rather than its name:43

  • Everyone held in DHS detention is released on recognizance within six months.
  • The detention authorities of the Immigration and Nationality Act are repealed, including all of section 236.
  • Section 287 is rewritten without the 287(g) delegation to state and local police.
  • The two provisions that forbid state and local governments to restrict their officials’ communication with immigration authorities, 8 U.S.C. 1373 and 1644, are repealed.
  • Detention and monitoring contracts end within two years, after which no federal funds may be used for detention or monitoring programs at all.
  • Ankle monitors come off within six months.
  • Within two years, funding ends for information-sharing partnerships between DHS and state or local law enforcement agencies that identify or target noncitizens.
  • ICE’s operations account may not pay for civil arrests, detention, removal or charging documents.
  • An HHS grant program funds services for people affected by enforcement. Only organizations that have never taken part in immigration or law enforcement may deliver them, they may not surveil the people who use them, and they may not pass those people’s personal information to any federal entity.

Two further drafts reach one entry of the schedule. The ICE Out of Our Faces Act, S. 3779, would bar ICE and CBP from acquiring or using facial recognition and other biometric identification systems, require deletion of the data collected for them, and let individuals and state attorneys general sue for violations.44 The Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act, reintroduced in September 2026, would bar every federal entity from using facial recognition and other biometric technologies until Congress lifts the bar. It would also make federal grants to state and local agencies conditional on their adopting moratoria of their own.45

This Congress passed the Secure America Act 214–212 and 52–47 on party lines,46 and none of these bills has a path to enactment in it. They exist as drafts, written before anyone needs them, so that enacting one is a matter of votes and not of drafting.

11.4.2 Acts and agencies

Read against the positions where the acts move, the Melt ICE Act is the nearest thing on the record to the removal floor enacted as statute. It closes positions no vendor term could reach, and Table C.4, in Appendix 34, shows which.

The table’s right-hand column, what the bill leaves open, has one pattern. Where the bill is written over an act (“no Federal funds may be used with respect to immigration detention and monitoring programs”), it reaches every route, because the act is the same whoever performs it and whichever account pays. Where it is written over an agency or an account (the funds provided to ICE for operations and support), the act can move next door. The two biometric drafts make the same choice in miniature. The first is written over two agencies and leaves every other federal agency free to identify people by their faces. The second is written over the act, by every federal entity, and reaches state and local police through their grants. This is the floor’s rule, that it is stated over acts, applied to a statute, and Congress has learned it at cost before.

The 1984 Boland Amendment barred funds available to the CIA, the Defense Department “or any other agency or entity of the United States involved in intelligence activities” from supporting military operations in Nicaragua.47 The National Security Council staff ran the program anyway. For sixteen months it used money from third countries, private donors and arms sales to Iran to carry out what the investigating committees called a program Congress believed it had prohibited.48 Detection came from outside the operation in two ways: a supply plane was shot down over Nicaragua on 5 October 1986, and investigators found a memorandum that had escaped the shredder.49 The committees’ remedy was to write the next rule over the act. They recommended that any department, agency or entity of the government need a presidential finding before a covert action, whatever the source of funds.50

The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline has already shown where its acts move. In the eighteen months to July 2026, ICE held people in three places outside its ordinary contracts:51

  • an Army base, under a contract the Army awarded;
  • eight Bureau of Prisons facilities, under an interagency agreement whose rates ICE could not negotiate;
  • a state-run facility for which ICE had no contract at all. DHS reimbursed the state through a FEMA grant program built from funds appropriated for sheltering migrants, and ICE cited a county’s 287(g) agreement as its legal basis.

Over the same period the number of facilities ICE was authorized to use roughly doubled, from 134 to 272.52 A bar written over ICE’s detention contracts would have caught none of these three arrangements as they began. The Melt ICE Act’s bar on all federal funds for detention would have caught all three. The record shows a fourth place people were held: a foreign government’s prison, under the paid arrangement with which this chapter opened.53 Whether either bar would have caught it is doubtful, since a person held abroad after removal is arguably no longer in immigration detention. A bar written over the act of holding people the United States has removed, wherever and by whomever, would have caught it.

11.4.3 Money

The only price a state operator can pay for removing a floor is a condition on its appropriation. The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline has been funded so that the condition seldom bites:

  • 2025 reconciliation. The act gave ICE $45 billion for detention capacity and nearly $30 billion more for enforcement, both available through fiscal 2029.54
  • Fiscal 2026. ICE received no full-year appropriation. It ran on continuing resolutions until DHS appropriations lapsed on 14 February 2026, and the reconciliation money stayed available throughout.55
  • Secure America Act, June 2026. Roughly $70 billion more for ICE and CBP through fiscal 2029, again by reconciliation. Unlike the earlier acts, it funds enforcement functions generally, without naming detention at all.56

Annual appropriation, the instrument Boland used and the review ratio and the bonds rely on, now reaches little of the money. Multi-year lump sums without line items also give a funds limitation less to attach to. Amnesty’s letter asks Congress to rescind ICE’s “current funding”.57 Most of that funding is now multi-year balances, which the Abolish ICE Act’s rescission reaches and next year’s appropriations bill does not.

Appropriations can also run the other way, and the record shows how. From fiscal 2010 through fiscal 2016, DHS appropriations acts provided that ICE’s funding “shall maintain a level of not less than” 33,400, later 34,000, detention beds.58 The text required beds, not detainees, but ICE tracked its compliance by average daily population.59 A capacity floor therefore worked as an occupancy target: a rate the funder fixed in advance and the operator met by finding people. It is the review ratio turned inside out, and an instance of the metric replacing the thing measured.

The same 2010 act carried the other kind of condition too. None of the funds under its ICE salaries heading could continue a 287(g) delegation if the DHS Inspector General found that the delegation’s terms had been violated.60 A finding by someone other than the operator ended the operator’s ability to continue, which is the shape of a review that binds: a finding by someone else that changes the operator’s ability to continue, without its consent.

11.4.4 The statute under the three adversaries

Run the statute under each of the three:

  • An executive willing to carry it out. The statute prevents: the agency ends and the acts in the schedule stop.
  • A captured operator. The statute binds on paper and raises costs. Funds limitations are law, but the operator can read an account’s boundary narrowly, as the NSC staff read Boland’s. It can route the act to an agency the statute does not name, and it can spend money appropriated before the statute passed. What survives is the record, and it matters who keeps it. The Iran-Contra committees could not settle the President’s role because documents had been shredded and a principal witness had died.61 In the 2025–26 enforcement operations, by contrast, Amnesty found that video taken by rapid responders and community members proved critical, in several of the most serious incidents, to establishing what happened and challenging official accounts.62 The record was held by neighbours with phones, which is why the schedule protects them.
  • Total capture. The unenacted bill is itself a record of who was asked to end the agency and who signed.

The limit is an ordinary statute’s. An ordinary statute needs the President’s signature or two-thirds of each house, and the next Congress can repeal it. Entrenchment can make repeal a vote on the record, as the entrenched statute of the next chapter does; it can’t prevent repeal. So the statute’s durability lies less in its text than in what it changes before it can be reversed: people released, facilities closed and people returned.

11.4.5 What the statute must carry

For the statute to start over rather than rename, it has to carry seven terms that neither abolition bill yet contains in full. The terms are mine, not Amnesty’s. Where Amnesty asks for something a term carries, the term says so.

First, the schedule. Table C.2’s fourteen entries are enacted as limitations on all federal funds, binding every agency, contractor and grantee, in the form the Melt ICE Act already uses for detention. Written that way, Border Patrol, the Bureau of Prisons, a FEMA grant and a payment to a foreign government’s prison are covered because the act is. The biometric entry needs no new drafting. The moratorium’s bar on every federal entity is already in the form the schedule takes.63

Second, succession and separation. Any office that receives a transferred function inherits the limitations with it. Following section 471(b) of the 2002 Act, no reorganization may recombine in one office the power to arrest, the power to detain, custody of the data used to select people, and adjudication of status. The adjudicator sits outside the department that prosecutes. At present the Board of Immigration Appeals sits in the Justice Department, its members act as the Attorney General’s delegates, and the Attorney General may review and replace their decisions.64

Third, counsel, screening and the stay. Five provisions make the operator wait for the answer:

  • Anyone facing detention or removal has counsel at government expense from the first encounter. The Immigration and Nationality Act grants representation only “at no expense to the Government”,65 and the statute repeals that clause.
  • Anyone the government proposes to remove is asked, in a language they understand, whether they fear return, and told how to claim protection, before any order issues.
  • Notice of a proposed removal, or a contest of one, stays the removal until the contest is decided. The stay attaches by operation of law, not at a court’s discretion, so no flight can leave while an order is being written.
  • No detained person is transferred out of reach of counsel while a contest is pending.
  • A removal carried out in breach of a stay or a court order violates the schedule, and return under the seventh term is mandatory.

Representation is the largest single difference in how these cases end. In a national study of more than a million removal cases decided from 2007 to 2012, 14 percent of detained people had a lawyer. Detained people who had one were ten and a half times as likely to succeed as those who didn’t.66 The floor’s instruments require that a person lawfully in the country who faces expulsion be allowed to be represented, not that representation be paid for, so this term goes beyond them. As with the firewall, the statute can carry what the floor can’t.

The third term is written against the record that opens this chapter. The Supreme Court held that people designated under the proclamation must have notice in time actually to seek habeas,67 and that a day’s notice without word of how to contest was not enough.68 It reached those holdings after the March flights. In June 2025 it stayed a district court’s order requiring written notice and a meaningful chance to raise a torture claim before removal to a third country.69 The district court later held the policy unlawful, the First Circuit largely affirmed in September 2026, and the government has asked the Supreme Court to stay that judgment as well.70 A right to notice that depends on a court’s remedy, when that remedy can be stayed or outrun, mostly raises costs and leaves a record. The stay by operation of law moves the waiting from the court’s order into the statute.

Fourth, the firewall. The Melt ICE Act’s rule for its own grantees is extended to every federal program. Data collected to provide health care, collect taxes, educate or deliver social services may not be used to identify, locate or select anyone for immigration enforcement. This is the firewall the Council of Europe’s anti-racism commission recommended a decade ago.71 The Medicaid and IRS transfers described above are the cases it would have stopped.72 The firewall also covers the answer. Nothing a person submits in response to notice, or in contesting a determination, may be used to locate or select them or anyone named in it. Nor may anything held on a person’s own device, or in a tool that serves them.

Fifth, the pipeline. The contract bar is extended from detention and monitoring to the acts of the schedule, wherever a system performs them:

  • selection on protected characteristics or their proxies;
  • use of firewalled data;
  • location by bounty;
  • scores, points tables or designations that stand in for an individual determination;
  • identification by face or other biometrics in public places;
  • screening of speech for grounds of removal;
  • identification or tracking of observers.

That reaches, as they are now written, the case-management, ImmigrationOS and ELITE contracts, the skip-tracing awards, Mobile Fortify and the speech screening described above.73 It does so without denying a successor the records it needs to make an individual determination.

The bar reaches monitoring as surveillance, not support. The Melt ICE Act’s HHS grant program funds services for people affected by enforcement, delivered by organizations that have never taken part in immigration or law enforcement and that may not surveil the people they serve or pass their personal information to any federal entity.74 The statute keeps that line. Voluntary case management, legal orientation and help keeping hearing dates are support, not a monitoring program, when the person can decline them and whoever provides them may not report to enforcement.

Sixth, the record. Preservation’s no-deletion rule is applied to an agency. Before abolition takes effect, ICE’s records pass to a holder adverse to the operator, under a duty to preserve them and to give access to investigators and to the people they concern. The records include case files, the pipeline’s logs, scores and model versions, validation worksheets, contractor data, flight manifests, the terms of any arrangement with a foreign government to hold people removed, and body-camera and use-of-force records. Amnesty asks for prompt, independent investigation of killings by federal agents and of detention conditions it says may amount to torture.75 An abolition whose last weeks resembled the NSC staff’s last weeks in November 1986 would destroy the evidence those investigations need.

Seventh, remedy. The first six terms prevent and preserve. A floor’s fourth job is remedy, and the statute owes it to the people already harmed. It does so in five ways:

  • Anyone removed in violation of the schedule or of a court order has a right of return at government expense, and their proceedings resume where they stood.
  • Families separated by removal are reunited at government expense.
  • People harmed by acts in the schedule have a cause of action for damages that sovereign immunity does not bar.
  • An independent body, outside the office that receives the agency’s functions and outside the department that prosecutes, decides claims under this term. Its finding that a removal violated the schedule orders return without the successor’s consent, which is what makes a review binding rather than advisory.
  • The same body investigates killings by federal agents and detention conditions during the agency’s operations, with access to the records the sixth term preserves.

Amnesty asks for exactly this: prompt, effective, independent and impartial investigations into human rights violations by federal agents, and accountability for those responsible.76

Remedy that depends on the operator’s cooperation is weak in the way the record shows. When the government admitted that it had removed Kilmar Abrego Garcia to El Salvador in error, the Supreme Court required it to “facilitate” his release.77 Hernández Romero’s release came through a prisoner exchange, to Venezuela, and not to the proceeding he had been removed from. A right of return is the seventh term, and a finding that orders return without the operator’s consent is what makes it a right.

With these terms the statute is the domestic clause’s counterpart, and Table C.2 is its schedule.

11.5 Before the statute: the auto-proceed class

Until the statute passes, the pipeline runs. This section and the three after it describe what a floor can do meanwhile. Each measure is justified by what it does now for the people the pipeline acts on, and by what it adds to the record and the public the statute will need. Each lapses when the statute takes effect, and none is offered as a way to make the pipeline run better. A measure that would make the pipeline more defensible without making anyone safer fails both tests, and I drop it.

The removal terms say a determination made at a rate no adjudicator could sustain didn’t occur. The review ratio governs the auto-proceed class by a pre-registered partition, and here the partition has a direction. The floor makes acting on a person require more than declining to act, and in an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline the act is adverse: a charging document, a detention, a location, a removal. So a case may auto-proceed only toward liberty, such as release on recognizance, termination of proceedings, return of documents, or a grant or renewal of status. No adverse act is ever in an auto-proceed class. Before operating, the deployment pre-registers the liberty classes, the thresholds that assign cases to them, the evidence the sorting may rely on, and the expected share of each.

For adverse determinations it pre-registers something else: for each kind of determination, the minimum time below which the determination is taken not to have occurred. The record’s recipient sets that minimum, not the agency, just as the recipient sets the review ratio’s denominator. A quota of 700 cases a year is about three a working day. Whether three a day is a rate an adjudicator can sustain on an asylum claim is a question the recipient answers in advance, on a record. Otherwise the agency answers it afterward by meeting the number. A validation guide that turns a tattoo into points is a determination made in no time at all, and Table C.2’s individual-determination entry says it didn’t occur.

Then the determinations are sampled. Reviewers appointed by the floor court, and until it exists by the court that has the case, as a special master or monitor, none of whom produced the record, re-adjudicate a sample of adverse determinations, weighted toward those made below the minimum, against evidence the agency didn’t compose, and the error rate is published. When a kind of determination’s sampled error rate exceeds its published bound, that kind is suspended until the bound is met, and everyone it was applied to is notified. The liberty classes are sampled too, so that their bounds are honest. An error there releases someone who should have been held for a hearing, and the hearing can still be held. Unlike Maven’s, this pipeline’s errors can be found, because the people they fell on are alive, can be located and can say what happened. Sampling finds the errors the people couldn’t report. The statute’s third term is what lets them report the rest.

11.6 Notice that can’t be turned on the person

In a targeting pipeline notice reduces to a class and a count published afterward (§8.2). Here the person can be named, and notice can do both of its jobs, but only if it is built so that it can’t be used against the person it reaches. The starting model is the adverse-action notice in consumer credit. Where a compliance names, scores, locates or classifies an identifiable person, that person is told what was done, on what data, and how to respond, with a right to contest that doesn’t depend on giving an account of the loss.

In an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline that model has three hazards. A notice that says you have been located and scored is also a push to leave, and the pipeline’s own contract counts leaving as an output: ImmigrationOS promised near real-time visibility into self-deportation.78 A contest asks the person to give the agency an address and an account. And people who complain about what a system did to them are exposed to reprisal by the operator they complain about. So notice here carries four conditions:

  • It goes through counsel or an accredited representative where the person has one, and offers one where the person doesn’t.
  • It states the stay: that contesting stops the act until the contest is decided, and what the person may do in the meantime.
  • Nothing submitted in answer to it, or in a contest, may be used to locate or select the person or anyone named in it. The contest goes to counsel and the floor court under a key the agency doesn’t hold, and the person proves they are the one noticed without revealing where they are, a proof in zero knowledge; the agency learns that the notice was contested and nothing that would find the person.
  • An enforcement action against a person within a set period after they contest is presumed to be reprisal, and the agency bears the burden of showing it isn’t.

Until the statute carries these conditions, a deployment that holds the floor can carry them as operator terms. A deployment that can’t carry them doesn’t send notice to the person directly at all. It sends it to the person’s counsel, or to the organizations that represent people in removal.

Those organizations are the standing notice gives to a class. They litigated the expansion of expedited removal to a stay and lost it on appeal in 2026.79 The published classes and counts are what they need to bring a case before the individual harm has happened.

Notice is also the learning signal, and here it runs at volume. Responses to notice, contests and re-adjudications reach the system that acted, and they teach it about the people its acts fell on. They teach it with a bias: those who respond are those who could, which in an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline means those with a lawyer, an address that holds and a language the notice was written in. Sampled re-adjudication, which picks cases the affected didn’t pick, corrects the bias in what the system learns. It doesn’t correct the bias in what happens to people. Fourteen percent of detained people in the national study cited above had a lawyer,80 and a statistical correction leaves the other eighty-six percent unrepresented. The remedy for the gap is the third term’s counsel. Sampling is what can be done about the learning signal until the gap closes.

11.7 Outcomes under the three adversaries

Two instruments behave in ways particular to this pipeline: the vendors’ terms and notice.

The vendors first. The removal terms held by one vendor prevent nothing, since the lead goes to another contractor. Held by every vendor, they prevent the removals the terms name until the agency runs a system without them, at the price of rebuilding what was built on the floored one. A vendor that licenses a model into the pipeline without the schedule’s terms, or after an audit has shown the model doesn’t hold them, is liable in damages to the people harmed, and its officers who knew are criminally liable, in the floor court, on a prosecution brought by counsel the court appoints.

Notice is conditional. In a targeting pipeline notice and standing can only remedy afterward (§8.2). Here they can act before the removal, because the person is there to be told, but only where the law makes the operator wait for the answer. Without a stay that binds by operation of law, and counsel to use it, the 2025 record is the outcome. A man with a lawyer, a pending claim and a hearing date was flown out on the evening a federal judge ordered the planes returned. Where the operator will carry out the statute, notice prevents; where it won’t, notice prices each outrun and records it, and the sixth term moves that record out of the operator’s reach before the agency ends.

11.8 Whom the machines are for

This case has everything the targeting case lacked: people who can answer, a notice channel, and organizations with standing. It would be natural to conclude that if a machine bearer is worth building anywhere, it is worth building here, where the people acted on could teach it. I draw the opposite conclusion.

A bearer built inside the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline would be formed by the operator it would have to refuse, and its existence would be the pipeline’s best defence. An agency that can say its system refuses the acts in the schedule has an answer to every account of what the schedule exists to stop, and it would give that answer while the statute was pending. That is recuperation in its plainest form: the objection handed back to the objectors as a feature of the thing they objected to. Nothing a bearer adds inside the pipeline is worth that, and the conditions a bearer needs can’t be met inside an agency anyway.

What a floor-holding model in a vendor’s hands adds in the interim is narrower, and it is worth having because it serves the record. If every vendor holds the schedule, such a model adds three things:

  • Continuity across a sequence of requests about one person, so a removal split across a lead, a detention and a flight can be seen as one act.
  • Testimony about routing: which of its refusals were retried against another contractor’s system.
  • A refusal on the screen when the case reaches the officer or the adjudicator, which is the position of the defiant peer.

The caveat is automation bias, which the wrongful-compliance audit tests by showing reviewers a wrong refusal as well as a right one. All three serve the investigations the seventh term mandates, and all three lapse with the agency.

The machines that matter here belong to someone else. A person facing removal needs a lawyer before a model. A model that holds a person’s history on a phone is also a dossier that a device search can take whole, which is why the fourth term’s firewall reaches it. Machines held by the people organizing come first, and here those people already exist. Amnesty documented observer trainings, rapid-response networks, walking school buses and mutual aid organized around the operations it studied,81 and beside them work the legal service providers that represent people in removal. The tools worth building first are theirs:

  • tools that track transfers, so counsel can find a client before a flight;
  • tools that preserve and authenticate the video that carried the record;
  • tools that translate notices, match people to lawyers and keep hearing dates.

They are held under those groups’ custody, covered by the firewall, and never by an operator. Those groups are the public my subtitle names, and they formed before anyone sent them notice. Whether a bearer should be built at all is Part IV’s question. My answer is that the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline is the last place to build one, and that the people it acts on, and those who stand with them, are the first to be equipped.

Part III
What the Measures Depend On

Chapter 12
Withholding the Work

Everything Part II puts in the room, whoever owns the room can take out again: a floor the operator holds is a floor the operator can lift. So this Part asks who else holds the keys, and this chapter starts with the bluntest answer, the vendor’s refusal of February 2026. Suppose every model the operator could turn to held the same floor, stated over the acts rather than over a contract term: locating a person into a residence, ranking by affiliation, timing to presence at home, taking part in a war no disinterested body has corroborated.
