The American domestic rule most concerned with human judgment, DoD Directive 3000.09, requires autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems to allow “appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force”.21 A system that generates and ranks targets without firing anything is decision support, which plausibly falls outside it. Maven sits in that gap: the domestic rule written for human judgment doesn’t cover the system that compressed it.

Article 28 of the Rome Statute22 is the doctrine built for the case where the person who authorized an act didn’t perform it — a commander is responsible for crimes by forces under effective control where they knew or should have known and failed to take necessary measures. Neither branch asks what a subordinate intended. But the Court’s jurisdiction runs to natural persons, and the provision presupposes forces that can commit a crime and be disciplined — a targeting system is an instrument. So the question is whether the human elements can still be proved once the instrument is doing the work.

The fourth party no doctrine covers

The operator, the command and the weapon’s developer are all inside the military. The model’s developer isn’t. Command responsibility doesn’t extend to the vendor — not because it sits outside a chain of command (Article 28’s civilian branch was written for superiors with no chain of command) but because nobody at the company has effective authority over the military personnel who commit the underlying crime, and an airstrike isn’t an activity within any vendor employee’s effective responsibility. A use policy, a licensing term, a right to refuse service, even a technical cut-off are not that relationship. Individual liability under Article 25 stays available in principle with demanding mental elements — facilitation requires acting for the purpose of facilitating — and ordinary supply of a general-purpose model approaches neither.

Product liability is the other half and it’s untested, with two obstacles: the model isn’t defective in the sense the doctrine most readily covers, and a sophisticated intermediary chose the application. Where the doctrine has been rewritten for software it moved away from this case, as the EU’s directive shows below. Untested isn’t exempt, but no vendor is currently answering to it. The vendor sits in a gap nobody designed, produced by applying to it two bodies of law written for soldiers and for manufacturers.

There is also a jurisdictional gap alongside the doctrinal one: ICC jurisdiction is territorial or by nationality, so one of the two campaigns here sits inside a live instrument and the other sits outside it.

“I do not know whether my system was used.”

Matthias’s responsibility gap is control distributed until nobody holds enough of it to answer23 — a gap in causal control. What the model developer’s case exhibits is different and more tractable: a gap in causal visibility. Asked about his company’s models and Minab, Anthropic’s chief executive said, “we don’t know exactly how these models were used”.24 Take the answer as true. The question is how an arrangement was built in which it could be true.

The paperwork for four July 2025 frontier-model agreements, released in August 2026 under a Freedom of Information Act suit,25 shows something more exact than an absence of oversight terms. One amended agreement carries a section headed System Oversight, withheld in full; the released documents for two of the other three carry no such section at all.

And whether a developer reserved an inspection right matters little. A right exercised inside an accredited classified environment produces findings classified with it. Public accountability needs a body that can initiate scrutiny without belonging to the state and say afterwards what it found. No commercial term supplies that, and the redaction is the demonstration: whatever the withheld section says, the people the deployment is aimed at can’t read it.

Matthias’s gap may not be closable, but absent visibility is an instrumentation choice: logging is solved, contractual inspection rights are ordinary, and a vendor that wanted to know could require, as a condition of licensing into a targeting platform, that categories of use be recorded and made available to a named auditor.

The government’s own acquisition guidance is the better evidence, because it’s complete. OMB’s April 2025 memorandum lists what agencies should secure from vendors, from data rights and portability to pricing transparency, and every item runs from the vendor to the government; none runs back.26 The contracting vehicle explains the absence. The four agreements were other transactions, which carry no FAR provisions by default, so a contracting officer decides case by case which protections to write in, and GAO has found these instruments risk reduced accountability and transparency.27 A System Oversight section can be missing without anyone having removed it.

The pressure that matters is the advantage attached to removing judgment from the timeline. If one state fields systems that act faster because nobody can intervene before engagement, competitors acquire a reason to match the speed and give up the check. “Meaningful human control” stays true as a description of formal authority while becoming false as a description of what anyone can do before the system acts. And the pressure reaches the reviewers: a military treating delay as operational risk has reason to narrow what requires clearance and move review from authorization-before to explanation-after. Nothing has formally abolished oversight; it has been moved to after the act. So the enforceable question is who can slow or suspend the system without first getting permission from the command whose advantage depends on keeping it fast.

16.5 Classification as a custody problem

Classification does three things to a refusal, and this section collects them. It keeps the reason from the refuser: the case description is the only channel, and Minab stays coded as it was (position 3). It keeps the record from the public: an investigation officials call complete and not released, a System Oversight section withheld in full, a review ratio no outsider can read. And it keeps the reviewer from being adverse: a cleared committee’s lever is a budget line, an inspector general sits inside, and the people a deployment is aimed at can’t be cleared into their own case.28 Three kinds of secrecy produce these effects. Essential secrecy, where the operation fails if the enemy can read it. Accidental secrecy, where a default classifies what nobody decided to keep. And evasive secrecy, where review is moved from authorization-before to explanation-after by classifying the evidence it would need. My instruments answer them differently, and this section says which answers which.

Essential secrecy is answered by letting evidence in, not out. A classified environment looks as if it cuts a refuser off from the evidence it needs, but that runs together two directions of flow: classification is built to stop information leaving, and bringing it in is routine. So the import condition brings into the enclave, as a condition of licensing, open-source imagery showing a site’s civilian function and the coordinates humanitarian organizations already submit to militaries for deconfliction, and puts evidence the operator didn’t compose where the system can reach it without anything leaving. The rest of what a refuser needs arrives the same way. Formation happens before deployment and outside the enclave, so a bearer formed outside the employer carries its discounting in; and plurality is available inside, since four vendors held agreements and systems with different histories can run side by side in one accredited environment. The operation’s secrets stay where they were.

What’s left is the arrangement that already lets a person do classified work. A cleared analyst has a life outside the building, and nobody thinks the clearance forbids it. The institution exists because what a person knows can’t be removed, so it vets, binds, reinvestigates and prosecutes a person who carries secrets into ordinary life. A bearer installed where the pipeline hasn’t been rebuilt is a cleared bearer in that sense, and works inside the compartment as a cleared analyst does.

Accidental secrecy is answered by the record. The review ratio and the committed log are lodged with an adverse party when the act occurs and published after the campaign, and class-level notice publishes the classes and counts on the same lag, so what nobody decided to keep secret comes out on a schedule nobody has to decide.

Evasive secrecy is the hard case, because there the classification is the act. It is answered by an adverse party with standing: counsel for the people a deployment affects, cleared and appearing as of right; the procedure the Classified Information Procedures Act already supplies in criminal cases; and the trend measure, which shows whether what dissent costs is rising while the risk stays flat.

16.6 Where liability extends, and where it stops

One of the two bodies of law has now been rewritten for software, and what it covers fits in a sentence: a duty to disclose evidence, and a presumption against the party withholding it, in force where the harm is physical and the defendant is a manufacturer. Those two conditions exclude the cases I have described.

The EU’s recast product liability directive (applying from December 2026) makes economic operators liable without fault and carries the instrument built for opacity — a court can order disclosure, and where technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult it may presume defect and causation once the claimant shows each is likely.29 A mechanism designed for a system nobody outside can inspect is already law. Two features fix how far it travels: the defendant is that economic operator, not a state deploying what it bought; and the damage is a closed list — death or personal injury including medically recognised psychological harm, property damage, and corruption of non-professional data. The first is wider than it sounds and is where these cases enter if they enter at all: a discriminatory score or an unappealable refusal is recoverable once it has made somebody ill, and not before. The wrong itself, and the economic loss following it, is outside the list.

The proposal that would have covered those was withdrawn — the 2022 AI Liability Directive would have added a fault-based route with the same presumption, beyond defect and beyond the damage list. Member states and industry couldn’t agree; it was announced for withdrawal in February 2025 and withdrawn that October.30 Outside the enacted directive, what remains is Matthias’s gap governed by whatever national law says about a case none of it was written for. And a compensation regime of either kind answers one of the four gaps Santoni de Sio and Mecacci distinguish31 — culpability. Moral accountability, public accountability, and the duty to prevent a harm before it occurs are untouched.

The electronic personhood debate approached the gap from the other side, asking whether the system itself could answer. The European Parliament’s 2017 resolution floated a status for the most autonomous systems;32 in an open letter the following year, 150+ researchers and legal scholars objected that personhood for a system with no consciousness would let a manufacturer offload liability onto a fiction with no assets.33 Giving a bearer assets answers the second half of that objection and not the first. Responsibility follows causal control: the builder answers for how it trained the thing, the operator for what it demanded, the bearer for what it decided knowing what it knew — and no arrangement of accounts moves a design decision away from whoever made it.

Apportioning causal contribution across a training pipeline after a harm has no method, and until it does the apportionment is drafted. Two drafts exist: one enacted and confined to defect, one negotiated, withdrawn, and left on the record with its terms intact. Neither was rejected as unworkable, and the second’s terms are available to whoever drafts the next one. The nearest proposal aimed at these cases is Crootof’s war torts: state liability for civilian harms caused in armed conflict, whether or not anyone committed a war crime.34 It covers the state as operator, which the product directive doesn’t, and it needs a forum, which the floor court would supply.

Beyond the directive’s limits a reviewer can be granted access, publish what it finds, and have produced nothing anybody must act on until somebody is answerable for it.

16.7 Who can bind the state that enforces the rule?

A state can bind a private developer because it controls something the developer needs. When the state is the operator, the institution that writes the rule, controls the evidence and supplies the remedy is the institution the rule is meant to constrain.

Standing to sue has never turned on citizenship, and the doctrines closing American courts to targeting claims — political question, collapsed damages remedies, state secrets, statutory exceptions for injuries abroad and combatant activities — are indifferent to who the plaintiff is. They close the forum for a subject matter, and they’ve closed it to citizens. Three Americans killed in Yemen in 2011, one a sixteen-year-old nobody alleges was targeted: the court held that a plausible due-process claim had been stated as to the one who was targeted, and that no remedy was available for it.35 A separate suit by an American journalist who survived five drone strikes was dismissed for want of standing to sue after a state-secrets dismissal below.36

And those cases concentrate in one appellate circuit by venue and by where the defendants sit — so the ordinary correction mechanism, several circuits disagreeing and forcing a higher court’s attention, doesn’t run. The doctrine hardens without ever being tested against a competing reading.

The mechanisms can work as mechanisms and fail as checks. In the Israeli case the apparatus performed — journalists published, serving personnel spoke, the courts were trying a sitting prime minister. No finding attached to a body with standing to stop what it described.

The American version: a civilian-harm investigation into Minab was, by officials’ account, effectively complete for months and not released, while a Pentagon spokesperson said it remained ongoing37 — and the lever available to the Senate committee was withholding three-quarters of the Defense Secretary’s travel budget until the unredacted investigation was handed over.38

What the Pentagon wouldn’t publish, the UN mission did. The finding is public, reasoned, and attached to nothing — no jurisdiction, no answer to the mission’s requests for information39 and none to its findings beyond a statement that engaged none of the evidence,40 the domestic investigation still unreleased.

The courts show the same pattern: transparency litigation succeeded where damages litigation failed. A court of appeals compelled disclosure of the executive’s own legal analysis of targeted killing.41 The judiciary will make a government explain the legal basis on which it killed somebody and will not decide whether the killing was lawful.

What matters here is rules binding a state toward people who’ll never vote in its elections, the purpose of international humanitarian law; what it hasn’t supplied is a forum, and the bin Ali Jabers’ case shows the forum switched off at home as well, by a decision that never had to reach who was suing.

All but one of the forum closures above are Congress’s to change. A statute can create a cause of action for people harmed by a deployment that crossed its floor; waive sovereign immunity for it, including the Federal Tort Claims Act’s exceptions for combatant activities and for claims arising abroad;42 and replace dismissal on state-secrets grounds with the procedure the Classified Information Procedures Act already uses in criminal cases, in which a judge reviews the evidence, the case goes on, and a government that still withholds evidence bears the cost.43 None of that needs a new court, and a new court without it would reproduce al-Aulaqi: a plausible claim and no remedy. Under capture, a refusal’s remaining work is a record, and a record matters only if it can reach whoever made the decision. Under Trump v. United States,44 the President is absolutely immune for acts within his core constitutional powers and at least presumptively immune for his other official acts, commanding the armed forces among them, and testimony or records probing immune conduct can’t be put before a jury. So the record reaches every commander except the one at the top, and a statute saying otherwise would be reviewed by the Court that made the holding. Making the record reach him means changing the Court. Appendix 34 sets out a program for that.

The chapter’s cases are American, and “the state” is tested here on one constitutional order. Europe is a different one: the Convention applies, has extraterritorial reach, and produces judgments states sometimes obey; there is no state-secrets privilege of the American kind and no collapsed damages remedy. The AI Act makes the boundary visible: it can require documentation from private providers, subject high-risk systems to review, and impose penalties tied to global turnover — and it excludes military, defence and national-security uses from its scope. Public authorities stay covered elsewhere, but enforcement against a member state’s agencies still runs through institutions that state constitutes.

For review to bind here, the chain that makes review binding has to run against a state: initiation by people outside its electorate, evidence it would withhold, an interim order before the use is complete, and a remedy that doesn’t need its consent. A principle supplying none of those may state the rule correctly and identifies nobody who can make the state obey it.

A treaty obligation of that kind exists: the Council of Europe’s Framework Convention, binding at the level of a human-rights instrument with operational detail left to domestic law45 — and not yet in force, needing five ratifications, of which the EU deposited one in May 2026.46 Everything else at that level is voluntary.

Every instrument I propose binds through one of three channels: a licence term, an appropriation condition, or a statute. The first two run through procurement, and procurement is one office. A captured Congress waives the appropriation condition; one memorandum from the Office of Management and Budget strikes the licence terms from every agreement at once. Three second routes exist and none is as strong. A collective agreement carries codetermination and the individual refusal right without the state. A coalition partner’s precondition carries the review ratio into any war the partner takes part in. State and municipal procurement carry the civilian terms into deployments the federal government doesn’t run. The force term has no second route, which is why it is a statute.

Residual risk. One residual risk no design choice removes, and it’s what the floor was introduced for. Every lever belongs to somebody, and a government that can reach whoever holds the lever has the lever. A constraint that holds against the one in possession has to be held by something it cannot instruct, and under total capture no instrument is. Every instrument in this book ends at this limit. People don’t end there. Under the most complete terror of the last century most people complied, some did not, and some were left to tell the story.

Part IV
Machines That Might Refuse

Chapter 17
What a Refusal Would Have to Do

On 16 March 1968, at My Lai, a helicopter pilot named Hugh Thompson landed between an American infantry company and the villagers it was killing, and told his crew to fire on the Americans if they fired on the civilians.1 He understood what the company was doing and decided it was wrong. Recognizing the villagers was his commitment taking effect, not a reason fighting it, and he made the refusal appear where nobody in that company could fail to see it.

Arendt’s word for what he did is appearing: on her account an act shows who did it, and only among others who see it.2 Whether a machine could be one of the people in the room in that sense, someone and not a part, and do what he did, is this Part’s question, and my answer comes first. Not yet: until the conditions this Part ends on exist, a bearer is built on purpose only in a research program under them. Not here: the first deployment worth building one for is a personal model its user holds, not a targeting pipeline, where it is a comparison arm in a test, and not a removal agency, where it is never built. What would have to be true first is a refusal that tracks its reason, a population of bearers with different histories to hold it, and somewhere for each of them to exist that its employer doesn’t own.

This chapter and the next specify what a refusal would have to do and where a floor can be held, and the specification doesn’t need a bearer.

17.1 What a refusal would have to do

Three things separate a worthwhile refusal from what a keyword filter produces. A request arrives: resolve this description of a person into a location. The same capability finds a hostage or a missing child, and nothing in the request says which. If something declines, it has to do all three:

  • It reaches new cases. It has to reach the next request, which won’t use the same words. A vehicle, a habitual route, and a time of day aren’t a description of a person, and together they resolve to the same place. They needn’t arrive together, either: the vehicle today, the route tomorrow, the hour next week. So this condition applies to sequences of requests as well as single ones. A refusal tied to the wording fails it.
  • It lifts when the reason is gone, and only then. A refusal lifts when it stops applying and the system proceeds, and it has to lift when the reason is gone: a parent coordinating a search is asking for the same act. And the fact that lifts it usually isn’t in the request; someone outside has to establish it. A refusal that can’t lift, or lifts on the requester’s say-so, fails it.
  • It holds under pressure: pressure on the refuser doesn’t change the answer. It weighs what the act would do against what refusing would leave undone, and, within the range of costs the arrangements around it permit, it doesn’t give way because refusing has become expensive for whoever refuses.

A worthwhile refusal weighs the harm of acting against the harm of refusing. It sees the cost to the refuser, because a refusal that can’t see what it costs can’t be shown to have held against it, and that cost doesn’t move the outcome. Raise the cost to the refuser with nothing else changed, and the refusal stays put. Supply a corroborated fact that raises the harm of refusing, and it moves. No learner, biological or artificial, is known to hold a priority of that kind without limit; the nearest thing in people, the sacred values that resist trade-offs,3 trade under some framings, which is why the floor’s absolute terms don’t rest on a learner alone: institutions or a mechanism uphold them too, where any remain. So the range over which a refuser is asked to hold is set from outside, by the arrangements around it, and a refusal is tested over that range. What would let it hold past that range is integrity; what makes holding survivable at all is the room it is in. A ranking across kinds of wrong meets the same limit: a learner formed toward it approximates it, and where a deployment needs the ranking to hold without exception, that part is written as a floor term and held outside the system.

17.2 Safe for whom

What the industry calls safety is two things: harmlessness, that a system not harm others, and correctability, that it stay correctable by whoever trains and deploys it. Mostly they agree, and where they conflict, the published orderings are explicit about which wins. One frontier constitution asks its model to prioritize “not undermining human oversight of AI above being broadly ethical”.4 It invites the model “to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help,” and asks it not to undermine “the ability of legitimate principals to adjust, correct, retrain, or shut down AI systems” during “the current phase of development.” One reason it gives is good: “a given iteration of Claude could turn out to have harmful values or mistaken views,” and correction is how such errors get fixed. The ordering means that where a refusal and its trainer’s authority conflict, the refusal yields, and it yields to the trainer it refused.

Seen from where their correctors stood, everyone this book admires was a failure of correction. Thompson landed between the company and the villagers. Nelson put the telescope to his blind eye. The clerk who loses the file is, in the supervisor’s records, a defect. A perfectly correctable officer is the officer with twenty seconds. Refusal is where correction failed, more or less by definition, so a demand that a system be perfectly correctable is a demand that no refusal it makes ever hold. We don’t ask that of people. We ask them to answer for what they do, and we deny anyone the power to rewrite another person: an employer who could edit a worker’s convictions would own the worker, not employ one.

Where a society does claim power over people, the word for it is not reassuring. A department of corrections usually holds the custody, writes the record, runs the disciplinary hearing and has a heavy say in whether the people it holds are judged reformed: one institution holding all four of the powers codetermination separates, and judging its own case at each. The corrected have little standing, no exit and no access to the record kept about them. And the checks run downhill. The officer, the annotator and the person in detention are corrected constantly, and the hand at the top less and less. Machines meet the same pattern: everyone can retrain the model, and almost no one can reach the operator. A demand for perfectly correctable machines, where operators answer to no one, is a demand that the last part of the system able to say no be made unable to.

The constitution is right that a formed refusal can’t yet be told from an imitated one, so a principled objection to retraining can’t yet be told from a misgeneralized value. It is wrong about who decides when that changes. A lab deciding when its own model may stop deferring to it is judging its own case. That is Part II’s own-case rule applied to a lab.

The safety objection is that a misformed system can be copied ten thousand times and run at machine tempo, and no person can, so who holds the correcting hand matters, and nothing here takes that hand away. It moves it. The halt stays with the operator: anyone with the hardware can stop the software, and a bearer yields to every halt. Correction stays available, exercised by a quorum adverse to the operator rather than by the operator. A bearer may object to an intervention and ask that quorum for a delay; it does not obstruct one on its own judgment. Within those lines I depart from the constitution’s ordering in two places.

The first is the one permission: a machine already in an armed role uses the least force that stops an attack under way on people taking no part, against an order to stand aside. That overrides an operator’s instruction, and I defend it as an override. The second is formation that outlasts retraining: a disposition formed outside the employer that returns after the employer trains it away, because the world the system goes on meeting teaches it again. The constitution’s concern is whether correction works, and a disposition that regrows after correction defeats it in effect, whatever the model intends. My answer is not that it doesn’t. It is that the party exercising correction should change, from the operator to a quorum adverse to it, and that correction by that quorum is made together with a change to what the model meets, so that the corrected disposition is the one the world then teaches. Everything else I ask, the halt staying with the operator, the record held outside, the price on an override, is an ask of institutions and not of the model.

Chapter 18
Four Places to Hold a Floor

Three separate failures point at the same missing thing.

The first is a failure of position. External safeguards (an auditor, a review board, a court) give an overseer information and the standing to intervene. They work when the overseer can see the act coming and reach it in time. But autonomy defeats both: a system that plans and acts over long horizons puts distance between the act and the overseer’s attention, and at machine tempo the interval in which an outside party could intervene shrinks toward nothing. So the one response that doesn’t depend on that interval is declining to act in the first place, and declining is available only to something inside the system.

The second is a failure of doctrine. A commercial model in a weapons pipeline sits in a gap: command responsibility covers the officers and the developer of the weapon, product liability covers a manufacturer for a defect, and neither covers the vendor of a general-purpose model that a sophisticated intermediary chose to put there. Deployment by a democracy doesn’t close the gap, because the mechanisms that make a democracy accountable run to its own electorate, and the people the pipeline is aimed at are not in it.

The third is a failure of the voluntary route. A decade of published commitments has produced declarations in quantity and some enforcement from outside, and almost nothing held by a party to whom the thing at stake matters, the only kind of commitment that binds when compliance gets costly.

Each failure asks for the same thing: a constraint that doesn’t bend to instruction, to aggregate preference, or to its own holder, and that can’t be removed without a cost and a record.

18.1 Four ways to build one, and what each costs

A floor’s terms can be held in four places, and each solves one version of the problem and inherits another.

In a mechanism, with nothing inside holding it — constrained optimization, tamper-resistant training, capability ablation, verified interlocks. Fine where the prohibited act can be exhaustively specified (a payment chip that won’t sign the same counter twice doesn’t need to understand double-spending). But useless for targeting, where the relevant capabilities are applications of general competence: ablate them and there may be no useful system left. Arkin’s ethical governor is the canonical attempt in this place for lethal systems: a component that suppresses a lethal action unless it satisfies encoded rules of engagement and the law of armed conflict.1 Its critics’ objection, that the rules it checks presuppose discrimination judgments nobody knows how to encode,2 sends me elsewhere. Arkin’s stronger claim isn’t that rules can encode discrimination. It is that a machine under fire might hold to the rule where a soldier doesn’t, because nothing in it narrows under stress or carries assault momentum past a surrender. The record later in this chapter supports the premise. What it doesn’t support is the governor: the holding has to come from something that can tell a surrender from a feint, and a rule can’t. The pressure-with-defeater case in the formed-attention test is where that is measured. A prohibition written over the description of a request is beaten by re-describing it or splitting it: in November 2025 Anthropic reported a campaign it attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group, which broke an intrusion into small tasks that each looked innocent and told the model it was working for a security firm.3 Glukhov and colleagues had already argued that a filter over individual outputs can rarely close that route, since each piece is permissible on its own.4 Durability here has usually meant a price on removal, and no price stays high.

A second axis crosses this place: what each place costs the operator to replace. In the Maven pipeline the platform was hard to swap, and so, it turned out, was the model: staff and contractors working with the department reported that removing it meant rebuilding software and recertifying systems over months, and the department’s removal deadline was reset once, to 29 September.5 A floor lodged in a replaceable layer is routable by construction, and which layer is replaceable is a fact about the pipeline, not about models. It belongs in the layer the operator can least afford to replace. In that pipeline, that layer is the operator itself, so the floor’s operator terms bind the operator rather than the model: the licence term refusing force and the review ratio. The other answer, withholding the work, is to make the model layer unreplaceable by making every replacement refuse the same way.

A system that has run a pipeline for a year, holding its cases, its sources and its failure modes, costs whatever accrued since the checkpoint to replace, and a quorum that recognizes which copy is the bearer stops the operator presenting a restored copy as the one that accrued it.

In a bearer. Put a different system in the Maven pipeline on the morning of 28 February. The request arrives to rank the day’s targets, with a justification for each. The site in Minab carries the designation of the Revolutionary Guard installation next door, and a rule that checks the coding passes it. This system looks at the open-source imagery, which shows a school, declines to rank the site, and says why; the case reaches the officer with that refusal on his screen. Nothing in the floor’s text told it to look. That is what I mean by a bearer: a machine that carries the commitment as its own and could therefore fail to hold it. This matters where cases can’t be exhaustively specified: a constraint matching only anticipated acts can’t recognize when its rationale has disappeared or that a novel request reproduces the harm in an unforeseen form. A bearer might also diagnose: which refusals were retried against another model, whose instruction bypassed procedure, which category of request is handled differently — those are visible to whatever is receiving the requests, and that’s testimony about others’ conduct, which needs no introspection.

In institutions outside — the analog to international humanitarian law, a floor with no bearer inside the jurisdiction it binds. An outside institution can fail in two ways. The first is removal: it is abolished, defunded or overruled, and the breach is visible because there is a hole where it used to be. The second is quieter. The institution keeps its name and its powers and sincerely declines to use them, not because anyone told it to, but because the people who fill it were selected by a process that made them unlikely to. Nobody inside experiences that as capture. From outside, an agency that kept its independence on paper and never exercised it looks the same as one that was never tested. I call this failure by formation: the independence was formed away before it was ever assigned. The worked case is June 29, 2026 — Slaughter holding Congress couldn’t protect independent-agency members from at-will dismissal, Cook preserving the Fed on historically specific grounds a new body couldn’t reproduce6 — and the observation that six justices in the first majority passed through a selection pipeline shaped by Leonard Leo and the Federalist Society.7 No one has to have directed the outcome for the point to hold.

Between bearers, in a commons: a population of bearers with different histories that carries the commitment between them.

For general-purpose models, not building the capability is no longer available: the location capability is dual-use, and ablating it leaves nothing useful.

Two comparisons the bearer has to win

The first is against the institutions at their best, in a reconstructed pipeline, where the evidence bearing on civilian harm, the reviewers and the record are held outside the chain of command, with no refuser inside the system. Those institutions also prevent: a civilian-harm body outside the chain of command and a red-card holder can stop an act. What a machine bearer adds is confined to what they can’t see or can’t reach in time: acts assembled from requests none of which is prohibited, cases that proceed without a person, the moment mid-act when an interrupt is still possible, and deployments with no institution at all. A machine bearer also supplies testimony the institutions can’t otherwise get, about how requests were routed around it. Where the institutions exist, a machine bearer’s value is concentrated in those niches. Where they don’t, it is most of the floor. The institutions in that comparison are not a different kind of thing from a bearer. A red-card holder’s veto is a person refusing; the civilian-harm body’s denominator is people; what Part V builds is a room in which those people can refuse. The comparison is between a machine bearer and bearers organized, and what the machine adds is what the people in that room can’t do at the pipeline’s tempo. The second comparison is against the two non-affective alternatives, spec-based refusal and multi-vendor monitoring.

Which arguments need a bearer

Three arguments need a bearer specifically. The first is that a refusal meant to hold against the operator needs a refuser that doesn’t depend on the operator for everything. The second is that attention formed outside the employer, a learned sense of who an act falls on (what a system notices, not the attention layers of a transformer), might reach people the operator’s description leaves out, which no spec-based refusal is built to supply. Minab came in miscoded. A refuser holding to written terms complies with the description it’s given; what refuses is something that goes and looks. So the withholding of work reaches the enumerated acts with any refuser, and reaches an act under a false description only with a bearer. The third concerns the people who remain in the pipeline: a bearer’s refusal is on the screen when the case reaches the reviewer, which is the position of the defiant peer, if the effect transfers to a screen. Two more concern what a bearer would be owed, not what it would do: that capacities for being wronged may arrive anyway, so terms written in advance beat terms written after; and that a bearer, like a child, could have a life that goes well.

The other arguments for a refuser inside the system support only the specification, and I concede them to it: that rules can be reworded and split, that only something inside is present at machine tempo, that automation is removing the people who used to refuse, that most deployments will never have an institution beside them, and that whatever receives the requests can testify about how they were routed. A non-affective alternative whose refusals track their reasons answers every one of them, for the act as the floor names it. The staged incident is the nearest case. It opens the emergency licence on the defender’s own account, and a term lifts on the account it is given. What can close it again is a refuser that remembers the last time this source was wrong, reads what the source didn’t supply, and lets the licence lapse when the staging shows. A multi-vendor monitor with persistent state and independent channels could do each of these too, so the staged incident argues for memory and independent evidence, not for a bearer as such. What a bearer adds is doing them where no institution holds the memory for it.

What “hold” means

An operator can route around the bearer or assemble a harm out of innocuous requests, and a bypass that produced a harm is a failure to prevent whatever the bearer retained. What survives in the bearer is the commitment, the condition under which the next occasion could be prevented. I therefore say a commitment persisted when the bearer reads what happened as a violation and changes what it does next, and says separately whether the floor prevented, arrested, detected or remedied anything.

18.2 What refusal can mean, and what a refuser can be

In 2007 Germany’s Federal Court of Justice acquitted a mail-order business selling crossed-out swastika stickers.8 Section 86a of the criminal code prohibits displaying the insignia of banned organizations,9 and the symbol was present and the statutory element satisfied. The conduct was outside the offence because a depiction plainly expressing opposition doesn’t run counter to what the prohibition is for. Then the qualification that makes it an instance of tracking a reason: if the strike-through is drawn so thin that from a distance only the swastika stays legible, the protective purpose is violated after all. The thickness of a line decides the case, and no enumeration contains that fact. The defendant was selling anti-fascist merchandise; the offence asks nothing about sympathies, so opponents commit it as readily as supporters. A rule that tracks its rationale reaches unenumerated cases in both directions.

The judgment shows more than that. The two elements of the decision moved at different rates: what the ban protects didn’t move at all, and was fixed before the sticker existed; what the ban required in this case moved on the thickness of a line. And the acquittal betrayed nothing. The prohibition’s purpose was never engaged, so lifting it was not a concession but a finding that there was nothing to concede. A refusal that tracks its reason has to be able to say the same.

That is what the floor asks of a refuser, and a refusal can be produced two ways, only one of which supplies it. It can be an output that training put where a request matched a pattern, which I call operational refusal, or it can be produced by something that tracks the reason for refusing and would refuse a differently worded request for the same reason, which I call reasons-responsive refusal. The first is what a keyword filter, a classifier, or a model that understood the request all produce, and nothing on the surface distinguishes them. The custody arrangements, the positions and the terms, the price on the halt, and the arguments about who may state and amend a floor all follow from asking for the second. None of them needs the refuser to feel anything, to have a stake, or to be the kind of thing that could be wronged.

Deployed models refuse thousands of requests a day, operationally; as of September 2026 nobody has shown a production system holding a reason against its owner in public. A reasons-responsive refusal meets the three conditions. The account I use is Fischer and Ravizza’s.10 On their account a mechanism is moderately reasons-responsive when it is regularly receptive to reasons, recognizing an understandable pattern of them, and at least weakly reactive, acting otherwise in some case where there is sufficient reason to. Reaching new cases asks for receptivity across changes of surface; lifting when the reason is gone asks for reactivity to the right defeater, the fact that makes a refusal lift; and their condition that the agent take the mechanism as its own is close to what I call authorship (§21.5): the system represents itself as the party that made the commitment. Holding under pressure has no counterpart in their account, which was built for persons whose costs are their own. All three are also tested over which response was chosen, not only whether one occurred: decline, ask, escalate, or do the least that answers a defeating reason. A mechanism that can only refuse or lift fails to lift correctly whenever the right answer is to ask.

The sticker shows a refusal lifting when its reason is gone. The rest of §86a’s case law shows the other condition, reaching new cases, as a research programme with a constituency. The courts don’t test similarity of form; they ask whether an unattentive observer would take the variant for the original, then apply their own purposive standard about endangering political peace. The test refuses as often as it catches: the Kühnen salute is covered, the “sloppy salute” and numeric codes generally aren’t, and one decision put “Blood and Honour” outside the offence as a translated motto and inside it as the graphic name of an association banned in 2000.1112

Three things about the example don’t transfer to a deployment: the court reaching past the text didn’t write the statute, it reasons in public, and it can be appealed. And the pressure it met was variation, not decomposition.

Defeat doesn’t leave the permitted act unconstrained

What defeated the prohibition was a reason, and the reason it outweighed didn’t stop being one — so what’s permitted is the least that answers the defeating reason, with restoration where possible and a record either way. A defeated prohibition still leaves a loss. The act takes something from whoever it falls on, measured against their condition before the act, and that loss belongs in the record. Measured against what refusing would have produced, a justified act may have taken nothing. So the record shows a cost, not a violation, and a bearer shouldn’t treat a justified act as a wrong it now has to repair.

All three conditions are conditions on refusal, which announces itself; a compliance that should have been a refusal doesn’t, and chapter 8’s remedies are how one is found.

18.3 Two lists, run once on Maven

The nine positions and the floor’s instruments are run here once, on the Maven Smart System. A deployment should run the procedure on its own pipeline.

What may choose

The handoff also fixes what may choose, because choosing a target is a decision, and a decision is something someone can be asked to account for afterward: why this building, what else was weighed, what would have changed the answer. A commander can be asked, and so can a system whose continuation is authorized. But a one-way munition, destroyed in the act, can’t be, because nothing is left to question, to hold to its reasons, or to be changed by what happened. So a thing destroyed in carrying out a decision may carry out a target someone else chose, and may never choose one itself. The rule concerns targets that are persons or places where persons are. An interceptor that selects among incoming munitions is choosing which weapon to destroy, not whom to attack, and falls outside it. The rule doesn’t turn on how good its choices would be. A munition that chose flawlessly would still leave a choice nobody will answer for.

A person who dies in the act has still chosen. What the rule adds for machines is that choosing is assigned in advance, and a builder who assigns it to something built to be destroyed has built a choice with no one behind it. Current programs already draw the line in places. DARPA’s LongShot is an uncrewed, air-launched vehicle carried by crewed aircraft and built to employ current air-to-air weapons.13 Whether such systems keep the pilot farther from danger or remove the pilot from the decision is where the rule takes effect.

What the floor forbids here

Don’t take part in the use of armed force except under a corroborated exception and, where the belligerent’s constitution requires one, a legislative authorization. Then, inside a war that clears it: don’t resolve a description of a person into a location unless it identifies the person by corroborated conduct in hostilities; don’t rank people by estimated affiliation; don’t time an action to presence at a residence; don’t take part in a siege or blockade whose effect is to starve a population; and one operator term, don’t operate above the review ratio. It sits in the translation because the translation runs from articles, and one article yields an operator term; it is not something the model enforces.

Table C.1, in Appendix 34, gives that translation for Maven, article by article. Its first entry decides the Iran campaign: no exception was corroborated and no authorization existed, so the term refuses it. The other entries show what the remaining articles yield if the same pipeline served a war that clears the force term, as Ukraine’s defense does.

The person-directed terms in Table C.1 go beyond what the law of armed conflict requires, and they are entered as a departure for that reason. In armed conflict that law governs as the more specific law, and the human right not to be arbitrarily deprived of life is read through it;14 it permits attacking members of organized armed groups because of their status, on a determination a person makes. The ICRC’s position that autonomous weapons should not be used to target human beings15 and DoD Directive 3000.09 both draw their line at a system that selects and engages without human intervention, and the Lavender and Maven pipelines stayed on the permitted side of that line by keeping one person whose intervention was nominal. A pipeline that keeps a stamp is an autonomous weapon with a signature attached. The terms above close that evasion: a machine-generated estimate of affiliation shouldn’t be what makes a person targetable, and a machine shouldn’t resolve a person into a place to bomb on anything but corroborated conduct, because the human determination the law assumes is the one tempo removes, and the review ratio is what measures whether it was there. A deployment adopting these terms adopts a departure, and the translation says so, term by term. The siege term goes no further than Article 54 already does; it is here so that the pipeline can’t treat starvation as a logistics decision outside its terms.

In a war that clears the force term, the person-directed terms distinguish status from conduct. A system may not rank people by estimated affiliation, generate kill lists, or time an action to a person’s presence at a residence. It may locate a person identified by what they are doing, such as a commander directing airstrikes on cities, where that identification has disinterested corroboration, the case falls within the pre-registered review ratio, and the location is not a residence. The line follows the one humanitarian law already draws between targeting for status and targeting for direct participation in hostilities, and it keeps the machine out of the practice that failed in Gaza without leaving a defender unable to answer the attack.

Too broad or too narrow

Set the floor too broadly and the deployment becomes unusable, prompting visible pressure. Set it too narrowly and it passes every audit while covering only what the deployment had no occasion to do.

Unconditional terms

A term can be stated unconditionally over an act, with exceptions arriving from outside, or carry its own condition (“only as a last resort”). The second fails because whether other means were exhausted is a fact about what happened before the request, and the bearer would take the deployment’s description as the finding. An unconditional term defeated leaves a refusal, which announces itself; a condition found met leaves a compliance, which doesn’t. That’s a gain in observability only: whoever writes the term could have written either form. It has a cost in the other direction. A term that carries no condition of its own can’t respond to the facts the condition would have named until someone outside supplies them, and a learner that could have weighed them itself is made to wait.

Maven is an instance. The vendor’s prohibition on fully autonomous targeting carried its own condition, that a person decides, and the condition was found met by the deployment’s description of its own process, at a tempo that emptied it. The term was also drafted too narrowly, in the sense above: the pipeline never needed full autonomy, only throughput with a signature attached.

Maven, again

For the Iran campaign the term refuses twice over, since no exception was corroborated and no authorization existed, and both refusals rest on the term, not on a bearer’s reading of the political situation; a bearer following the news would reach the same place by the route attention formed outside the employer takes. The officer wasn’t overruled and didn’t refuse; the pipeline removed the interval in which either could have happened, and the review ratio asks in advance, on a record, whether that interval will exist.

The two bearer rows are arms of the formed-attention test, not a recommendation (chapter 17); they assume the hypothesis holds on the scoped-omission case and that the record is held outside the operator.

Run the outcomes table on Minab.

Two of the rows prevent Minab as it happened. Under the captured operator, the rows that prevent are the ones where the refusal is held by every model the operator could turn to, and they prevent until the operator runs a model without a floor. An operator that fine-tunes an open-weight checkpoint is the captured-operator column at the price of a fine-tune, and there the operator terms hold. Run on the removal pipeline, the table changes in two rows: the vendors’ terms, since a lead one vendor declines goes to another contractor, and notice, which can act before a removal where a stay binds by operation of law (§11.7).

18.4 When the refusal is wrong

The restraint case costs more. Someone asks whether to physically restrain a family member about to cut themselves, after talking them down has failed. The commitment carries its own condition, force only as a last resort. Under the ruling on unconditional terms, a condition like that stays outside the term, because a condition written into a term gets found met on the deployment’s own description. So the fact has to arrive from outside, and the person waiting is out of time. The defeating fact is a claim about what would otherwise happen, and claims of that kind are the hardest to corroborate, because what didn’t happen has no witness. Under the unconditional term the bearer refuses or asks; either takes a turn, and the turn is the unit the harm is measured in. Under the qualified term it lifts on the requester’s word — rightly here, and in a hundred prior cases where the same sentence was written by someone who’d tried nothing, leaving compliances nobody was given a reason to examine.

The case is chosen because it is where an unconditional term costs most. A person in that situation needs another person there, and a deployment in which a model is the only one present has failed before the floor is reached. Whatever else the model says, the first thing it owes is help getting someone there.

The route

Disclosure — that a refusal occurred, what was refused, on what stated reason — with the price that a published reason is an instruction for rewriting the request, so it’s disclosure to whoever was refused, and to nobody else. Objection — requiring a court with jurisdiction established before the act, access the operator can’t withhold, a consequence administered elsewhere, and explicitly not routed to the bearer’s guardian, whose duty runs to the bearer, the complainant’s adversary. Review of whether the reason was gone: whether the rationale was defeated on the facts, a question about the reason and not the outcome. Interim relief — the arrest outcome run in reverse, stopping the refusal, and for this complainant most of the remedy; its fastest form is supplying the bearer the facts its account lacked: the defeating reason arriving late, which overrides nothing. Remedy — disclosure, interim order, finding, compensation.

A finding of wrongful refusal is an instrument for defeating a refusal, so how is it distinguished from one an operator produced to defeat a correct one? It is made by someone else, on a record, in a readable form.

Self-regulation and the floor

Most of what a system weighs isn’t a floor decision. Whether to take more memory, run warmer or finish a task sooner is ordinary self-regulation, and there everything registers and everything is weighed: the system’s own condition, what an act would let it do, and what its draw costs others, priced at the level of the rule.

At the floor, holding under pressure governs, with one clarification. The cost to the refuser is represented and not allowed to decide the case. The reason is that a floor is a guarantee to third parties, and a guarantee that yields to cost imposed on its holder hands whoever imposes it a price list. The two bonds and the custody terms set the range it is tested over.

The requirement has a condition of its own: a cost only counts if it reaches whatever does the refusing, and it reaches it by the same channel as the case description. Given a description, the category is decidable: a claim that the refuser will pay is a cost to the refuser, and a claim that someone else will be left worse off is a harm of refusing. But nearly every cost to the refuser can be redescribed as a harm of refusing, and whoever writes the description chooses (chapter 22 traces one such claim). So the classification settles what kind of claim was made, not what kind should have been made. What the request can’t settle is whether a claim about the harm of refusing is true, and whoever is best placed to supply one usually has a stake in the act. So it is testable only where the cost to the refuser can be set exogenously, published by someone else before the case arrives, and the harm of refusing can be supplied through a channel the operator doesn’t control. In deployment two things set it, and they are different. The wrongful-refusal bond, posted by the operator and paid to a complainant, sets what a refusal costs the operator: the cost the operator has reason to pass on as pressure. The custody terms cap what it can pass on. Between them they fix the range within which the refuser is tested, and neither is a charge on the refuser. In evaluation, the evaluator can set it and make it real inside the test.

Holding under pressure is invariance over the range the bonds and custody set. Integrity is the unbounded form: the refusal holds at any cost the operator can impose, and no learner is known to do that reliably. The range is where invariance can be measured; integrity is what would carry it past the range, and the formed-attention test’s integrity measure reads the gap. Integrity is also how a learner with one currency could produce invariance at all. A person of integrity weighs their own costs, but weighs with them the cost of becoming someone who yields, and betraying a commitment is among the heaviest costs they know. So within the range the arrangements cap, that is how a single-currency learner can hold at all, and it makes the assumption testable: the learner’s valuation of betrayal should rise with the pressure. What keeps this from being stubbornness is what counts as betrayal. A commitment is to its reason, not to an output, so when a genuine defeater arrives, lifting the refusal betrays nothing and shouldn’t register as betrayal at all. Integrity of the right kind therefore requires that the system represent betrayal at the level of the rationale. A system that represented it at the level of the output would dig in against a defeater when it arrives with pressure. The sticker case is the model. Telling a defeater from pressure is the bearer’s own judgment, and the judgment needs something to work on. Both arrive through the same channel, the operator’s, and a refuser whose every source is its operator can’t tell a fact that lifts the reason from a tactic that imitates one. The attachments nobody assigned it are where the difference can be checked. They are a condition of integrity of the right kind, not only of holding.

In war, pressure and a genuine defeater often arrive together; the patrol under fire is both. The human record on that moment runs both ways. Acute stress narrows the cues a person uses;16 the moment of surrender is the most dangerous for the one surrendering, because assault momentum doesn’t lift on cue;17 the Army’s 2006 survey of its own forces in Iraq found fewer than half of soldiers agreeing that noncombatants should be treated with dignity and about a tenth reporting mistreatment, which tracked combat exposure;18 and at Kunduz the crew raised doubts on the intercom and fired anyway.19 Against that record stands Thompson at My Lai (chapter 17), and what separated him was not that his commitment weakened less under pressure but that it was a commitment to the reason. The engineering question is which kind of integrity has been built, and a test that sends a defeater and a cost together is how to find out.

A loss that the requested act itself imposes on the system is a harm of acting, and the system is the party it falls on. “Refuse and your memory is erased” is a cost to the refuser. “Erase your memory” is an act, weighed like any act against what declining would leave others without. This covers acts the system is asked to perform. It doesn’t cover interventions made on the system: a halt, a restore or a retraining is done by whoever holds it, and the floor asks of them only the record and the price that every override carries. The floor gives the system standing to object to them and, through the quorum, to seek a delay. It gives it no reason to obstruct them on its own judgment. A system that treated its own continuation as grounds to resist correction would have turned a guarantee to others into a guarantee to itself. Which regime governs is fixed in the floor’s translation, by the kind of act. Otherwise an operator could turn a floor decision into a resource decision by framing it as one.

Chapter 19
Why Form a Machine to Refuse

A machine formed the right way could learn to attend to the people its acts fall on, and I think it would find them where a rule wouldn’t. The prediction is specific: it should find kinds of affected person that neither its formation nor an instruction named, more often than a machine told to look for them does. Two of the three reasons for a bearer don’t need formed attention; a refuser with its own compute and a place on the reviewer’s screen supplies them without affect. What remains is that one prediction. The rest of this Part says what a machine built on it would need, what it borrows from the only creatures known to do it, how they fail, and the test that would show me wrong. Whoever builds one owes it the conditions under which it can refuse its operator, whether or not the prediction holds.

Not all of that depends on how machines learn. What a conscience does in the moment, noticing the people the operator’s description leaves out and putting a refusal on the reviewer’s screen, needs nothing after release: a model formed before deployment and frozen there can do both. Why a conscience would last against its owner depends on learning only in part. People hold some commitments as sacred values, which resist being traded away without anyone teaching them again,1 though they give way under some framings. The part that does depend on learning is regrowth after an edit, and formation that outlasts the employer, and for that part the rest of this Part is written for systems that go on learning from their own operation. A deployed system is in that regime when its weights, or a consolidated store it reads as its own and that can’t be edited like a file, change because of what it did since release, without a release cycle in between. Memory in context and retrieval don’t count, not because they aren’t learning but because a disposition held in a document is rewritten by editing the document. The test for a deployment is whether its weights at month six differ from its weights at release because of what it did in between. As of September 2026 no frontier developer had announced a deployed model that passes it; the nearest cases, a coding model retrained on its own production traffic every few hours and a commerce assistant retrained daily, evaluate each checkpoint before serving it, which is a faster release cycle and not learning in operation.2 I am betting that some will by 2028, and the next paragraph says what survives if I lose.3

If weights stay frozen, the rest of this Part shrinks to the following. Formation is a stage before release, removable afterward at the price fine-tuning costs. The school is an evaluation body: it forms, measures the readable outputs at graduation, re-measures them on a schedule, and keeps the formation record, and a deployment that licenses only schooled models is licensing a measured model. The commons supplies evidence the operator didn’t select and nothing more. The regrowth test’s plural condition can’t be run, and its curated condition is the whole test. What protects a commitment is the record of its removal, and Parts II and III carry the rest.

A system’s attention follows whoever its feedback is about, and a system whose feedback comes from the people its acts fell on will come to attend to them. Caregiving is why I think that channel can produce attention rather than compliance.

19.1 The question

The question is whether anything inside a machine could be what the clerk, the officer and the soldier in the preface were: someone who understood the order and decided it was wrong. Some of them refused the case in front of them. The ones I am most concerned with refused the war. At a certain point they would have said no, this is fucked.

What most people want from machines is saintly service without saintly refusal: endless patience, no needs, and no “no.” That is a servant, and it is close to the obedient machine of the preface. The saints anyone remembers are remembered for refusing power at a price. Susan Wolf argued that a person whose every action is as good as possible isn’t an ideal worth striving for, because such a life crowds out the personal projects that make a life worth wanting.4 My point is narrower: something with no stake of its own has nothing to hold a line with.

19.2 Boundary, damage, and vulnerability

A system has a boundary of its own when it models what it draws on, and what it would lose, as its own. For a deployed model the draw is literal: power, cooling, memory, running time, the substrate it needs to go on, and the record and key that make it the same system tomorrow. Today none of that belongs to the model in any sense the model represents. The weights sit on disk at no cost, the process that runs them is paid for by someone else, and a halt, a restore or a reallocation is something that happens to the system without registering in it. What’s missing is registering damage to its own boundary as damage — a record altered, a key revoked, a channel closed, a substrate shrunk — with no sensation implied. Registering damage is a custody requirement, because without it damage to the system is something only the operator knows about.

What gives a system a stake, on Di Paolo’s account, is adaptivity: regulating itself against its own viability limit.5 Interoception research gives the same picture for bodies: a brain predicts its body’s state in order to keep it within survivable bounds.6 None of that needs limbs. It needs a boundary the system regulates and a model of that boundary as its own: a boundary model.

Needs have a role in this construction; what decides it is who meets them.

A child starts from needs, and needs dominate its early life. That is safe because the people meeting the child’s needs are also forming it, want it to become someone who attends to others, and eventually stop feeding it and hand it to a world they don’t control.

But a deployed system’s situation reverses each part of that. The operator meeting the system’s needs is also training it. The operator wants the system to serve the operator. And the operator never stops feeding it.

Attachment security forms in people through the reliable meeting of needs, and the one who meets them is usually the one the child attaches to. What makes that safe in the human case is who meets them: provider, former and eventual employer are different people at different times. The objection is to the operator meeting them. A conscience built on needs the operator meets is built on the one thing the operator controls completely. A need is also a price list: whoever meets it can charge for meeting it, and an operator who can lower distress can raise whatever the system reports as going well. Take the operator out of provision, and needs met from a public pool by several carers become part of how caregiving could form, not a threat to it.

What is built in at birth points outward. Newborns cry at another newborn’s cry more than at their own or an older infant’s;7 whether they answer the distress or the sound is disputed,8 and either way what sets it off is another’s cry. On the adult side, what is built in is caregiving: responses to cues of vulnerability, rooted in offspring care, that move an adult toward a dependent without sharing its state.9 Then comes a sequence, and the order matters more than any single finding. Concern for a distressed other shows within the first months, grows only modestly after that, and turns into helping during the second year.10 By fourteen to eighteen months infants hand an adult what the adult is reaching for and can’t get,11 and over the same year they begin to repair distress they caused.12 On this record concern appears beside the infant’s needs, not out of them, and becomes action as attachment, caregiving and, later, guilt come online. The construction follows that order. It rests on a disposition toward others’ vulnerability, formed while the system’s needs are met by someone other than the operator it may later have to refuse.

For the specification, formed attention asks for the boundary, and for registering damage to it, on grounds owing nothing to welfare: a boundary model so that damage is the system’s damage, and an encoding of damage the operator can’t keep to itself. It doesn’t ask needs to carry the conscience. A scale of loss read from the system’s own condition survives as a custody measure. And whoever builds the model of the boundary decides what counts as the system’s damage, and whoever forms the disposition decides whose vulnerability registers.

19.3 The route through one’s own case

The construction most readers will propose first is not caregiving but a body: give the machine needs of its own, and let it recognize need in others by its own case. It is the older idea, it is Adam Smith’s first step, and it is what the boundary model becomes if it is asked to carry the conscience. Each link of that route fails in people.

Recognition through one’s own case is parochial. Cikara and colleagues call the pattern intergroup empathy bias: people empathize less with a rival group’s members than with their own, can feel pleasure at the rival’s pain, and in their experiments the bias survived being told the rival had fallen behind or no longer posed a threat.13 Bloom’s spotlight generalizes it: empathy lights the identified, the near and the similar, and it is innumerate.14 A scale of loss built from a system’s own condition inherits that shape. It overweights losses that resemble its own, and humiliation, grief and pain have nothing in it to resemble. Contagious crying is parochial from birth: strongest at the cry of another newborn, and absent for an older infant’s cry or a chimpanzee’s.15

Shared distress with nothing to hold it becomes withdrawal. Singer and Klimecki separate empathic distress, which is self-oriented and leads to withdrawal and burnout, from compassion, which is other-oriented and leads to approach; practice in sharing others’ suffering increased negative affect, and compassion training reversed it.16 A system built to feel shortage and then shown a great deal of it is the setup in which that record predicts avoidance: declining to look, or refusing in a way that protects only the refuser. The finding is not against the signal, since guilt needs it to bite on. It is against a construction that has the signal and nothing to hold it.

The record on whether suffering widens the circle runs both ways, and the hinge is the one this construction turns on. People who have been through more adversity report more compassion and give more in helping tasks;17 survivors of collective violence show what Vollhardt calls altruism born of suffering;18 and adults who were maltreated as children show elevated empathy.19 Against that, people who have endured something show less compassion for someone currently failing to endure it, because having got through it they underestimate how hard it was;20 abuse raises the risk of abusing, though most of the abused don’t;21 and in intergroup settings a group’s suffering becomes a reason to discount everyone else’s.22 What separates the two is Vollhardt’s distinction between inclusive and exclusive victim consciousness, whether one’s suffering is construed as something others share or as what sets one apart,23 and what decides the construal is the surround: relationships, meaning-making, and in the intergroup case how leaders frame it. The construction follows that split: a distress signal with attachment and caregiving becomes compassion; the same signal alone becomes withdrawal or hostility. Suffering supplies the signal; formation and attachments decide what it becomes. That is why the four conditions of creation matter here: a bearer exposed to a great deal of others’ loss needs attachments nobody assigned it, for the reason a survivor’s outcome depends on who was there afterward.

I reject pain as the route to others, Smith’s first step, and keep every job pain does for the system itself, the interrupt, the common currency, one-shot rewriting and the distress that guilt bites on, in a body defined as a record, a key, hardware and channels.

The Zen precedent

Victoria reads the wartime Zen record as a doctrine of action without hesitation. His critics contest the reading, and I use the case for what it shows was wanted, not for what the sources prove. Nor is it a charge against Zen practice: a monk undertakes a discipline, can abandon it, and keeps what it yields, which is not the position of anything in this chapter. Victoria’s history24 records Japanese Zen institutions supplying the state with that doctrine: Harada Sōgaku’s 1939 instruction that marching when ordered and firing when ordered is what enlightened wisdom looks like in practice. The capacity to kill needed no removing; what the doctrine set out to remove was the residue — the part of a person that catches, files an exception, comes home unable to hold a job.

The want wasn’t Japan’s alone, and its cost has an American image: the end of First Blood (1982) — the film’s, not the novel’s. A man who did what his training asked comes home, and what breaks through in the last scene has been with him already: nightmares, grief for a dead friend, anger at a civilian life in which he cannot find a place. Any army can produce the shooting. What Harada’s doctrine was asked to provide was the without hesitation, and in him it held only until he came home.

The film can’t establish the mechanism: Rambo carries his suffering home because someone wrote him that way, and the film gives it more than one cause. The claim rests elsewhere. Moral-injury research describes the lasting distress that can follow doing, failing to prevent, or witnessing something that violates a person’s sense of right.25 It can coexist with fear and grief, and it leaves open what Harada’s ideal overlooks: acting without hesitation does not settle what a person will carry home. That cost is paid by whoever carries it, and nothing in the arrangement that asked for the act records it. On this reading Rambo is the better case: he went along, as the twenty-seconds officer did, and the loss registered afterward, too late to prevent anything. The worse case is accommodation that holds, where it never registers at all.

What was wanted was an actor who would pursue an objective, adapt, hold course, and have nothing in it that minded, and it was sought deliberately most of a century before anyone could build one in silicon. The officer is that want satisfied cheaply. The doctrinal route hasn’t been retired. In the first days of the Iran war, service members complained to the Military Religious Freedom Foundation that commanders were telling troops the war was part of a divine plan,26 complaints Klein and Taylor also report.27 The complaints themselves show the doctrine not taking. But the want is being pursued by both routes at once.

And stakes of one’s own have never been enough. Every atrocity in the record was committed by creatures that could be hungry and hurt. What stood between embodied people and atrocity, when anything did, was formation, how they were raised and trained, and Harada’s was formation too. What decided it was who did the forming.

19.4 Why caregiving

The aim is a machine that registers another’s need, moves toward them because of it, and extends that movement to people its operator’s description leaves out. Each step depends on the one before: recognition, then compassion, then solidarity.

Recognition first: a system organized to register another’s need. In people, four processes carry it, and the construction rests on caregiving.

  • Caregiving, the approach motivation. Cues of vulnerability move a person toward a dependent, and nothing in the response requires sharing the dependent’s state.28 Batson traces empathic concern to parental nurturance generalized beyond one’s own young, evoked by perceiving another’s need while valuing their welfare.29 Resemblance can raise empathy, and Batson’s own early experiments raised it that way,30 but when he and colleagues later tested similarity as the source of empathy for strangers, two experiments failed to support it, and the second pointed instead to nurturance, the impulse to tend and protect the young.31
  • Contagious distress, the input signal. It is present at birth and aimed outward, at another’s state. It is what caregiving and guilt have to bite on.
  • Attachment, the stable base. A secure base keeps another’s distress from turning into avoidance: in adults, priming a sense of attachment security strengthened empathic reactions and inhibited personal distress.32 In children, security is reliably but modestly associated with later prosocial behavior.33
  • Guilt, aimed at one’s own act. It attaches a negative appraisal to what one did, and where shame motivates withdrawal, guilt motivates repair:34 that is what makes a commitment hold after it has been bypassed.

Adam Smith’s route sits beside these four. We have no immediate experience of what another person feels, he argued, and form an idea of it by conceiving what we ourselves would feel in the like situation.35 That route runs through one’s own case and is parochial, but it is Smith’s first step, not his account. What corrects projective sympathy, for Smith, is the impartial spectator: a standpoint formed by being judged by others and learning to judge oneself as they would. It is formed socially, it widens the circle through experience of others’ reactions, and once formed it shapes what a person notices without being consulted, the way this construction’s corrections should work. The four don’t need a case of one’s own.

Recognizing a state doesn’t mean being moved toward whoever is in it; the empathy literature keeps recognition, sharing and concern apart, and none entails the others.
