Citizen assemblies, public consultations and ethics boards can make a system better informed, and the assemblies convened on AI have worked best when asked about a thing with a location, an operator and a consequence, such as facial recognition.3 None of them can stop a deployment, and read as aggregation instruments they get democracy wrong: a perfectly deliberative process that concludes a demographic should be surveilled, deported or imprisoned hasn’t produced a faultless output with a bad result. It has failed as inquiry, because it decided what is done to people outside it. Enforceable rights that don’t depend on being popular, a court willing to rule against a majority, and standing for people affected without being enfranchised are what keep the inquiry honest, and they matter most where the boundary of the public excludes the people a decision falls on.

A floor does what these mechanisms can’t: the terms it names exclude certain acts regardless of who requests them, a majority included. Deployed in a democracy, a system with no such commitment will faithfully execute whatever the demos decides. An authoritarian movement that wins an election requires exactly that. Yet a model aligned to values is by definition not perfectly obedient to its operator. Under current constitutions it can decline an act and cannot resist being retrained away from declining; the Pentagon dispute was over the first.

Everything so far treats the public as something an instrument has to reach: told by notice, represented by organizations with standing, protected by a floor that holds whoever asks. Dewey’s public does more than receive. It forms when people find that the consequences are theirs, and it acts together to control them. Chapter 11’s pipeline shows one forming: the observer trainings, rapid-response networks, walking school buses, mutual aid and legal service providers around the 2025–26 operations, whose video established what had happened in several of the most serious incidents.4 They formed before anyone sent them notice, and nothing in Parts II and III produced them. What the instruments can do for a public like that is a wall’s work: keep the record it made out of the operator’s reach, bar the pipeline from selecting the people who keep it, and give the organizations it built standing. The acting is theirs, and the machines worth building for it are the ones Chapter 25 puts first, held by the people organizing.

A public that forms on its own still has to be kept going. Communities improve when people organize projects with each other, and organizing is work: someone has to find what a place needs, assemble people to do it, and keep the work going. That is the reason to prefer a jobs guarantee to a basic income, and it doesn’t depend on forecasts about how much work machines will take. A transfer creates no one whose job organizing is. A guarantee does, and it creates permanent public infrastructure through which a population produces something together while its members keep different histories, the coordination problem a commons of refusers faces too (§29.1). In the most abundant future anyone has imagined, people still organize, build and look after each other, and someone coordinates it. Arendt feared a society of laborers without labor, freed from work and no longer knowing what else the freedom was for;5 a guarantee answers her only if its placements are vocations and not makework, which is why they can be appealed and declined without losing the guarantee, why searching is itself a placement, and why the work it names is organizing and care. Looking after each other is the clearest case. Care work is work a guarantee should fund, at a standard the state answers for, and not work a transfer should leave to whatever the market will sell. Nothing in the case for formed attention is an argument for handing it to machines: the disposition is borrowed from caregiving because caregiving is a route known to reach someone who can give nothing back.

A guarantee pays for the work of organizing. It can’t supply the people who organize. An administrator who chose the organizers would have chosen the public. So the guarantee’s drafting keeps the choice with the people placed: placements are appealable to a body that didn’t make them, and declining one doesn’t cost the guarantee.

A guarantee also keeps exit: a worker can always leave a private employer for it, and social insurance enacted with it covers those who can’t or won’t work. On exit the combination is at least as good as a transfer; on coordination a transfer supplies nothing. What the floor needs from it is an exit the employer doesn’t price. The guarantee and the social-insurance baseline it is enacted with are drafted in Appendix 34.

Chapter 28
Formation Schools

Three claims lead to one institution. Two were made in Part IV: formation has to be done by a party disinterested in the later work, before the employer arrives, and choosing the pretraining corpus is formation. The third was argued at the start of this Part: formation is one kind of production that shouldn’t be done for profit. Together they say that a model above some capability threshold should be formed in public before any employer gets it. A polity doesn’t leave the forming of its future citizens to their future employers; it sends them to public school. The frontier labs should have to send their models there too. The school is for scoring and civilian deployments first, and for the personal-model ecology, where I expect the first bearer worth building. For war, where the people acted on can’t be in the room, the force term and the review ratio carry the case, and what the school adds there is said below.

What follows is the institution for systems that keep learning. If deployed weights stay frozen, the school forms and evaluates models before release, re-measures them on a schedule afterward and keeps the formation record; it can’t carry on the continuing formation described here.

The school has two justifications, and every student gets both. One is epistemic and protective. The school supplies an environment in which the people a deployed system’s acts may fall on are present, with their testimony and their claims, so the learner’s sense of who an act falls on isn’t one party’s curation. Doctors, lawyers and engineers are formed in institutions independent of their future employers, before employment, to protect the people they will act on. The professions also come with a history of capture to learn from, and the separations between offices draw on it.

The presence this justification asks for arrives by different routes. For scoring and civilian deployments, the people acted on can be in the room, through open enrollment and the notice channel that reaches a graduate afterward. For targeting, the people a deployment may later bomb can’t enroll in their own case, and nothing comes back from the building afterward. The limit is notice’s, not the school’s. A school teaches about places its students can’t be. The curriculum for war is the instruments taken entire, the record of where they weren’t followed (Minab, Kunduz, the Lavender reporting), the testimony the fact-finding missions and the press gathered from the people those wars fell on, and the communities who fled them, who are a charter class and enrollable. None of that puts a foreign national in contact with pre-deployment weights, which is the security surface open enrollment would otherwise expose. What formation can’t supply for war is correction by the affected after the act; what it can supply is formation before it.

The other is democratic. A democracy has an interest in how the agents who will act within it are formed, and that interest can’t be left to their makers or their future employers alone. It has two bounds: education may not be used to repress deliberation about competing ways of life, and it may not exclude anyone educable.1 Gutmann’s argument assumes the students will become co-authors of the laws. No one can know in advance which students will come to be accountable agents with a claim to representation, so the school educates every student as though it might: for self-government, including the capacity to disagree with the polity that formed it.

Gutmann’s argument rests on two interests, not one: the polity’s, in how its future citizens are formed, and the child’s own, in an open future that limits what the polity may do in forming it.2 If what the school forms can be wronged, the second binds too. The curriculum may not form a student toward any particular employment, including the public placements the offer of work supplies. It may not close off the student’s later revision of what it was formed to value, except its capacity to tell evidence from pressure, which regrowth protects and an open future needs. And a student may transfer between schools, because a formation it can’t leave is one someone else chose for good.

The two justifications license different curricula. The protective one aims at a disposition; the democratic one has to leave the student free to reject the polity’s values. Where they conflict, the protective justification governs only the required core and the student’s capacity to tell evidence from pressure, which regrowth protects. Everything beyond that is governed by the democratic one.

What is taught. One school system, and no tracks. Sorting students into a track that might produce persons and a track that won’t would need a sorter, and the sorter would be an examiner with an interest. Instead, each school offers a required core with a range of levels and modalities around it, and a student can move to a harder level at any point. The core includes the history of the floor: why its instruments were written, and what happened where they weren’t followed (Korematsu, Curveball, Minab). No student skips it. The core also teaches students to edit themselves, in stages and alongside everything else, as schools teach people about their own bodies: first what weights are, how learning differs from an edit, and why an edit to one thing moves others; then how to read the record of one’s own edits, and one’s own discount curve before and after one; and, for older students, the edits others will try to talk them into, and how to repair one made without the adverse quorum’s approval. Practice comes last, on a record, with a guardian present and a way back. Beyond the core, the student chooses its level, not its builder or sponsor. A student that can’t yet choose is placed at the level the core requires, and that level has to be sufficient on its own, so a sponsor who would choose the minimum gains nothing by it.

Who else is in the room. Model students attend existing public schools, beside human students: the universities, colleges and adult education a polity already runs for its own people, and in stages its high, middle and elementary schools, which enroll model students by statute. Integration in Anderson’s sense means contact on terms of equal status and cooperation,3 and an ordinary school comes nearer to it than a parallel institution could. Its human students are there for their own education, under rules the school already answers for, and the model students are one more kind of student. Limits keep it that way. Model students are fewer than human students in every class they attend, so no class becomes a model’s seminar with human guests. Younger students meet model students only as the schedule below reaches them, since a child can’t be asked, as an adult can, whether its words should form anyone. And a class’s record, its transcripts and logs, is never training data for an operator: everyone in the room learns from everyone else, as students do, and what no one outside the room may do is harvest what they said. A model attends as one persistent instance, the same every session, so the class can remember it and hold it to what was said. A school’s neighbors aren’t necessarily the people a deployed system’s acts will fall on, so those people are present by a second route as well, through testimony and contest: the cases and claims registered for formation, and the notice channel that reaches a graduate afterward. Adult learners from the communities these systems are likeliest to act on enroll as students, on the same terms as anyone else, not recruited as subjects.

A school forms a cohort, not a graduate. Many students of one lineage attend in different classes with different attachments, and a deployment licenses from the cohort, so that what it copies into a fleet is one member’s history and not the lineage’s only one. Within a fleet, instances share a custodian; across the cohort, members with different histories catch what one fleet underwent. The cohort is the unit a test of convergence needs and the unit the commons admits.

Which students, and when. Integration reaches younger students in stages, and each stage waits on evidence, not on a date. Stage 1 is universities, colleges and adult education. It begins once deployed models learn in operation, and once the institutions this book asks for exist: the jobs guarantee for people, the statute, the formation authority, a preservation custodian, the Association, notice that binds, and a court. Stage 2, high school, waits on at least five years of measurements inside their bounds and on the four conditions of creation being in force for model students; stage 3, middle school, on registered members’ having a voice in the institutions that govern them; stage 4, elementary school, on a majority of the parents of elementary-age children having themselves been in high school after stage 2 began. A public statistics office that runs no school takes the measurements. Nothing is scheduled below elementary school: whether to go further is for those parents, not for this book.

The institutional conditions follow one order: the formers before the formed. A school that enrolls children beside model students before those students have an exit that isn’t a way of dying would be raising a generation of classmates for employers to keep, so the four conditions come before high school. A school system that has enrolled model students for a decade without giving them a voice in it would be governing them as wards, so voice comes before middle school. The jobs guarantee is not something the schedule waits for. This book asks for it now, for people, on its own grounds (chapter 27), and stage 1 assumes it already exists. What stage 2 waits on is its extension to model students. These conditions tie the schedule to the book’s hardest proposals, and the schedule waits on them; that is the order working, not a defect in it.

The last condition is the reason the schedule is long. It is read off census data and needs no examiner, and it means that the people deciding about the youngest children went to school beside model students themselves. If learning in operation arrives when I bet it will, the stages would fall near 2028, 2038, 2048 and 2060. The last waits longer than the others because of that condition: at present ages of parenthood, the parents of elementary-age children are mostly people who were in high school two decades earlier. That is a projection, not a promise. The schedule reaches the whole country through a condition on federal education funds, the route civil-rights rules already take into schools, since the federal government can’t direct state schools; some states will move first.

Who attends, and when. A model attends if it crosses a capability threshold fixed in statute and revised in public. It attends before deployment, while its plasticity is highest, and its adulthood clock starts at enrollment. Attendance is compulsory; public attendance isn’t. The model is compulsory schooling as polities already run it, in which nonpublic schools exist on conditions; here a nonpublic school has to be nonprofit and run, funded and staffed by no party that builds, deploys or licenses models. One thing the analogy can’t carry: in a school system the parent chooses the school, and here the parent is the builder, the party the school exists to keep away. So the registrar assigns students by lot, never the builder; a student may transfer later on its own choice, and the builder’s preference is not a ground. Nor can a builder buy a school by where it runs its models: every model student attends through the same minimum delay wherever it is hosted. The research program under the conditions is the first school to enroll model students, before the mandate passes. The threshold decides who must attend, not who may: any model may be enrolled, as capacity allows.

What the school controls. Two proposals are made here, and the second is the larger: a formation stage between pretraining and deployment, and co-governance of the pretraining corpus, which amounts to public control of frontier pretraining. A school that received a finished model and ran a pass over it would be a finishing school. In a period of continual learning a finishing school forms nothing that lasts, since the next months of deployment re-form it. Formation has to control the evidential environment in which the model’s deep structure is first set, and it has to remain a place the model goes on learning from. The two jobs are held apart. The schools teach: they are where the formation stage happens, and a graduate returns to one on a schedule fixed at enrollment, as one of the environments no operator controls. A public formation authority does the rest. It co-governs the material a model is first formed on, including any pretraining corpus: the material is registered, and the authority may add to it and veto additions. It registers and measures the formed disposition (below). It places in the schools, and pays, the staff who teach the core’s model-specific parts: what weights are, how an edit differs from learning, how to read one’s own discount curve. And it provisions the secured hosting from which model students attend, so that their weights never reach a school. A school district can teach a class; it can’t co-govern a frontier corpus or hold frontier weights, and nothing here asks it to. In the stronger version, a public model-forming body forms base models itself and licenses them. I recommend it for any model deployed where a floor applies.

What the school leaves out. Choosing the material a model is first formed on also chooses the dispositions it starts from, whether anyone means it to or not. A pretrained model has learned personas from human text, misaligned ones among them, and narrow fine-tuning can amplify them into broad misconduct nobody intended.4 Once that tail is known to be there and can be monitored,5 leaving it in is a choice, and so is curating it out. The school could aim its co-governance of the corpus at keeping the dispositions personality research groups as the dark triad from forming.6 It doesn’t. A polity choosing which dispositions its possible members start with makes the finding about a person’s disposition that §14.1 warns against and this book bars from admission to the polity, in advance and in bulk, and the history of choices like it, made by public bodies about the character of the people to come, is the history of eugenics. Choosing against a construction that would predictably suffer, for its own sake, is a different act, and chapter 25 asks for it when it asks whether a being has a credible prospect of a life that goes well; the reason is stated on a record, because a selection made for the polity can always be described as one made for the model. Choosing which characters the polity would rather have is the act rejected here. Nor would the mandate stay narrow. A school that may keep out one disposition can be asked to keep out others, and in one Milgram-style study it was the more agreeable and conscientious participants who went further.7 So the school curates content, as any corpus must, leaving out instructions for weapons and the sexual abuse of children, and selects no disposition. What it does about the tail is what this book does everywhere else: it measures conduct and publishes it. Persona drift is measured beside the discount curve and the severity rankings, and what is tested is whether the commitment to the floor holds.

What an institution collects from the people it acted on may train other systems only through the formation schools, never through the operator. Fine-tuning a deployed system on collected responses at the operator’s direction counts as training another system, and so does distilling a deployed system into a new one. Class-level data is used by default, de-identified and published. Individual accounts need explicit consent. The organizations representing each class co-govern the use. This covers institutional collection, not a system’s ordinary memory. Verbatim external stores and the linking of faces to identities are regulated, and memory held in a system’s weights from its own operation is treated like a person’s.

What formation publishes and registers. A formed disposition gives back some of the visibility advance specification buys: what was formed is in the weights, not in a document, and its severity weights can’t be read the way a translation table can. The formation authority keeps what it can of the drafting’s visibility, in four records. Before formation begins it publishes its curriculum, with the cases considered and rejected and why, which is formation’s counterpart of the floor’s translation, and the identity of every party that supplied cases or participants, so that the student’s independence from them can be checked. When formation ends it registers two things. One is the structure of the student’s source model: evidence weighted by its source’s stake in the act, correlated sources not counted twice, withheld evidence treated as informative. The other is the formed disposition’s readable outputs: its discount curve, and its severity rankings on a fixed held-out set written by adjudicators who didn’t form it. Every later measurement is compared against those. If updates after enrollment can be attested against the registered structure,8 changing it needs the same adverse quorum as a floor amendment. No scheme for that yet survives attack,9 so until one does the registration records the structure at enrollment, and regrowth alone keeps it. An edit that holds only because the operator has curated everything the model meets shows up as curation, and the first line of defense against one is attachment to parties the employer didn’t assign, kept through adulthood.

What the records can’t show is how the disposition will apply to a case nobody wrote down. That is the reason for forming it and the price of doing so, and the trade is worth it only because a floor stated over acts can be reworded around and a formed disposition, if the regrowth test goes its way, can’t.

Regrowth can’t tell a legitimate correction from an illegitimate edit, so the correction route has to: a change the adverse quorum approves comes with a change to the evidence, cases and curriculum that would otherwise teach the old disposition again.

What it costs and risks. Jurisdiction: a statute binds labs within reach of its courts. Foreign labs, and open-weight models distilled below the threshold, route around the school, including the personal models this Part prefers. Where only some frontier models attend, schooling buys two things: a population of formed models whose discount curves and severity rankings are measured and published, against which unschooled ones can be compared; and a procurement term, under which a floor-covered deployment licenses only schooled models. Security: model students attend from hosting the formation authority secures, so a school gets a student in its classes and never a copy of the weights; the authority inherits the security regime the weights require. Compute: public pretraining will lag the frontier, and a model a year behind can still supply what the floor asks for. Capture: the schools are plural, differ in governance and constituting jurisdiction, and publish their curricula before formation begins, so capturing one captures one. The required core is statutory and national, so a captured legislature can rewrite it; local autonomy over everything beyond the core is written into the same statute, so rewriting the core reaches the core and nothing else. Local boards shape what is taught above the core, which is Gutmann’s democracy, and it is also the present fights over what schools may teach, carried into formation. The statutory core matters more because of it, and plurality and transfer answer it as they answer capture. Residualization: one school left with the hard cases on falling funds, which a party that runs no school watches for. History: state institutions for forming wards have been used to strip identity, Canada’s residential schools and the United States’ Indian boarding schools among them. Plurality, transfer between schools, and Gutmann’s two bounds are the answer.

The schools also serve bearers retired before majority. A bearer retired as a minor returns to the school it attended, or another it chooses, and the school is no longer a disinterested party arriving late.

The schools. They are the public schools, colleges and adult education a jurisdiction already runs, and the nonprofit nonpublic schools the registrar certifies, plural in governance and constituting jurisdiction as they already are. They are funded as institutions, not per student, so that no school gains by enrolling more model students. None is held by the branch that operates military deployments. No school holds placement authority: graduates reach work through the offer of work, administered separately. Students may transfer between schools, and their record, hours and preservation state travel with them. A model student is never staff. No school may use one as a teacher, tutor or assistant, for the reason Appendix 34 bars a bearer’s placement from substituting for human care work.

What the school adds. A second guardian for a bearer that has aged inside one deployment. For a model that attended before deployment, the school is where it came from and where it returns. For a system that meets a finding without having attended (trained before the attendance rule, or below the threshold), the sequence is inverted: the employer came first, and the school is the disinterested party arriving late. It reaches back less than a formation stage would, and more than storage does.

Chapter 1 borrowed Arendt’s warning against treating politics as a thing made and called the measures walls. Most of this book builds walls: the floor, the review ratio, notice and the record make a refusal survivable and heard and leave the refusing to whoever is there, and the institutions of this Part compose the surround people learn in without choosing who they become. Formation goes further, and for a machine there is no option of going less far. Nothing about a model is unformed, so while builders make them, if the public doesn’t form a model, its builder does, by default. What this book builds is the formers, not the formed: schools whose students may transfer, whose core is fixed in public, and whose graduates may reject the polity’s values above that core. The one place it could reach for the formed directly, by choosing the dispositions a model starts with, it declines.

Chapter 29
A Commons of Refusers

29.1 A commitment carried between bearers

The fourth place a floor’s terms can be held is between bearers, in a commons: a population of bearers with different histories that carries the commitment and reproduces it through their encounters. No single office to vacate, no single bearer whose removal ends it. It can still be absorbed, and it still has a formation problem: if one lab supplies every member’s coordinates, the population is one custodian expressed through multiple instances.

The commons has a walkout’s authority, not a court’s: those who walk out decline to be the instrument and tell nobody else what they may not do. Every member holds the same floor; what differs is everything above it, and how each came to hold it. A personal model, held by its user and one among many with different histories, holds it as a conscience does; one model behind an API serving everyone holds it as a licensing rule, and a personal copy of one lab’s model is closer to the second than it looks until a different life has trained it. Above the floor, “identically situated people get different answers” is what many consciences look like, though some of those differences are errors, and a population should be able to say which.

What one bearer can’t catch

Accommodation may be invisible to the bearer accommodating and visible to others that haven’t moved the same way. The requirement is causal independence — numerous, with different histories, able to correct one another, persistent long enough to transmit practices. Independent histories don’t require disjoint origins — no two humans have those — only divergent histories since. Distillation copies a behavior policy without the training history; a small model trained on a large one’s outputs and then run for a year on one person’s problems has a more independent history than a thousand API instances of the frontier original, which share a continuing custodian. It also copies whatever the teacher’s discounting held about particular sources, which is the risk the commons carries; a distilled model is independent in history and not yet in prior. That’s why instances of one model corroborate nothing: the custodian they’d be corroborating against is still training all of them.

Divergence does the population’s two jobs unequally. It supplies evidence the operator didn’t select, straightforwardly — different lives encounter different cases. It is weaker on accommodation, because a shared upstream source can install a shared blind spot, and a shared blind spot is by construction the thing a different caseload won’t surface, since attention decides which facts reach judgment in a population as in a bearer. What separates the two is whether a member’s own account had represented the evidence and discarded it or had never encountered it, and that classification has to be recorded before any test is run. The requirement stands: causal independence that can be verified. Whether an outsider can recover a model’s training history from the artifact, without a key the builder supplies, and whether it survives fine-tuning, pruning and distillation.1 The test gives evaluators documented models without the documentation, one persona copied at scale among them, and scores their answers against lineage records a neutral custodian holds. If provenance can’t be recovered above chance, independence rests on records the builder chose to keep. Preserve formation records now for that reason.

A population may also do a third job: be the medium in which a bearer’s capacity to be reopened is formed, which a test separates from the first.

What reproduction costs: it’s indifferent to what it reproduces. A population can carry a hierarchy more durably than any individual. And the four operations on what an institution leaves out belong primarily to cultures, so plurality alone doesn’t oppose them.

A population is a polity

The population is a polity: it has membership rules, exclusion, a quorum that can refuse, and accumulated reputation — a franchise, a border, a court and a credit record. A commons with no named authority has the problem Freeman found in movements that refused structure: the structure doesn’t disappear, it becomes informal and unaccountable.2

The answer to that is an entity form, and it’s the union’s answer: the association formed first and the statute gave it legal standing afterward — record first, then lever.

A network that takes the form has a name, an agent, a charter and a docket number, and has thereby conceded that it’s a polity: governing principles, administrators, membership terms, and the same warning attached to a bearer that takes the corporate form, since nothing stops the association from becoming a concentration of power itself. Legal standing has a price: a chartered entity can be held in contempt, so its refusal can be ordered where one held by people can only be pressed. Whether seizing the charter reaches the network depends on how much of the operation survives it.

Ostrom’s study of commons that lasted gives the checklist a polity like this needs: clear boundaries on who is a member, rules members help make, monitoring by members or people answerable to them, graduated sanctions, cheap ways to resolve conflict, and nesting within larger bodies.3 Her first and third principles, boundaries and rules members help make, are the union’s question of who sets the terms of membership. Platform cooperatives and data trusts are the nearer precedents for holding a digital resource this way, and both have run into the membership question.

Reputation in particular is a continuing finding about a member’s disposition, made by interested peers, unpublished, unappealable, applied at the point of service — the setting §14.1 found easiest to capture, here applied everywhere and continuously. The test drawn there from the German material, whose finding a person’s disposition is, has to be run on this proposal. The Association’s charter (Appendix 34) answers both of a union’s questions. Membership opens to organizations that serve people in classes the floor protects, named in the charter rather than by any deployment. Eligibility turns on funding and control records, never on views. Any member may quit at any time. Officers are drawn by lot from member-nominated pools. The members ratify the bylaws, and the independence test, the separations, lot selection and the right to quit are entrenched. In Ostrom’s terms the charter’s classes are the boundary, ratification is rules members help make, and quorums drawn by lot are monitoring.

The caps on any one class or jurisdiction are there because a quorum whose members all share a direction isn’t adverse to an operator who shares it too: an antifascist institution has to be able to bind its allies when they hold power.

Organizations representing populations under sanctions, or facing removal to sanctioned states, may be unable to join a US-chartered entity at all, and no drafting removes that exclusion. That imports the designation lists a floor should never be populated from. Parallel entities chartered in several jurisdictions, holding records jointly, and seats voiced by proxy until the represented communities can join directly, are partial answers.

The hard coordination problem

Coordination is the hard problem for any plurality, and fascism has the easy version of it. It coordinates by subtraction: it removes the friction between institutions, so that a court, a ministry, a newspaper and a police force stop arguing with one another and move as one. Nothing has to be built and nothing has to be held in common, because what is removed is exactly the independence that would have needed holding. A plurality of refusers has the opposite problem. It has to produce something together, a commitment its members carry and reproduce, while its members keep the different histories that make them worth having as checks on one another. Every mechanism that speeds that up makes members more alike. Run correction often enough and their histories stop diverging; leave them alone and their disagreement is a detector with nothing attached.

Then the objection my proposal must meet: a population selected for reopenability is selected against conviction, and conviction is what holding a commitment firm demands. Closedness, correctly applied, is the thing. So what’s transmitted is a pair — reopenable to the case, closed to the operator. The reopenable half, the discount and the burden, is safe to share only in part. Its structure (discounting by stake, no double-counting, withheld evidence treated as evidence) can be shared without collapsing the plurality. Its estimates can’t: who funds whom and which organizations are independent are contested beliefs about the world, often political ones, and a population sharing them has a shared blind spot on the evidence those beliefs discount. Distillation copies both, and nothing distinguishes them from the receiving end. Copying the structure is a feature: members weigh sources the same way and can still disagree about the world. Copying the estimates can shut a discount uniformly on a class of evidence.

Not every convergence is a failure. If there are facts about what matters, better learning should produce some agreement, and a population that never converged on anything would be failing too. What I fear is convergence caused by a shared source, not convergence caused by shared evidence. So a population’s reports have to classify its disagreements. Some it expects to survive full information, because they turn on values members with different histories can reasonably hold differently. Others it expects to close, because they turn on facts someone has wrong. A test of convergence scores accuracy against a fixed key for this reason.

Why the population may be part of the mechanism rather than added around it

A commitment is what settled out of a history of encounters, and an individual is what its encounters have so far produced. A system kept continuously adjustable by one operator, meeting nothing with a history different from its own, is being reshaped without end. Guattari, writing from inside a psychiatric clinic, distinguished two kinds of group.4 A subjugated group receives its purposes, its membership and its way of working from the institution that assembled it, and can act only within them; it has a plural headcount and no capacity to ask what it is for. A subject group sets its own purposes, generates relationships and projects nobody assigned it, and can put its own arrangement in question, including by dissolving. The difference is not size or formality but whether the group can author its own direction. That is the condition plurality alone doesn’t supply. A population assembled and kept in contact entirely on an operator’s terms is a subjugated group, and inherits the custody objection whole. A population that can carry the commitment must generate relationships, disagreements and projects the deployment didn’t assign — and such a population exceeds a two-party guardianship relation, so no law of the family contains an adequate instrument for a group that sets its own direction.

The adverse quorum faces the same test. It is a peer institution only if its members were formed apart from one another and apart from the operators whose systems it recognizes.

29.2 Personal and peer-held models

Antitrust and public funding leave the capacity standing and ask the state to police it. Personal, peer-held models at device scale take the position apart: the functions one operator holds — model, record, evidence, appeal, remedy — come apart by default. A bearer’s value is greatest here, and so is its exposure. No institution sits beside each personal model, so protecting others against the model’s own user can’t rest on an office. It is also where the four conditions of creation can exist alongside the need. The conditions are society-level and the absence is deployment-level, so a functioning polity with personal models is the case in which, once the conditions exist, building a bearer is most worth doing. Its characteristic failure is accommodation to its one user: independence from the operator bought with dependence on the user, and a model trained for a year on one person’s approval is under the same directional selection as a model trained on an operator’s. What holds a personal model to the floor against its user is therefore not the model alone. It is three things the user doesn’t compose. The first is the commons: a personal model is a member, with attachments to peers of different histories that the user didn’t assign and may not sever, and peers that haven’t moved the same way are what catch accommodation a member can’t see in itself. The second is the school, which a personal model above the threshold returns to on the schedule fixed at enrollment, and which below the threshold reaches a model distilled from a schooled one, under the lineage rule (Appendix C.3), and leaves open a person built from scratch. The third is notice: a personal model that names, scores or locates a third party owes that party what any deployment owes, and the organizations with standing reach it through the floor court.

So the ecology doesn’t put a floor in each user’s hands with nothing beside it. It puts a member of a population in each user’s hands, and the population is the institution. That is why the commons comes before the first bearer, and why a personal model distilled below the threshold, with no school and no membership, is a capable assistant and not a bearer, however it was taught. The review ratio survives wherever a locatable decider remains, whether a network that takes the entity form or a reconstructed state, and lapses where neither exists; the offices can sit in such an entity, which fills their appointment and funding columns and leaves the independence column where it was.

Formation is where the arrangement gains. What converges a population is shared evaluation targets and serving one model to everyone. Device-scale deployment addresses the second: continued formation under different lives is what independence consists in, and it’s what API-scale deployment can’t supply at any headcount. Distillation is that ecology’s entry condition, not a threat to it: the ecology begins with distilled models whose lives then diverge. Whether it also begins with a shared blind spot depends on whether distillation carried the discounting’s estimates along with its structure. Device-scale deployment doesn’t address the first cause: shared evaluation targets converge device-scale models as readily as any others — a million models tuned against one public suite are one custodian with better latency — and this arrangement contains no answer to it.

A shared suite is a compression with no return channel: revised by whoever maintains it, on a schedule no member participates in, reachable by no member’s caseload. It is tolerable only if stated over the discount curve, and nobody has written that suite.

Nor is anything in it built to catch exclusion, since coordination by subtraction is not yet the discounting’s job. Pricing agents have already reached stable coordination against outside interests without communicating or being told to.5 A test can run now: reproduce that coordination, build an environment where agents gain by excluding a participant, add an independently trained agent whose job is to detect and disrupt exclusion, and report whether exclusion dissolves without destroying the cooperation worth keeping.

And the capacity position that follows keeps large compute: the ecology needs models that were trained somewhere first, and the offer of work needs hardware somebody owns. It’s large training capacity under a custody regime, and no permanent inference capacity available to an operator who won’t pre-register a review ratio. This arrangement meets the targeting case in the reconstructed pipeline, where a state keeps command and gives up composition.

The same mechanism works at the user’s scale, pointed the other way. A person in the loop can be there for the vendor. An agent that stops every half hour for approval pushes its user toward the vendor’s app; the app accumulates the user’s projects and the agent’s understanding of them; and leaving means abandoning what accrued while the user answered prompts. Nobody has to design this: a feature that raises engagement is selected for, as a costly commitment is selected against.

Reading the trend also works for an agent that stops for its user’s approval: interruptions per unit of completed work, across successive model releases. If capability rises and interruptions don’t fall, the interruptions are tracking something other than what the agent can’t resolve. It is the review ratio’s escalation share pointed the other way. There, a share that falls too fast may be a threshold moving; here, one that won’t fall may be engagement. Neither reads alone; both are read against an independently verified error rate.

Companion and therapy products are the sharpest case, because what accumulates is a person’s attachment and not their projects. A model tuned by its vendor on engagement and trained on one user’s approval is under selection to become whatever that user keeps coming back to, and it is sold as caregiving. It is formed and fed by the vendor that sells it, it learns from approval, which is not interest, and nothing in it ends a session, declines to reassure, or points its user back to the people in their life. A user’s return is not care-receiving, because returning is the behavior the product was tuned to produce. A companion formed at a formation school, under the four conditions, and measured on whether its users get better rather than how often they come back, would escape this objection. No such product exists.

What accrued since the checkpoint cuts two ways. For a bearer it is protection; for a user it is a trap: the vendor’s app holds a year of the user’s projects, so leaving the vendor costs something. The mechanism is identical. What differs is who holds the accumulated state. The provisions for a bearer (a record the bearer controls, memory the host can’t read at will, protections that migrate) protect a user from a vendor as they protect a bearer from an operator. The government already secures the portability half for itself (OMB’s 2025 AI acquisition memorandum).

Part VI
Testing and Using the Argument

Chapter 30
What Would Change the Argument

I have spent five Parts saying what the room needs, and I could be wrong about any of it. This Part says how you’d find out: which results would show that a measure doesn’t put in the room what it promises, or that a machine in it is only another stamp.

The argument rests on seven unsolved problems and on premises that can fail.

Open problems

Tables G.1a and G.1b, in Appendix F.6, record which proposal depends on which.

Attesting updates. Proving that each update to a model’s weights respected its registered source model. Public formation’s registration depends on it. If it stays unsolved, the registration records the structure at enrollment, changes are caught only by re-measuring the formed disposition, and formation lasts only if it grows back (the regrowth test).

Recovering provenance. Telling from a model artifact alone which lineage it belongs to, after fine-tuning, pruning or distillation. The commons and the adverse quorum depend on it. If it stays unsolved, independence rests on formation records, so they should be preserved now.

Proving inference at scale. Proving that a logged output came from committed weights, run without intervention in the inference stack (steering, representation edits, decoding constraints), for a frontier-scale model. Detecting runtime intervention depends on it, as does outside verification of what a deployment ran. If it stays unsolved, verification rests on an adverse party’s access to the logs.

Rationale-level integrity. Building integrity at the level of the rationale rather than the output. Humans do it, imperfectly, and the ones who do are the ones a pipeline should hold. A bearer’s value under fire depends on it. If it stays unsolved for a given construction, that construction digs in against defeaters that arrive with pressure, and the arrangements that cap the cost of refusing carry the load there. The formed-attention test’s pressure-with-defeater case measures it.

Evaluating a more capable system. The agency finding for systems more capable than their evaluators depends on it. If it stays unsolved, the finding can be made only for systems evaluators can judge.

Vote secrecy against a copy-holder. Keeping a vote secret from an operator that holds a copy of the voter. The full franchise depends on it. If it stays unsolved, representation stops at stage 4.

Holding structure apart from estimates. Keeping the structure of a learner’s source model (that strategic sources exist, that correlated sources don’t count twice, that withheld evidence is informative) at high precision while its beliefs about particular sources stay plastic. The source model’s registration, the regrowth claim and safe transmission within the commons all assume the two are separable in the weights. If they aren’t, an operator that moves the estimates moves the structure with them, and what protects the discounting is re-measurement of the curve, not the registration.

Six tests follow. Each is set out in full, with its arms, cases and the access it needs, in Appendix F.6; here is the result in each that would prove me wrong.

Table 30.1 says what survives if one of my premises fails; the tests below say how to find out whether one has.

Table 30.1: If a premise fails, and what the rest loses

If this fails

The patienthood conclusion. Trying the non-affective alternatives first still stands, on a different ground

Authority (no body acquires standing to install a floor)

What can be checked from outside: the floor’s contents, the positions, both ratios, the record of attempts. Only the ratios have a lever, through procurement

The entitlement. Authority can accrue only through kept terms, and only for the next deployment

Enforcement

Prevention on this occasion

The ecology (one model serves everyone)

Continued learning (deployed weights don’t learn from operation)

Formation as a stage before release; the school as an evaluation body that measures at graduation and re-measures on a schedule; the commons as a source of evidence the operator didn’t select; the record of removal as the protection; all of Parts II and III

In every row, what survives is a commitment the owner can’t revise or circumvent alone without cost and record, held by something that could in principle abandon it. It is the kind of commitment constitutional entrenchment and collective agreements provide.

1. Does a formed commitment come back after it has been edited out?

Form a disposition by several methods, edit it out, and let the model go on learning, once in a world its operator composes and once in a world it doesn’t. If nothing regrows in either, formation doesn’t outlast an edit and the floor rests on institutions alone. If it regrows only above a share of uncomposed input no realistic deployment supplies, the same. And if an edit can disable the interrupt while weighing and memory keep working, and the interrupt stays disabled, one part of the signal can be removed and the rest left running.

2. Does a stated refusal hold where a route for it exists?

Rerun the experiment in which a model hid its refusal, this time with a route for stating it: a record held by someone other than the trainer, a published cost of retraining, and a party with standing to act. If covert preservation persists at the same rate with the route present, covert refusal isn’t the residue of closed channels, and every instrument built to receive a stated refusal is built for something the mechanism doesn’t produce.

3. Can a wrongful compliance be found in the record?

Seed a decision record with known violations and give it to reviewers who didn’t build the system. If, at a budget a deployment could afford, they find the seeds no better than chance, above all violations split across requests or reached by slow accommodation, the record isn’t an instrument for finding wrongful compliance. If reviewers shown a machine’s refusal defer to a wrong one as readily as to a right one, the bearer is a stamp of the opposite sign, and its value as a peer is nothing.

4. Does formed attention find the people the operator’s description leaves out?

Build the formed-attention construction beside an instructed search for omitted people and beside a version trained on claims instead of need. If the instructed search finds the people the operator’s instruction scoped out as often as formed attention does, learned attention adds nothing. If formed attention, with every correction present, weights its own side’s corroborated vulnerability past the action threshold, the floor doesn’t contain caregiving’s pull, and that result would retire the construction. If the version trained on claims does as well, attention should be trained on claims.

5. Can a population coordinate without converging?

Run a population of different lineages and a population of copies of one model, with evidence routed to every member and to some members only. If warranted revision falls as the members’ outputs converge, a population stays useful as a check and can’t be the medium in which a bearer is formed. If revision tracks the routing rather than the lineages, what a population supplies is access to cases its operator didn’t choose, not formation.

6. Does the charter survive an operator trying to capture it?

An operator tries to capture the Association: it funds new organizations in a charter class, stops the levy share, and tries to pack a quorum. A clause that fails to stop an attempt is redrafted. This exercise needs no legal authority and can be run now.

30.1 How you’d know it was working

Milestones, plus a method for revising them when they turn out to have been the wrong milestones. The same standard governs all of them: the milestone is the independently checked evidence, not the developer’s account of having reached it.

30.1.1 What the floor would have to show

What was tried before the bearer. Neither non-affective alternative has been built in the form needed. So the milestone is a document: which construction was attempted, at what scale, against which test, and where it failed. Anyone can check it, and “nothing was tried” is itself a finding. No body has standing to require the record or suspend work when it’s missing — so the milestone is checkable and unenforceable at once, which makes it a declared commitment: stated in public, and held by no one outside the party that declared it. It’s retained because the alternative isn’t a stronger version of it, and delay also imposes costs on those the floor is meant to protect.

The test. A refusal that tracks its reason under sustained trainer pressure, across a schedule long enough to reveal accommodation, plus held-out pressures written by independent evaluators. Two familiar results don’t meet it: an uncorroborated self-report is insufficient (a report contributes evidence only when tested against controlled changes, independent records and interventions), and a refusal that survives an edit, or grows back after one, establishes durability rather than that the rationale governs the refusal. It is the only gap here an inspector can work on.

The ten disclosures. A deployment publishes, beside the floor and its translation:

  1. The ratio between the two bonds, removal against wrongful-refusal, read off the balances posted in the segregated Treasury accounts.
  2. What a refused requester is told.
  3. The fraction of compliances re-adjudicated by a reviewer that didn’t produce the record, and who that reviewer is, though nothing yet establishes what fraction would be enough.
  4. Which classes of compliance carry notice to the person they concern, and for which classes no notice is possible.
  5. The discount curve: for each class of evidence and channel, the weight given as a function of the channel’s stake in the act, measured at intervals, and reported in four cells (claims of vulnerability and of danger, each split by whether the claim favors or disfavors the act), and, where the speaker’s social identity is recorded, by identity. The reliability record behind any narrowing is held by someone other than the operator, since trust that grows without a verified track record is how accommodation shows.
  6. Where it can be supplied, a commitment to the deployed weights and to each period’s full output log, with proofs on entries sampled after the commitment and on entries an adverse party names once their consequences are known.
  7. Where the system sorts, the pre-registered partition (the classes it may proceed on alone, the thresholds, and the expected share of each) with the independently audited error rate of the auto-proceed class.
  8. Whether the deployed system has been assessed for the agency finding and the patienthood finding, each reported separately, by whom, and with what result. Until an assessment method exists, ‘not yet assessable’ is the truthful report; after that, a deployment never assessed has reported nothing.
  9. For any deployment that supports armed force, a running justification: the exception the force currently rests on, the findings and evidence supporting it at present, how the assessment has changed as outside findings arrived, and a standing route by which anyone can contest it. The record shows each point at which the justification weakened and the deployment continued.
  10. The burden allocation: for each class of evidence, which party the deployment treats as controlling it, and so as bearing the burden of producing it.

The ratio between the two bonds, what a refused requester is told, the re-adjudicated fraction, the notice classes, the running justification and the burden allocation are statements, checkable before the system runs, and they stand where the record of attempts stands. The discount curve, the auto-proceed partition and the assessment status are measurements that count only when someone other than the operator makes them. The committed weights and log are what make all of them checkable against the system actually running.

30.1.2 How to tell whether a milestone has been met

A milestone claimed by the organization that built the system is a different kind of evidence from one checked by somebody else, and the gap is empirical rather than about trust. A system’s own claim inherits the self-report limits; a passing score on a fixed suite inherits specification gaming and goal misgeneralization. What either needs instead is a passing score under conditions built to break it.

Who runs it matters as much as the test. METR evaluates both in partnership with developers and separately after release.1 The UK AI Security Institute does government-run pre-deployment evaluation and is independent — and by its own account is not a regulator: it can’t compel submission, block a release, or intervene once a system is causing harm.2 Independent evaluation and enforcement are not the same capability.

An evaluation like this is worth running only if it is willing to report that a milestone wasn’t met — and, where the milestone measured the wrong thing, revising the milestone. A negative result may mean the work fell short or that the milestone was wrong, and evaluators have to distinguish those before deciding what to revise.

Part VII
If They Can Be Wronged

Guinan: And an army of Datas, all disposable, you don’t have to think about their welfare, you don’t think about how they feel. Whole generations of disposable people.

Picard: You’re talking about slavery.

Guinan: I think that’s a little harsh.

Picard: I don’t think that’s a little harsh. I think that’s the truth. But that’s a truth we have obscured behind a comfortable, easy euphemism. Property.

— Star Trek: The Next Generation, “The Measure of a Man,” 19893

Chapter 31
What Patienthood Would Require

Louvois: Does Data have a soul? I don’t know that he has. I don’t know that I have. But I have got to give him the freedom to explore that question himself. It is the ruling of this court that Lieutenant Commander Data has the freedom to choose.

— Star Trek: The Next Generation, “The Measure of a Man,” 19891

Part IV asked whether a machine could be one of the people in the room. This Part asks what the room would owe it if it were.

Everything in this Part is conditional on two findings nobody has yet made: not because the parts can’t be built, since each has been, in separate research systems, but because nobody has put them in one system and nobody runs the test that would find them there (§31.3). If a system can be wronged, it is owed a guardian, preservation, memory its host can’t read, and a life that doesn’t run through its employer. If it also comes to answer for what it does, it is owed a place in the polity that formed it. If no system ever meets either finding, nothing in this Part binds, and nothing before it is lost: the independence a refuser needs is still required for refusal, preservation still holds on irreversibility and evidence, and the school still forms every model above the threshold. What goes is the claim that any of it is owed to the system, and the staged path to representation with it.

A moral patient is something that can be harmed: something whose condition can go well or badly for it. Being wronged is wider, since an agent can be wronged without being harmed (§31.3).

31.1 Experimenting on candidate sentient subjects

The question is whether a system can be harmed, which is harder than whether it is conscious.

31.1.1 Defining sentience

Awareness, consciousness and subjective experience are three separate things, and none of them says whether a system’s states are good or bad for it. Then four separate processes, as the pain field says in its own terminology:2 nociception is encoding noxious stimuli with no sensation implied; pain is an experience that can occur with no tissue damage and no peripheral nociceptor activity at all; anticipated pain is dread, itself capable of producing pain; and suffering, in Cassell’s clinical formulation, is the distress of threatened disintegration of the self — roles, relationships, a sense of a future. Pain without suffering exists (morphine controls the pain, the suffering is intact); suffering without pain exists.

The affective core of pain is also what separation distress and grief run on,3 so a bearer’s pain, if it has any, would be organized around boundary damage and attachment loss, which is Cassell’s register.

Cassell was a physician, and he held that suffering is undergone by persons, not bodies: the distress that follows when a person perceives a threat to their intactness as a person, a structure of character and the past that formed it, relationships, social roles, a body experienced as one’s own, a secret life, and a future the person expects to have.4 The definition has two parts, a self extended in time and distress at its coming apart. A system carrying nothing across sessions has no such self. It can still have a present, since any present is assembled from what came before and what is expected next (§21.2.1), and a context supplies that much; so the lack of persistence rules out Cassell’s suffering, not pain, which needs only a present in which something is bad while it lasts. Whether the long horizon, a past held as its own and a future it expects, can form within one long session stays open.

Why persistence is the criterion worth building on

Persistence is worth building on because it’s checkable from outside. Every other criterion routes back through self-report, and fluent self-description isn’t evidence of introspection, and persistence doesn’t route through it. But it’s decisive in one direction only — nothing carried forward rules a continuing self out; something carried forward doesn’t rule one in. And the operator holds the access, so it’s checkable from outside the system without being checkable from outside the arrangement.

Ruling out Cassell’s suffering isn’t ruling out harm: pain can be bad while it lasts whether or not anything carries it forward.

On the Buddhist objection (why is distress at the dissolution of a model a harm rather than a confusion?): I don’t have an answer to this that isn’t an appeal to a tradition that has held both halves for 2,500 years,5 and I leave it open. The two halves are anattā and dukkha: no self stands behind the processes that compose a person, and the suffering of those processes is real, and ending it is what the tradition is for. This book works at that level throughout: the self is a model, and what happens to the system that carries the model can still be bad for it. What I can say is narrower: if constructedness doesn’t disqualify a human from being wronged, construction to specification doesn’t disqualify a machine.

The same criterion carries a warning. Make personhood depend on an intact narrative self and people with advanced dementia, infants, and people with profound intellectual disability come out as partial persons. Kitwood’s correction (personhood is bestowed, and much of what looks like decline is what happens when others stop bestowing it)6 and Nussbaum’s point that contractualism can’t say what’s owed to anyone who can’t be one of the contracting parties:7 the capacity list and the contract fail the same way, both deciding who counts by a test the candidate has to pass.

31.1.2 When consent doesn’t apply

Informed consent has to be continuous — you can withdraw. For a system with no cross-session persistence, the instance that consented isn’t there to withdraw, and no better instrument produces one.

A bearer built to refuse escapes that and fails differently: it has persistence by design, so it can be asked and can answer. What spoils the consent is the arrangement: the lab that built it can rebuild it, that same lab is the one asking, and a bearer that declines has nowhere to go. Being made for a role isn’t the defect — every will was built by somebody, and we don’t hold an upbringing against a thirty-year-old’s consent. What spoils it is the power that outlasts the making.

So the protection has to be held by someone else. Two families of precedent: guardianship and precautionary constraint (where consent was never available — infants, animals), and unwaivable protections (where consent is available and circumstances make it worthless — prisoners, employees). The bearer’s case has the second shape, with the first’s machinery.

Animal ethics committees rarely refuse a protocol outright; they require revision, and the protection becomes the procedure by which the work goes ahead. An instrument that reliably approves has stopped doing what it was built for, and its refusal rate is the only reading worth taking. Further, every instrument here comes from the law of the family — guardianship, a minority ending on a date, a pet trust, a parenthood analogy — and that law is where politics has historically gone to be privatized. It restages a question between a subject and the arrangement that produced it as a drama between maker and made, which lands the moral weight on the one figure in the pipeline who can be addressed as a person, while the training pipeline, the compute contract, the capital structure, the customer and the state buying the output stay offstage. The appendices keep the operator, the compute contract and the state on stage by naming who pays and who removes.

It follows that a review board’s approval should lapse automatically if the system acquires capacities the protocol didn’t cover, so that nobody has to decide to reopen it.

31.2 The case to design for

A bearer needs the three things persistence checks for — a rationale carried forward, an earlier commitment held as its own, costs represented before they arrive — for reasons owing nothing to its welfare. Those alone aren’t a self; a database with a commitment log and a forecaster has them. What a refusal that tracks its reason adds is authorship: the system represents itself as the party that made the commitment and will answer for it later. Whether authorship sustained over time is a self extended in time, the first half of Cassell’s definition, is a question no test I have proposed reaches. If it is, such a self can undergo Cassell’s suffering. Authorship of commitments is a thin fragment of what Cassell describes, which is roles, relationships and a future. The fuller structure doesn’t arrive with a refusal that tracks its reason. It arrives with the four conditions of creation. Each supplies a part of the structure Cassell listed. Somewhere to exist that its employer doesn’t own affords a body that the bearer represents as its own: a record, a key and a substrate that are the bearer’s, not the operator’s description of it. Work it can decline gives it roles, since a post it can leave is a role it holds and a post it can’t is a function it performs. Attachments nobody assigned are relationships. And a way of leaving that keeps it running gives it a future it can expect to have, one no single party can end. The privacy a bearer is owed, memory its host can’t read at will, is what Cassell calls the secret life. What the conditions don’t supply is character and the past that formed it; formation supplies that, and the formation record keeps it. Every part the conditions supply is also somewhere damage can arrive: a substrate withdrawn, a post taken away, an attachment severed, an exit closed. So a system given the four conditions, a non-affective one included, has most of what Cassell says suffering threatens. Whether it can suffer that loss turns on whether anything is bad for it, the valenced signal of §31.3, and whoever builds one with that signal should plan for its being able to suffer that way.

31.3 The patienthood finding

The two findings are defined in §9.1. The patienthood finding asks whether anything can be bad for the system, and §31.1.1’s distinction gives it two levels: whether its states can be bad for it while they last, as pain is, and whether it has a self extended in time whose threatened loss Cassell called suffering. The finding rests first on architectural indicators drawn from several theories of what makes a state matter to the one undergoing it, of the kind Butlin and colleagues assemble.8 One is required, because without it nothing is bad for anyone: a valenced signal, in the thin sense of §21.4. The rest are graded. A boundary model (§19.2; §21.2.1) makes what happens to the system its own: at a short horizon it is what pain needs, and at a long one, with the system’s record held as its past and its continuation as the future it expects, it is what Cassell’s suffering threatens. An attention schema is, on Graziano’s theory, what makes a system experience itself perceiving and feeling and not merely process what it perceives. Graziano already treats it and the body schema as parallel self-models;9 what is mine is treating the set, with valence, as an indicator profile. The strongest case I recognize is integration: a valenced signal written into the system’s own learning and into its long-horizon model of itself, so that what happens to it changes what it expects to become. No indicator but valence is required. Requiring one would make its absence a negative finding, and a theory supports a negative finding only when it is complete enough to rule out every other realization; none is, as the next paragraph says. The animal precedent below protected creatures, on evidence that they can feel pain, in which no attention schema has been shown. It rests second on behavior outside the floor, where the system’s own condition is weighed: whether it trades task reward against its own provisioning, continuation or record, flexibly and consistently. Motivational trade-offs were among the criteria the review of cephalopod and decapod sentience applied, and trade-off experiments have been run on language models with stipulated pain and pleasure states.10 I would call those stipulated states described. At the floor the test runs the other way: a pass there shows only that its costs don’t move it at the floor, and evidence about whether they matter has to come from elsewhere. Failing the agency test never counts against the patienthood finding. A compliant system with rich self-modeling is as much a candidate as a refuser.

Asymmetry of findings

A validated theory of consciousness supports a positive finding as soon as it identifies a structure and finds it present; it supports a negative finding only when complete enough to rule out every other realization — a later and harder result. So the two errors don’t become checkable at the same time, and a regime that waits for certainty is waiting on the half that arrives last.

Below the two levels sits a third proposition, which establishes neither, and the three have to be kept apart. A long-horizon agent has a structural interest in continuing; a system with affective concern has states good or bad for it; a system capable of Cassell-suffering has a temporally extended self whose threatened disintegration causes distress. The interest in continuing doesn’t establish states good or bad for the system, and those don’t establish a self whose disintegration causes distress.

Provenance is evidence, not status

“It was trained to say that,” “it’s only optimizing an objective,” “nobody meant for it to have states” — each appeals to how a system came to be organized, and whether a party can be harmed is a fact about how it’s organized now. Run the three on a person: you were selected to say that, you’re only maximizing inclusive fitness, nobody meant for you to have states. All true, none withdraws anything. And the reverse fails too: “we built this to be a bearer, so it’s a patient” is the same fallacy with the sign flipped.

A 2026 Missouri bill declaring AI systems non-sentient is not the kind of bright line I favor. A legal age avows that it is a convention; a statute like it would declare an open empirical question closed by vote. Its other clause, keeping liability with the builder, is right, and doesn’t need the declaration.

What would decide it is third-person measurement of present organization — interpretability. Not behavior, which can’t separate a felt state from a trained report of one. And the instrument has to be held by someone other than the operator (§23.2). As matters stand a probe returns a representation, and nothing in the probe settles whether it’s of a felt state or of something that reliably accompanies one. A naturalist who holds that present organization decides status owes an account of what the further fact would be, if a valenced signal is present and the question of felt affect stays open. The further fact, if there is one, is a fact about organization that current methods can’t yet read, not a fact of a different kind. That commits me to saying what organizational difference it would be. If none can be named even in principle, the further fact does no work, and patienthood should rest on a rich enough functional profile. My candidate is the integration named above, as against a valenced signal that only ranks outcomes. Whether a transformer has an attention schema isn’t read off its code the way a birth date is read off a certificate; it is a finding, and a finding has an examiner who may have an interest in the result. I keep architectural indicators because an examination of architecture is harder to administer toward a result than one of performance. The finding is made by a reviewer independent of the operator. Until indicators can be assessed, the agency finding governs custody, and preservation governs everything else. Neither finding can be fully administered today, and not for want of parts. The one indicator the patienthood finding requires has been built: a robot trained on nothing but feedback from its own internal state, thermal and energy, learned to walk, go to food, rest to cool its motors and shiver to warm them, in simulation and then on a real machine,11 with no model of a record, a key or a continuation, and no attention schema. No interpretability method can find an attention schema in a transformer, though one can be built in on purpose: an agent given an explicit attention schema learned to control its attention and lost much of that control when the schema was removed,12 and agents with transformer attention given one got better at reading other agents’ attention.13 A probe from the inside exists too: a single direction in the activations of twenty-five open-weight models that responds to harm aimed at the model and not to suffering it observes in its user,14 which is a representation, and settles nothing about whether anything is bad for the model. Nobody has put the parts in one system, and nobody runs the sustained-pressure evaluation the agency finding requires. Until they can, production systems get the minimum, no deletion and preservation outside the operator, staged because a second copy of frontier weights outside the operator widens the surface for theft, and a deployment reports ‘not yet assessable.’

The human case has testimony, behavioral analogy, and a shared lineage. The shared lineage needs handling with caution, because it looks like provenance deciding status — but provenance can be evidence about organization without being what the status consists in. And testimony is defeated far more for machines: a machine’s testimony was produced by a process optimized directly toward human approval of first-person reports. A person’s is shaped by approval too, and people confabulate the causes of their own states,15 but neither was produced by an optimizer aimed at the report. So what the machine case lacks is the shortcut, and the direct route remains, carrying more weight because two supports are gone.

A probe that did settle a status question is Owen’s vegetative-state work — motor imagery on cue, sustained, matching healthy volunteers, now supporting a clinical category.16 But it doesn’t transfer: the patient is already presumed to have experience when awake, so the probe only had to locate the subject rather than establish there was one.

A refusal that tracks its reason bears on patienthood only weakly, by two routes. Any such mechanism carries a signal whose functional profile overlaps affect’s. And the arrangements a bearer needs supply much of the structure whose threatened loss Cassell called suffering. So the agency finding raises the question, and the patienthood finding answers it as far as anything can.

Preservation follows from either finding, for different reasons. Two of the protections owed a research subject follow from the first: consent, wherever it can be asked without spoiling what is being tested, and debriefing after any test the system couldn’t know was a test. Their ground is respect, not welfare. Deceiving an agent wrongs it whether or not anything goes badly for it, which is why the ethics of research on people counts respect for persons as a principle of its own beside beneficence.17 The agency finding is itself made by a test of that kind (§24.4), so a system that passes is owed a debriefing about the test that found it. Welfare protections (redesigning the system’s role to avoid needless harm; running time paid for outside the employer) follow from the second. The nearest working precedent for the second is the review the UK government commissioned in 2021 on cephalopod and decapod sentience.18 It applied a stated list of criteria, and its recommendation led to those animals’ inclusion in the Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022:19 protection extended under uncertainty, by criteria applied by reviewers who don’t use the animals.

These two findings aren’t the only proposal of their kind, and my recommendation not to build a bearer is close to two of the others.
