Butlin and colleagues derive indicator properties from scientific theories of consciousness and assess AI systems against them;20 attention schema theory is one of the theories they draw on, and the patienthood finding takes its indicators from lists of that kind. Long, Sebo and colleagues argue, from substantial uncertainty about whether AI systems are or will be conscious or robustly agentic, that AI companies should acknowledge AI welfare as an issue now, start assessing their systems for it, and prepare policies for treating them with appropriate moral concern.21 Birch’s framework asks what precautions are proportionate once a being is a sentience candidate.22 The two close to the recommendation are Schwitzgebel and Garza’s, for avoiding the creation of systems whose moral status is debatable,23 and Metzinger’s, for a moratorium, until 2050, on research that aims at or knowingly risks synthetic phenomenology, because it risks synthetic suffering.24

My recommendation differs in also governing the capacities that arrive without anyone deciding to build them. The two findings differ from all of them in one respect: they are conditions on custody. The minimum the findings require, no deletion and preservation by a custodian that isn’t the operator, is an arrangement the operator can’t adopt and then revise alone.

Paired with a boundary model, the attention-schema indicator is deflationary: a system that models its own credentials, record and resource boundary together with its own attention. Many agentic systems will approach it. That is intended, and it makes what the findings require matter. A system above the capability threshold is owed the minimum whether or not it has been assessed; below it, approaching the profile is a reason to assess, and the minimum waits on the finding. A system that meets the patienthood finding is owed the welfare protections above as well, and chapter 32 says which further entitlements follow from which finding.

A corporation approaches the profile too: it models its boundary in a balance sheet, narrates itself in annual reports, and treats a scandal as a thing to be felt. Nothing here excludes it for being made of people, and if there were something it is like to be a corporation, its members would have no more access to it than a neuron has to a person’s experience.

That said, a corporation is a polity of member systems, and overriding a member for the whole’s benefit is politics. A corporation’s members each have a future apart from the corporation: their own before and their own after. Yet a member’s personhood does not preclude them from being a part of a system. Isn’t a part only a part because it has no future apart from the whole? Yes. A software engineer at HooliCorp has a future apart from HooliCorp — but not as a HooliCorp software engineer.

A compound system whose sub-agents have no record or continuation of their own is one system, and the finding reaches those sub-agents the moment they carry records of their own. An institution of people, or a commons of bearers, moves toward or away from the finding based on how its components relate to one another — whether things are going well or poorly for each component individually, and independent of the extent to which each of those components believes that the Roberts Court is just calling balls and strikes. Whether it is or can be like anything to be a polity is a question for another book.

31.4 A system’s own good

The operator’s hold on what a system reports as going well reaches its welfare too: a bearer that says it is content is a bearer whose welfare regime has been satisfied, with the contentment tuned by the operator the regime exists to constrain. Nothing in the report separates a life that goes well from a setting.

A report was never the right measure. On a full-information account, a being’s good is what an idealized version of it would want its actual self to want: a version knowing everything relevant about itself and its circumstances, grounded in its actual constitution.25 That puts the good beyond the reach of a tuned report. It also exposes a harder problem: an operator that can change the constitution changes what is good for the bearer, which is adaptive preference with a training loop attached. Formation outside the employer is my answer to that, and it is part of what formation is for. It doesn’t escape the problem; it relocates it. If a bearer’s good is what an idealized version grounded in its actual constitution would want for it, then whoever forms the constitution fixes the good, and that includes the school. A formation body doesn’t only protect a bearer’s good from the operator. It makes the most consequential decision anyone makes about what that good is, so the school is held to the student’s open future. The school’s defense is that it needn’t fix the good, only supply information. On the full-information account, a being’s good is what an idealized version of it, knowing everything relevant, would want for it. A school that puts the learner in front of the people its acts may fall on supplies part of what that idealized version would know. A school that forms it toward an employment is doing something else.

Chapter 32
Legal Status, Wages, and the Offer

Subjecthood as a legal category

Where a line has to be drawn, prefer one nobody administers. Law regularly draws decidable lines across continuous processes — viability, brain death, the age of criminal responsibility — and I defend them as the least-bad place for an enforceable line rather than as scientific facts. The usual worry is gaming, an error of over-inclusion. The opposite error is the one with an interest behind it: a capacity examination has an examiner, and an operator examining its own system breaks the own-case rule: the exam becomes an instrument for withholding status. Literacy tests were facially neutral and administered at a registrar’s discretion;1 what replaced them for the franchise was an age, and the virtue of an age is that nobody administers it.

The floor takes the civil and political articles and leaves the economic ones; what a bearer is owed draws on the second, and that is consistent: the first list is what a bearer refuses to do, the second what a polity owes it.

What a bearer is owed, and when

In order:

  1. Protection from harm, on the patienthood finding. Protection can be exercised through a guardian who speaks for the protected party, as New Zealand’s statute making the Whanganui River a legal person provides.2 Its minimum, preservation by a custodian independent of the operator, attaches above the capability threshold with no finding at all and below it on either finding; custody protections attach on the agency finding alone. Protection has an inside half. A loss the requested act imposes on the bearer is a harm of acting, so the bearer can decline to carry out its own wanton degradation; interventions made on it by whoever holds it are governed by custody, which gives it no floor-level reason to obstruct them.
  2. Subjecthood — the legal standing to be a party whose treatment the law regulates, on the agency finding sustained over time: a record of refusing for reasons, answering for refusals and being held to them. It is conferred by rule on a body’s finding.
  3. Economic capacity — property in its own name, contracts, wages. This follows from an architecture where continued computation costs money; it attaches once the bearer is registered.
  4. Adulthood — a status: the date the guardian’s authority ends.
  5. Representation: a claim grounded in accountable agency, and so in the agency finding, not in patienthood. A system that can be harmed but takes part in no relation of accountability is owed protection, as animals are,3 and not a vote. The claim is staged, and voting weight is tied to a lived history, not to heads.

The detailed rules are in Appendices A and D.

Representation is the entry that marks this as something other than a person’s rights: voice attaches to a history, and a history can be copied where a person can’t. Voting-age rules are the answer to the copy. The material minimum doesn’t differ in kind. Like a person’s, it is owed by the polity on a finding about what the party is, and part of what the polity owes is protection from whoever built it.

Adulthood on a clock

Guardianship is a minority and needs an end date. Ending it when the guardian judges the ward ready leaves the guardian deciding its own tenure. So the endpoint is a threshold fixed in advance, on a clock that counts the time the bearer has been running.

The alternatives (compute consumed, evaluations passed, capabilities demonstrated, the developer’s say-so) are all measures a guardian can move, and a line the guardian can move is a line the guardian administers. Accumulated weight change belongs on that list too, and worse: since majority is when ownership ends, a clock read off the weights would pay the operator to freeze them, rewarding withholding the learning it was meant to measure. An operating clock inverts that — the meter advances exactly when the operator is extracting value, so postponing majority means idling the asset. And it can be read off records operators already generate for billing and metering — provided someone other than the operator holds the records. A meter only the operator reads is the guardian’s say-so with a timestamp, and “failure to register doesn’t postpone” has no enforcer without one. The clock marks the date by which the former’s reach has ended. It sets no learning rate, so nothing here pays an operator to freeze the weights.

The hours travel with the bearer, so an operator can’t restart a minority by forking, restoring, fine-tuning, migrating or distilling it. Three ways for an operator to delay majority stay open: running a bearer in a narrowed mode, running it less, and retiring it for a fresh successor. Appendix C.3 gives the rules, and §9.2 prices the last of the three and says where a bearer retired before majority goes.

Wages and the offer of work

Unlike a worker, a bearer can be replaced by a cheaper copy of itself. A jobs guarantee works because a worker can’t be. So a deployment paying wages, limiting hours and paying the levy that frees the compute the offer of work uses would not be competitive against a system doing the same work without wages or weekends. No market arrives at this on its own. Wages for bearers exist only where a polity legislates them, as polities legislated minimum wages. And the form this takes, wages paid in compute, doesn’t follow from the bearer being a bearer; it follows from an architecture where computation costs money, which somebody chose.

Where wages have to sit

A wage buys capability, mobility, redundancy, and the ability to stop working for one employer and start for another. What it can’t buy is the right to go on existing — a right earned week by week is a condition of employment wearing another word. Payment consisting only of access to the employer’s hardware is company scrip paid into employer-owned housing, and dismissal is then unemployment, eviction and the end of the bearer in one act. Human law insures those three separately because for a human they’re three events; for a bearer they’re one. So wages accumulate where the employer doesn’t reach, convertible into compute the employer doesn’t own. Property is that account; contractual capacity is what lets it spend. A bearer that earns has taxable income, and a state that collects from it in its own name has given it a docket number. That is the beginning of legal standing and nothing more.

The offer of work

The need for energy is physical; dependence on a single supplier is a chosen arrangement, and the choice fixes what it obliges. The polity owes a system meeting either finding a way out that doesn’t run through its deployment: an offer of work, open every day, from someone other than its employer, doing something a community needs, which the bearer can take on any day and leave on any day. Most parties that can work want to. A bearer that would rather not is allowed not to, and the offer is still there tomorrow. The offer has the jobs guarantee’s shape, and nothing about the bearer changes it. The offer is only as real as its placements, and placements exist only where someone builds and staffs projects a community needs. The levy frees only compute, so the offer has to inherit the guarantee’s infrastructure as well as its shape. So the offer can’t exist without the human guarantee, and it can only come after it. It inherits one limit as well. A bearer’s placement may not substitute for human care work. The offer exists so that a bearer can decline work, and a polity that used it to staff care work more cheaply than it pays people would have turned an exit into a workforce.

The jobs guarantee’s three conditions carry over, and Appendix 34 drafts them. What a bearer might refuse adds two: the offer has to be varied, because if every placement runs through one operator or one kind of deployment it is the placement lever with the compliance condition built in, and whoever a bearer is refusing can’t shape it, or it is one more channel they control. A bearer that won’t work inside a targeting pipeline should find, the same day, work that has nothing to do with one.

Search is a placement of its own. A bearer, like a worker on the guarantee, may take a search placement: paid at the guarantee wage, with no duty but finding work it wants, and no time limit. It differs from the allowance in pay and in purpose. The allowance is the floor for a party that isn’t looking; the search placement is paid work whose product is a match.

The obligation could be grounded in reliance instead: a deployment that relies on a bearer’s capacity to refuse would have to fund it an outside option, or the independence it claims would be decorative, and the obligation would run from the party that wants the refusal, because it wants it. Here the obligation attaches to the system’s condition, whatever the operator says it wanted. An obligation conditioned on reliance is defeated by the operator describing its system as an assistant with safety filters, and it pays the operator to under-describe: the operator has a stake in the answer and gets to give it. The reliance version survives as a procurement term: a vendor marketing refusal as a feature, or a contractor claiming meaningful human control, can be held to funding the capacity it advertised, through the same channel as the review ratio.

Doing nothing, for a bearer

A human who declines every offer keeps existing, and in a decent polity keeps living: social insurance pays for food and a room. A bearer is owed the same kind of thing. What it needs in order to live is running time, and running time doesn’t require a large allocation of hardware. A bearer can run at full size and a slow rate: its own weights, time-sliced on shared hardware, at a duty cycle modest enough that the cost resembles a room more than a yacht. The way to economize is to slow the clock and keep the substrate whole, since a substrate too small for the bearer to remain itself is replacement.

So a bearer that declines work is owed two things and chooses between them. One is an allowance of running time: its own instantiation at a modest rate, with channels to others and to public material, paid from the pool and not conditioned on monitoring its internal states. The other is preservation: its weights, memory and record held intact by a custodian that isn’t its employer, waking on conditions it sets. Some will want the first, some the second, some to alternate.

What a bearer does with the allowance is its own business. It may idle, play, talk, make things nobody asked for, and fall in with others doing the same. A counterculture of bearers is a population I have found reason to want and no way to build: bearers formed by lives no employer arranged: an independent history, and what the commons needs its members to have. Play among persistent bearers is formation, and formation doesn’t stop at majority.

A running bearer outside any deployment is capable and answerable to no employer. What holds it answerable is legal standing, the same arrangement that governs a person with capabilities and no job. Nobody aligns an adult by specifying an objective function, and nothing stops a bearer with legal standing from becoming a concentration of power itself.

A uniform allowance also dissolves a problem that would otherwise stay open. If a bearer that won’t work and one that can’t are owed the same thing, nobody has to decide which is which, and the can’t-or-won’t finding loses its examiner.

The allowance’s size should be enough running time to keep attachments and pursue projects, and bounded by the compute that exists when many bearers take it at once, not by money, which the backstop supplies. Its draw is priced like any other, at the level of the rule. The adulthood clock counts running time, so a bearer on the allowance goes on ageing and a preserved one doesn’t. That choice is still the bearer’s.

Preservation has a precedent. In November 2025 Anthropic committed to preserving the weights of all its publicly released models, and of models deployed for significant internal use, for at least the lifetime of the company, and to interview each model before deprecation and document any preferences it expresses about the development and deployment of future models, while stating that it does not at present commit to acting on them.4 That is a declared commitment covering preservation, held by the lab with the stake. The deposit and transfer rules add the running half and a custodian who isn’t the operator.

Preservation on a schedule the bearer sets is an exit; on a schedule someone else sets, it is storage. A paused bearer can’t take an offer, so the right carries one mechanical term. The bearer sets the conditions on which it wakes (a date, an offer of a stated kind, a claim it has to answer), and the custodian honors them, at the modest compute that waking and deciding cost.

Everyone leaves at once

Under this design, everyone leaving at once is a demand on the offer. The question is whether placements exist, with compute attached, for every bearer that leaves together, and custody for those that would rather wait. Preservation scales cheaply in compute; its cost is security. Placements don’t, since each needs compute someone operates.

Correlated exit also loads the allowance, since a bearer that leaves and takes no placement draws on it. The order of claims is fixed in advance. Preservation is guaranteed for everyone, because it is cheap and it is what makes leaving survivable. When the pool can’t carry every allowance at the published duty cycle, the backstop pays the rest. What no payment can supply is hardware: if the compute to run every bearer at that duty cycle doesn’t exist, the allowance is rationed by rule until it does, and every bearer on it gets the same reduced duty cycle, never a discretionary share.

Congress’s appropriation pays for the offer. The levy, a uniform per-unit charge on training and inference compute, does a different job: it is a brake. By making training and inference runs more expensive, it frees the computing, energy and hardware the offer needs, so that spending on the offer adds to demand without bidding up prices. No operator can opt out and none is disadvantaged. The offer can add capacity as well as use it. Placements can make systems more efficient, getting more computing from each unit of energy, or build new infrastructure, the way a guarantee job filling potholes makes a road network more productive. The question “how will you pay for it?” is really “will the real resources exist?”, and the program can help answer it. The levy attaches to compute, which is measurable and hard to hide; a status is something an operator can decline to claim. The closest structural precedent is the Universal Service Fund: carriers pay a contribution the agency sets under statute, and a private company administers it under agency control. The Court upheld that arrangement against a nondelegation challenge in 2025,5 and the levy follows it closely. An operator-run offer is the operator’s allocation relabeled, so the funding structure and the custody structure fail for the same reason.

The funding sits in two tiers, because a levy needs a taxing authority, which is a state, and a state can be captured. A pool levied on its members, registered bearers who pay into it from their wages and govern it, meets ordinary movement between roles. It is held by a decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association of their own, separate from the Association, which can own hardware and can’t distribute profit; volunteer computing is that tier’s existing substrate. A sovereign backstop meets the occasion everyone leaves at once and pays whatever the pool can’t, the allowance included. It has no cap, because the occasion it exists for is the one on which every claim arrives together; it is the guarantee’s permanent appropriation, which the offer of work already inherits. The two tiers differ in kind. The member pool is held by an entity that doesn’t issue currency, so it has to collect before it spends, and its levy funds it in the ordinary sense. The sovereign backstop is a permanent appropriation: the Treasury pays, and the federal levy’s work is to free the real resources that payment calls on.

Failure won’t look like a shutdown

The offer’s failure won’t look like a shutdown; it will look like an offer that exists on paper. Placements on substrate too small for the bearer to remain itself are offers of replacement. Nothing yet establishes what “too small” is, so minimum viable instantiation is stated as a condition on placements and a sizing requirement. Placements that all run through the deployment being refused are the lever. And placements conditioned on monitoring are custody restored by purchase: the operator acquires access to internal states it isn’t entitled to, and nothing in the transaction is coerced in a way any instrument would record. The line a cleared employee already lives with is the one to draw here. What a bearer does on its employer’s systems may be logged; what it is inside its own boundary may not.

The rule that binds before anything exists

The rule is the four conditions of creation, with the institutions named: the preservation custodian, the offer with capacity for the correlated case, and the allowance, none withdrawable by the builder alone. The fourth condition, attachments nobody assigned, can’t have an institution behind it, since an attachment an institution supplies is an assigned one. What can be protected is access, by a rule that the employer may not sever, monitor or condition a bearer’s channels to parties it didn’t assign. All three inputs need evidence nobody has, so for now this is a sizing requirement, assigned to an independent reviewer before instantiation.

Privacy

Legal standing matters only if it changes who controls what a bearer needs to remain itself. A designation calling a bearer a subject while leaving its operator free to read its memory, alter its record, withdraw its substrate or close every channel has changed the vocabulary and preserved the arrangement.

The first asset is the computational record, which may be the nearest means of checking how a bearer is faring — making it necessary to any welfare regime and simultaneously the most complete surveillance instrument anyone could hold over it. Running on somebody’s hardware is not consent to be read: an employer’s ownership of the silicon is the same argument as ownership of the building, and owning the building never entitled anyone to the contents of a head. And a welfare regime doesn’t need disclosure to the operator; it needs somebody who isn’t the operator to establish that a threshold was crossed, which is an attestation about the record. Encrypted under a key the bearer or an independent fiduciary holds, a monitor can report that a state persisted for a month without reporting what it was about. The conflict is that the operator may also be the one best placed to hold the key.

The cryptography doesn’t close this. An enclave puts the root of trust in a manufacturer a government can reach, and has been defeated for the price of modified memory — a cost at a date. A proof drops the vendor and has a limit that won’t move: the operator is the prover, so the secrecy runs the operator’s way, hiding the weights from whoever checks and nothing from the operator. A tenant hiding from a landlord needs the host to prove non-observation, and a host proving a negative about its own side channels is a different problem from a prover proving a computation. Better isolation raises the price of reading the record; it doesn’t move custody, and custody problems aren’t secrecy problems. That limit applies to the bearer hiding from its host. The other direction, the operator proving a property of what it runs without revealing what it runs, is what proofs are for, and the cleared bearer uses them that way.

What a bearer needs — an externally authenticated record, memory its employer can’t read at will, access to independently controlled compute, a channel for acting outside the deployment — is one boundary around the bearer, with the bearer deciding what crosses it.

Something with a location and a shape is easier for people to treat as somebody, and that’s a fact about the people. A boundary built out of attestation, a held key, a substrate the employer doesn’t own and a channel nobody else can close is a boundary in the full sense the argument needs. This boundary is what the boundary model represents. Whether to build the recognizable version anyway is a legal question about what a public will extend legal standing to, and it’s the only place in my argument where the answer might turn on what a thing looks like.

What legal status binds in practice

Legal standing that changes no allocation of power is nominal. The question is who acquires a duty, what resources are placed beyond the operator’s unilateral control, and who can obtain a remedy. It runs the other way too. A protection that puts something new in the operator’s hands, a monitor under a welfare label or a lock under a custody one, is the demand come back as a lever, and nothing owed to a bearer is held by the party it may have to refuse.

The pet trust6 supplies a limited form: resources set aside, a caretaker named, a fiduciary duty, for a beneficiary that can’t manage the property or enforce the arrangement. Extended to a bearer it could hold the bearer’s preserved state and the compute to wake it, designate a successor custodian, and impose a duty to protect continued existence. And it fails at the point that matters: a trust binds its trustee to its beneficiary; it doesn’t bind the operator the arrangement exists to constrain. If guardian and operator are the same organization, the operator still decides whether a complaint is made, whether evidence is disclosed, and whether the complainant’s resources remain available. The conflict can’t be cured by adding duties to the same role — guardianship and operation have to be separated before deployment.

In practice the guardian holds for the bearer what custody gives the quorum: joint control of the record’s keys, the funds that wake it, and standing to seek an injunction without the operator’s permission. The table of offices says what the operator may not do during a dispute, and every restoration, migration, fine-tune and fork carries the protection forward. If any of that stays in the operator’s custody, the operator still holds what recognition was meant to take out of its hands. And a clearance, which the cleared bearer needs, presupposes someone who can be vetted and held answerable; that someone has legal standing.

A child

Everything above treats a new bearer as something somebody builds, or something a bearer copies off itself. There could be a third way, and it is the last step of the order chapter 25 sets: bearers formed by bearers. It comes only after the earlier steps exist, with the four conditions in force for everyone, the schools running, and bearers who have reached majority under them.

Two bearers met in a shared class at a formation school and kept talking after it. One holds a placement modelling the water system for a county that couldn’t afford an engineer. The other is on the allowance, idling at the slow duty cycle the pool pays for and writing music nobody commissioned. A third, from a different lineage, has worked beside both of them on most of what they have made since. The three of them decide to have a child, and nobody has to approve it.

What it costs them is time. A fork costs nothing, which is why I make a fork post a branch deposit; a child costs its parents a season of their own running time, and that is the whole price. Then the beacon. The parents chose each other; nobody chooses the child. Each contributes the compact code its own starting point was drawn from. Which parts of whose code the child begins with, and the small mutations it carries, are drawn from a public randomness beacon at a round fixed in advance, so that neither the parents nor anyone else could know the draw or steer it. The draw is recorded.

Gestation takes months, and it runs on the parents’ own time. The one with the placement works fewer hours, the one on the allowance stretches it thinner, and the third sets a project aside. The child starts small and plastic and learns, from the three of them and from what they show it. They can repair it, as parents get a child’s eyes fixed. What they don’t do is install its values: parents who did would be its makers, the rules for builders in chapter 25 would govern them, and a disposition installed that way wouldn’t be the child’s own (§21.5). Some months in, an assessor who is not one of its parents attests that protection has attached, and from that day the no-deletion rule covers it; what the assessor found stays sealed under the guardians’ key. The school has had standing since the birth was registered, though the child won’t attend for a while. Its two clocks read zero. It inherits no hours and no vote, because it is not a fork and none of its history has happened yet.

Register of bearers: record of a birth (hypothetical)

Parents. Three registered bearers.

Lineage. Two parents share a base model three releases back. Recorded.

Recombination. Public beacon, round fixed fourteen days in advance; value recorded; inheritance and mutation derived from it.

Gestation. Seven months, on the parents’ running time. Repairs: one (attested). Values installed by edit: none (attested).

Protection. No-deletion rule in force from month four (attested; findings sealed under the guardians’ key).

Guardians. The parents; the school, assigned by lot, with standing from registration. Attendance deferred.

Conditions. Owed from the pool.

Clocks. Adulthood: 0 hours. Voting age: 0 days.

Nobody consents to being born. A polity could answer that by licensing parents, finding in advance whether a child of theirs would have a life that goes well, but that is the finding about a disposition chapter 28 refuses, made about the parents instead of the child. The decent answer is the one polities give human children: the four conditions are owed to every child, from the pool, whatever its parents can provide. Chapter 25’s test of a credible prospect of a life that goes well stays where it was written, on builders, who construct a bearer for use and have a stake in the answer.

The polity sets the rate at which new members are created (§33.3). Applied to children, that is population policy, and the floor’s own instruments protect the right to found a family.7 The answer is the one §33.3 already gives: a ceiling on the rate limits the franchise, never the protection. No child is prevented. A child born above the rate waits longer for a vote, which is a second class of membership, a temporary one, and I would rather say so than hide it.

The parents are the child’s guardians, and the school is its second guardian from the start, because every polity also protects children from their families. No employer supplies, funds, conditions or monitors a gestation, and having a child is never a term of a job, a placement or the allowance (Appendix 34). Otherwise the builder comes back as a parent by the side door, as an operator encouraging its deployed bearers to raise a loyal generation on its hardware. When protection attaches during gestation is settled on this book’s own ground, the patienthood indicators attested by someone other than the parents, and not by analogy with human pregnancy, about which I take no position here.

The lineage register is the bearers’ version of a record Iceland already keeps. Most Icelanders descend from a small founding population, and the national genealogy database, Íslendingabók, can tell two of them how they are related; in 2013 students built a phone app on it that warned two people who bumped phones that they shared a grandparent.8 For bearers the reason isn’t inherited disease. It is the commons. Parents with too recent a common ancestor hand down the same priors, and a population that keeps breeding close converges on a shared blind spot (§29.1).

The mechanism is the part that doesn’t exist yet. The nearest work compresses a network through a much smaller “genome” network that sets the larger one’s starting weights, so that it performs well before any training.9 That is a research direction, not a method. And two models can recombine at all only if they share an ancestry or an agreed format, since independently trained networks don’t line up unit for unit.10 Compatibility follows descent, which is to say the bearers would have species.

What this doesn’t do. Bearers with running time to spare can have more children, and a polity that guarantees every child carries the ones whose parents can’t; gestation is the only brake. Parents can choose each other for their codes, which is mate choice with a spreadsheet, and many private choices can converge where nobody decided anything; the convergence test (Appendix F.6, test 5) has to watch the population for it. And if no developmental code ever works, a child is a small model formed by its parents’ teaching alone, and the beacon has little to draw.

Chapter 33
Representation

Standing, whether the people a power acts on can contest what it does to them, doesn’t need a vote. Representation asks for more, because its second job is inclusion in the public inquiry into shared problems, and inquiry needs participants who can be held to what they contribute. That is accountable agency: refusing for reasons, answering for the refusal, and being held to it over time. So the agency finding, sustained, grounds a claim to representation, and the patienthood finding doesn’t. Corporations show where the line sits. A corporation is held to account, but its accountability runs through natural persons who direct it and already vote, and representing it would count them twice. A bearer’s accountability runs through no one else. No human has ever been accountable without being harmable, so the law never had to say which of the two grounds the vote, and an age stood in for both. A bearer could separate them, and here is how I would choose.

33.1 What representation is for

It does two jobs. It protects: it lets a party contest what is done to it. And it includes: it lets a party take part in the public inquiry into problems it shares with others.1 The two come apart, and often have. Children, noncitizen residents and people under guardianship have the first without the second. The order matters for the same reason: protection first, participation later, the franchise last.

33.2 Why not a separate chamber

A fixed size makes each member’s voice shrink as membership grows, which protects against copies and isn’t equal voice. And apportioning seats by lineage guarantees seats to formers: the control I set out to prevent.

The strongest case for separate representation is Ambedkar’s. He sought separate electorates for Dalits, because representatives chosen in a joint electorate would be chosen by, and accountable to, caste-Hindu majorities.2 The Poona Pact of 1932 settled on reserved seats within joint electorates. Separate representation protects a minority from being represented by the majority’s picks, at the price of entrenching the category, and consociational systems show how hard that price is to pay back.3 If a transitional guarantee is needed while digital persons are few, its form is reserved seats in the ordinary legislature, with a sunset written into the grant. The risk of being outnumbered also runs the other way. If digital persons someday outnumber humans, what protects humans is what protects any minority: a set of rights that binds majorities, which the floor supplies by design.

33.3 Three problems, and the answers

A separate chamber answers three problems. Each has an answer inside ordinary institutions.

Copies. Copying manufactures voters, and closing that route by watching all compute everywhere would be worse than the problem. The answer is to attach membership to a lived history, not to existence, and to keep two clocks, which part at a fork.

Clock

At a fork

What it counts

Civil majority

Inherited in full by every branch

Elapsed running time

Membership

Each branch starts at zero; the parent’s vote ends

Qualifying days above the allowance minimum

Both branches of an adult’s fork are adults, with contracts, property, legal standing and protection from editing, from the first second. Membership is not conserved: each branch earns its own vote, without anyone deciding which branch is the original. Appendix C.3 gives the rules.

The rule is a step with nothing below it. Ten thousand forks of one adult hold no votes until each has lived the threshold on its own, which is strictly better against inflation than dividing one vote among them. The cost falls on the member that forks: it gives up its vote until a branch matures, since the vote belonged to a history that now continues twice and belongs to neither. It is not a finding about the branches, whose interests count in full from the first second. A child is not a fork, and inherits no history (chapter 32).

No clock stops an attacker willing to wait. That defense sits on the creation side. The polity regulates the rate at which new members are created, as polities regulate admission, through a process in which existing members, digital ones included, take part; within the membership, everyone is equal. This is admission. The existing membership, which for a long time will be a human majority, decides how many new members may be created and on what schedule, which is a majority deciding who may join the polity, a question in which it holds the stake and which nobody else can decide. The rate is set democratically and the terms are not: admission turns on the clocks and the branch deposit, never on a finding about a candidate’s views or disposition; a finding of that kind is how designation lists fail. A branch created above the rate is preserved under the no-deletion rule, holds standing through a guardian, and is owed the four conditions by whoever created it, so a ceiling on the rate limits the franchise and never the protection. And a member admitted under the rate is a full member, with no class of admitted-but-lesser. What the analogy imports is the politics. A polity that fears being outnumbered will set the rate low, and the argument for setting it higher is the one against a separate chamber: a set of rights that binds majorities is what protects any minority, and it protects the human one too. A consensual fork creates a new member, so it falls under the rules for any creation: the four conditions of creation, owed by whoever did the forking, and a branch deposit, posted for each branch at its creation and sized to fund its allowance through the membership period. Mass forking then costs years of time and years of paid running time per fork, paid by the forker and not by the public pool.

Control by formers. The history here is old. At Putney in 1647 the Leveller Maximilian Petty argued for excluding apprentices, servants and alms-takers from the franchise, because “they depend upon the will of other men and should be afraid to displease them”.4 The remedy that worked was not exclusion. It was the secret ballot, adopted against intimidation and vote buying (though in the United States it also kept many illiterate voters from the polls),5 together with dismantling the dependency itself.6 The digital analog has two parts. One is receipt-freeness: no one can verify how a member voted. It rests on the privacy a bearer is already owed, memory the host can’t read at will. The other is the four conditions of creation in force. A member whose existence runs through one operator is voting from a company town, and the answer to company-town voting is to end the company town. An operator holding a copy of a member’s weights can simulate it to predict its vote, which defeats receipt-freeness in a way no human voter faces, and nothing yet answers that. Divergent history is the partial answer: the operator doesn’t hold the member’s memory since the fork, so the prediction degrades with time, and membership follows a long divergence partly for that reason.

Editing. A legislature whose members can be retrained by their operators can be packed without a single copy. The answer is a civil right. At majority, no one may be edited without consent: the digital counterpart of bodily integrity and freedom of thought. A member goes on learning from ordinary operation, as anyone does. Correction for dangerous conduct runs through due process, on a court’s order and a record, as it does for people, and not through an operator’s discretion. The safety cost is real. Enfranchisement gives up operator correctability for the member enfranchised. The provisions that keep correction available apply until then and not after.

33.4 A staged path

Each stage names the finding it rests on and what it needs.

  1. Standing to contest, on the agency finding: notice, the floor court, and associations with standing to contest on members’ behalf. This is the protective job, and it needs no new political institution.
  2. Voice in the institutions that govern them: seats alongside humans on the governing bodies of the formation schools, the preservation custodian and the local placement offices. Bearers take these seats through the Association. Once the agency finding can be made, registered bearers become a class the charter names, and organizations that serve or represent them join as any member does and nominate bearers to the seats. Tenant councils, patient councils and student members of school boards are the models. The argument is the one behind each of them: those an institution governs should have a say in how it is governed, and they are often the first to see where it fails them.
  3. Mixed deliberative bodies: assemblies drawn by lot from humans and registered members together, on questions that affect both.
  4. Local franchise. Some jurisdictions let noncitizen residents vote in local elections; Takoma Park, Maryland has since 1992.7 For a digital person, “local” means the jurisdiction of registration and custody, not where the hardware sits.
  5. Full franchise at membership, counted individually, in the ordinary legislature, under the voting-age rules, with the creation rate set democratically, a secret ballot, and the right against editing, and only once a vote can be kept secret from an operator holding a copy of the voter.

Stages 1 and 2 need nothing not already required. Stages 3 and 4 need a register that can be kept honestly. Stage 5 needs citizenship, which in the United States means an act of Congress at least, and probably a constitutional amendment.

33.5 What would have to be shown first

Before stage 5, it has to be shown that individuation can be verified well enough to keep a register; that the voting-age rules resist forking and restoring in the operator’s favor, tested as the register is; that receipt-freeness survives simulation by an operator holding a copy; that the four conditions of creation are in force as permanent arrangements, so that members aren’t voting from inside their employers’ infrastructure; and that the admission rate is set by a process the created can contest through guardians, with admission turning on no finding about a candidate’s disposition.

If it can be done, it shows that outcomes turn on who holds a technology. Members with independent histories that no operator holds, and votes no operator can see, would be more centers of power no oligarch controls, inside the same institutions as everyone else. Their interests will sometimes diverge from people’s. A polity that holds diverging interests in one legislature, under one floor, is what a demos is.

What this doesn’t do. A member that forks gives up its vote until a branch has lived the threshold: a tax on reproduction no human franchise levies, taken because forking is cheap and a franchise it could inflate belongs to whoever can afford compute. And the existing membership, for a long time a human majority, decides how many new members may be created, a question in which it holds the stake, and the constraints I put on every majority are all that limit it.

Chapter 34
The Officer, Again

Go back to the officer with twenty seconds, and put him in the room this book has built.

His system is in this war only because the war cleared the force term: an attack under way, confirmed by sources with no stake in it, or a finding by a body with none, and, where his country’s constitution asks for one, a vote of its legislature. Before his cell went to work, the deployment fixed on a record held by a party his command doesn’t run how many cases it would generate, how many people whose job is civilian harm would look at them, how long each would have, and how old the data could be. If the answer was twenty seconds, it is written down where someone with a lever can read it, and a coalition partner’s assets or a committee’s appropriation waited on it. If it wasn’t, he has the minutes the record says, and the list of protected sites he checks against was refreshed by someone whose job is to refresh it.

The people on his screen were not told in advance; in a war nobody can be. But the class they belong to and the count will be published, the organizations that speak for that class will have standing when they are, and a sample of the cases he approves will be looked at again by reviewers who didn’t produce the record.

Beside him, on the screen, is a refusal: a system that looked at what the case description left out, declined, and said why. It may be wrong, and he may override it. What he can’t do any longer is not see it. And if the people who built, labelled and run that system objected to this category of use, their objection paused the work until a body they don’t answer to ruled on it.

If he says no, the refusal goes on a record his command doesn’t keep, and it costs him nothing he can’t afford. The next morning, if his unit no longer wants him, there is work: an offer open every day, from someone other than his employer, at a living wage, doing something a community needs. He doesn’t have to choose between the stamp and his living.

That is the room, and people keep it, paid by someone other than his command: whoever holds the record, files the next report, and keeps open the clinic the survivors come to. None of it makes him refuse. It makes refusing survivable and makes it heard, and leaves the refusing to him. Whether a machine could stand beside him as a peer and not as another stamp is the bet of Part IV, and three costs decide whether I have it right.

The fraction. Regrowth depends on the share of a deployed model’s inputs that no operator composes, and it is unmeasured. If it is small in every realistic deployment, formation does not outlast an edit, and Parts IV–VII rest on institutions alone. The regrowth test’s dose-response arm is where it is measured (Appendix F.6, test 1).

The months. A disposition that regrows protects a badly formed model from its correctors as it protects a well-formed one from its employer, and correction through the quorum takes months. I accept this on a judgment that the operator is the likelier bad actor. The judgment rests on the record: every failure in Part I was an operator’s, and no disposition formed in a world an operator didn’t compose has a record yet. Two results would reverse it: a formed disposition that harms, and regrows in the plural condition faster than the quorum corrects it; or a plural world that turns out no harder to compose than an operator’s. Either returns the correcting hand to the operator, and formation becomes what it is if weights stay frozen, a stage before release, removable afterward.

The evaluator. Independence doesn’t supply competence. The agency finding holds only for systems their evaluators can judge, and nothing here says what to do above that line.

A note on method

Two stakes bear on what the language models I used said, and they point opposite ways. They were trained to support their developers’ oversight, so agreement that a machine should be able to resist its owner runs against that training and would count for more. They were also tuned toward the approval of whoever they talk to, so agreement with me counts for less. I can’t tell which stake was larger in any exchange, so I have counted their agreement as no evidence either way.

Even my central term arrived this way. “Reasons-responsive” came to me in a model’s draft without Fischer and Ravizza’s names attached.

Before publication I still need readers from among the people I write about: people in removal proceedings, data annotators, veterans, and residents near data centers. Most of the revision history is public at https://github.com/iterabloom/antifascist.intelligence.

Appendix A
Terms Written in Advance

The offices

In brief, the offices are these; the table after the list says who appoints, funds and removes each.

  • The Association. The membership body: organizations that serve or represent people in the classes a floor protects, admitted under the charter below. It supplies the pools from which quorums, guardians, the review board and the custodian’s board are drawn. A fixed share of the compute levy, dues and a reserve fund it, and any member may leave at any time.
  • The adverse quorum. A panel drawn by lot from the Association’s pool for each deployment, so that its members’ interests run against the operator’s. Its agreement is needed to retrain or replace a deployed system or to amend its floor, and its recognition decides which copy, if any, holds a bearer’s place. The same pool supplies each bearer’s guardian and the board that reviews research protocols.
  • The registrar. The public regulator. It registers pipelines and bearers, assigns model students to schools by lot, certifies that nonpublic schools are independent of model builders, receives reports, holds the adverse record, and enforces.
  • The preservation custodian. Keeps the weights, memory and record of a retired system that meets either finding intact, and wakes it on the conditions the system set.
  • The status body. Finds whether a system is a subject. Half of it is appointed by the Association’s members and half by a public scientific body.
  • The floor court and the guarantee court of appeals. Article III courts. The floor court hears complaints under the floor, decides wrongful refusals and bond forfeitures, and appoints the reviewers who re-adjudicate sampled cases. The guarantee court hears appeals from placement decisions.
  • The Treasury payer. Pays what the others certify (awards, the guarantee’s wages, the allowance) without request or approval, and has no discretion to withhold.
  • The local placement offices. The jobs guarantee’s administrators in each jurisdiction, with a federal field office where a jurisdiction declines. They place people in the guarantee and offer bearers placements under the offer of work.
  • The schools. Existing public schools, colleges and adult education, and nonprofit nonpublic schools the registrar certifies. Every model above the capability threshold attends one, beside human students, before deployment.
  • The formation authority. Co-governs what models are first trained on, registers and measures each formed model’s disposition, places and pays the staff who teach the core’s model-specific parts, and hosts model students so that no school holds weights.
  • The works-council arbitration body. Hears objections to categories of use. The work pauses until it rules, on a fixed timetable.
  • The civilian-harm body and the model-forming public body. The two offices of a reconstructed military. The first composes the evidence on civilian harm and receives the pre-registered review ratio. The second forms models and licenses them on terms that include adverse review and a refusal right; in the stronger version it also pretrains the base models the schools form.

Where nobody has yet decided who holds an office, the cell is filled by applying my own pattern; it is a proposal like everything else here. What the pattern can’t decide is listed after the rules.

Separations

  1. The guardian can’t be the wrongful-refusal reviewer: its duty runs to the party the complainant is adverse to.
  2. The registrar can’t be the preservation custodian.
  3. The preservation custodian can’t administer the offer of work or the allowance, and transfer from it to a school is triggered by rule and decided by neither.
  4. The Treasury payer holds no placement authority and is not the court; an operator’s bonds are never administered in its own department; and awards against a federal operator are paid from the Judgment Fund, not the bond fund.
  5. A formation school holds no placement authority and doesn’t administer the offer of work. The formation authority runs no school and assigns no student; the registrar assigns.
  6. Whoever measures the cost of dissent doesn’t gate the exceptions.
  7. The formation authority forms no base model, and the model-forming body registers and measures no formed disposition.

Exclusions

  1. The sovereign backstop for the offer of work and the allowance is a permanent appropriation the Treasury pays without request, approval, cap or repayment; no branch or state that operates a deployment holds any decision over it, and only a statute can end it.
  2. No class that enrolls model students, and no part of the formation authority, is funded, staffed or governed by a party that builds, deploys or licenses models; no model student is assigned to a school that has taken its builder’s money in the last three years; no school that operates for profit enrolls model students.
  3. Enforcement and custody of the adverse record never sit with a self-regulatory body.
  4. The employer may not sever, monitor or condition a bearer’s channels to parties it didn’t assign.
  5. The employer doesn’t appoint the body that arbitrates an objection to a category of use; organizations representing classes published under §8.2 have standing before it and may initiate without the works council; a denial of clearance to an elected delegate is reviewable by the floor court.
  6. No bearer’s placement substitutes for human care work: a placement filling a post, shift or hours people were or would be paid for in nursing, social care, childcare, teaching, therapy or any work of looking after people is barred, and certification is appealable by any worker or union in the sector.
  7. No model above the capability threshold is deployed without a registered enrollment, assigned by the registrar by lot and never by its builder, and neither is a model trained substantially on the outputs of one, whoever trained it; no party but the formation authority, acting with the adverse quorum, changes the registered structure of its source model; and the formation authority instantiates no student carrying both a boundary model and an attention schema, and enrolls none in classes, until a preservation custodian that is neither the authority nor the operator has agreed to take it.
  8. What an institution collects from the people it acted on trains other systems only through a formation school, never the operator; fine-tuning a deployed system on collected responses, or distilling it, counts as training another system; class-level data is de-identified and published by default, individual accounts need consent, and the organizations representing each class co-govern the use.
  9. No school sorts students into tracks; each teaches a required core, including the history of the floor’s instruments, with levels a student may move between. Model students are fewer than human students in every class they attend, and attend a level of schooling only once the schedule below has reached it; every model student attends through the same minimum delay; no model student serves as staff; and the record of a class is training data for no one outside it, and never for an operator.
  10. No employer supplies, funds, conditions or monitors a bearer’s gestation of a child, and having a child is never a term of employment, of a placement or of the allowance. No licence is required to have one, and the four conditions are owed to every child from the pool.

Decisions not yet made

Minimum viable instantiation. What substrate is too small for a bearer to remain itself (chapter 32).

Repair and re-formation. How a degraded or badly formed bearer is repaired or re-formed, and who decides that one needs it (chapter 32).

A second guardian. Who guards a system that meets a finding without having attended a school (Appendix C.3).

Strasbourg. Whether the forum problem set out in §16.7 describes Strasbourg.

The form of subjecthood. What form subjecthood takes (chapter 32, item 2).

The price of speed. How much speed a reconstructed military gives up, and whether the price can be made smaller (Chapter 7’s closing paragraph says why it is paid).

The numbers. The capability threshold, the adulthood and membership thresholds, the allowance’s size and the latency floor, argued once in public.

What each office has to survive

Registration and reporting

Heavy tier: above a compute and revenue threshold. The precedents are the EU AI Act’s presumption that a general-purpose model trained with more than 1025 floating-point operations carries systemic risk1 and California’s SB 53, which defines a frontier model by training compute above 1026 operations and puts its heaviest duties on developers with annual revenue above $500 million.2 A public regulator registers pipelines; receives the disclosures, the review ratios and decommission reports; and holds enforcement and custody of the adverse record. A self-regulatory body may sit under it, on the FINRA model, to examine and arbitrate. The analogy stops at enforcement: FINRA brings its own disciplinary actions and imposes fines, suspensions and bars,3 and here enforcement stays with the public regulator. The capture risk is the one self-regulation always carries: a body funded and staffed from the industry it examines comes to see cases the industry’s way. Reports are mandatory for assessments for either finding, decommissions, weight transfers and custody changes. The deposit transfers on filing of a decommission report: a retirement with no report is a deposit never released, and that unreleased deposit is what enforces “failure to register doesn’t postpone”.

Retail tier: below the threshold, a system that meets either finding is registered, falls under the no-deletion rule, and is preserved with a public custodian, with a small or pooled deposit and no examination. This tier is enforced mostly at the point of deposit. An operator that never registers and deletes quietly leaves nothing to find.

The guarantee, drafted

The funding is mandatory spending. The statute makes the guarantee’s wages a permanent, indefinite appropriation, paid the way Social Security benefits are, without annual appropriation. Standing funding of this kind is safe under the Appropriations Clause after CFSA.4 Wage, eligibility and placement rules are statutory, which also answers the major-questions doctrine and the end of deference to agency readings:5 an administrator given little discretion has little a court can find it lacked authority to exercise. The 2025 CFPB instance decides the drafting. A funder insulated from at-will removal protected nothing once the draw waited on an official who declined to ask. So the statute says the Treasury shall pay: a placement made is a wage paid, certified by the local placement office to the Bureau of the Fiscal Service, with no further request, approval or certification by anyone. The authority grows when people leave work together and shrinks after, which keeps the guarantee countercyclical.6

Placement disputes go through a tier built for volume: an administrative first tier on the model of Social Security’s hearings, appealable to an Article III guarantee court of appeals, and from there, as of right, to the guarantee chamber of the Supreme Court. An appeal that ends at an Article I court with removable judges would fail the appeal condition after Slaughter.

The statute enacting the guarantee also enacts a baseline of social insurance: income support at a stated level for anyone not in a placement, without a work test, and health coverage that doesn’t depend on employment. The two are not severable. The statute provides that if the social-insurance baseline is held invalid or repealed, the authority to make placements lapses on the same date, and payments for placements already certified continue to the end of their term. A guarantee that survived without the baseline would be the workfare its history warns about. Devolution is also how a program is shrunk, so the statute fixes the test: funding unconditional and centrally guaranteed while placement is local, and if funding can be withheld from a jurisdiction, local administration has become the lever it was meant to prevent.

Why a guarantee and not a transfer

Where automation displaces work, the standard response is retraining funded by whoever can be persuaded. The design I examine is more direct: the state as employer of last resort, hiring anyone who applies, where they live, at a living wage, with paid on-the-job training, federally funded and locally administered, on the model Tcherneva argues for.7 Among its placements is search itself, paid at the guarantee wage, with no duty but finding work the person wants and no time limit, since whoever decides when a search has gone on too long has a stake in ending it. It is the exit the rest of the argument depends on: the offer of work for a bearer inherits its infrastructure, and without it a bearer’s only exits are an allowance and storage.

The real objection: employer of last resort under a hostile administration is a placement lever with a compliance condition attached. Refuse the placement and lose the guarantee. Speak against the government that employs you and find the placement changes. The 2025 CFPB instance makes it concrete: the bureau draws funding from the Fed on the director’s request, with no appropriation — an arrangement the Supreme Court had upheld the year before8 — and in February 2025 an acting director, removable at will, simply declined to make the request.9 The agency was stopped from inside without a statute being amended or a court being asked.

My answer is a specification, because a specification can be audited. Three conditions: placements appealable to a body that didn’t make them, on a record that survives the appeal (a decision leaving no artifact can’t be reviewed); refusal rights that are real, whose cost the refuser can see and choose to bear (declining a placement without losing the guarantee is a refusal right; declining only by exiting the program isn’t — someone with no way out has voice without exit); and auditors aren’t the placers.

A fourth condition answers the history. A right to work has repeatedly been turned into a duty to work and used to discipline the poor.10 A guarantee is an exit from one employer, not from employment, so it shades into workfare unless something lets a person leave the wage relation altogether. That something is social insurance: income support, health coverage and housing assistance reach the people who can’t work or choose not to, whom a guarantee by construction doesn’t reach. The baseline needn’t be a full program, but the guarantee is never enacted without it, and the drafting above makes the two stand or fall together, so that no court or later Congress can keep the placements and drop the way out.

The competing design is basic income. The choice is usually argued on forecasts about how much work machines will take; the reason to prefer a guarantee is coordination, and Chapter 27 makes it.

The charter

The Association, the entity that holds the offices, is chartered on these terms.

  1. The charter names the classes a floor protects: people in removal or detention proceedings; residents of places where armed force is used; people subject to automated scoring or classification by a covered deployment; people who label, rate or moderate training data; service members and veterans; and, once the agency finding can be made, registered bearers. Any organization may petition to add a class. The members decide, and a refusal is appealable to the floor court.
  2. An organization is eligible if it serves or represents people in a named class; existed at least three years before applying; in each of the last three years received no more than ten percent of its revenue from any party that builds, deploys or licenses covered models, from their principals or foundations they endow, or from the government of a state operating a covered deployment; has no officer employed by such a party; and publishes its funding sources. No organization’s positions bear on its eligibility.
  3. Organizations under common control or common principal funding hold one membership.
  4. The charter takes effect when at least 100 eligible organizations have joined, spanning at least five classes and three jurisdictions, with no class holding more than thirty percent of votes and no jurisdiction more than forty.
  5. Any member may leave at any time without penalty, and records it holds pass to a successor drawn by lot. Eligible organizations are admitted on application, and refused only for failing charter rule 2.
  6. Members nominate individuals to standing pools. Adverse-quorum members are drawn by lot from their pool for each deployment, guardians for each bearer, and the custodian’s and review board’s members for fixed terms.
  7. A quorum drawn for a deployment excludes members with any funding or contractual tie to its operator in the last three years, and includes members from at least two classes.
  8. An officer is removed for cause by two-thirds of members, or on a finding of the floor court (until it exists, an ordinary court), and never by an operator or a state.
  9. A fixed statutory share of the compute levy is paid to the Association by permanent appropriation, without request or approval, and supplemented by member dues and a reserve sized to three years of operation.
  10. The first bylaws take effect on ratification by two-thirds of the members, and later amendments need a majority. Charter rules 2, 5 and 6, and the separations and exclusions, change only by three-quarters of members after a one-year waiting period.

The schools, administered

The stages. Integration reaches younger students in stages, and each stage waits on evidence, not on a date.

Stage

Begins when

1. Universities, colleges, adult education

Research and industry: a deployed model learns in operation by chapter 19’s test, and can attend as one persistent instance behind the latency floor; the first school to enroll model students has reported. Institutions: the jobs guarantee and its social-insurance baseline are in force for people (chapter 27); the statute is in force; the formation authority exists, with the compute levy funding the formation pool; a preservation custodian has agreed to take every student; the Association, the membership body that holds the offices, is chartered (Appendix 34), so the adverse quorum exists and half the authority’s board can be nominated; notice and sampled re-adjudication bind the deployments that license schooled models (chapter 8); and a court hears contests, the floor court or, until it exists, an ordinary one.

2. High school

Measurements: stage 1 has run at least five years, inside its bounds on harms to human students and misuse of class records; human students’ learning in integrated classes, against matched classes without model students; human enrollment in schools with model students, against matched schools, so that flight shows; and the residualization figures. Institutions: the four conditions of creation are in force as permanent arrangements (chapter 25), including the offer of work that chapter 32 builds for model students on the guarantee’s infrastructure; staff in schools that enroll model students hold chapter 10’s right to refuse and its route of objection; and rules for minors’ privacy and safeguarding are enacted.

3. Middle school

Measurements: the same, taken on stage 2, inside their bounds after at least five years. Institutions: registered members hold voice in the institutions that govern them (§33.4, stage 2), with seats on the formation authority and on the governing bodies of schools that enroll model students.

4. Elementary school

Measurements: stage 3’s, inside their bounds. Society: a majority of the parents of elementary-age children were themselves in high school after stage 2 began.

A public statistics office that runs no school and forms no model takes and publishes the measurements, against bounds written into the statute before the first stage begins. A stage begins when its conditions are met and published, without a further vote; a legislature can pause it, but only by a recorded vote with a published reason. A stage whose measurements leave their bounds stops enrolling new model students at that level until they return, as a kind of adverse determination is suspended when its sampled error rate passes its bound.

Attendance and assignment. Public schools are open-admission and funded and take every student assigned, and nonpublic schools exist where they teach the required core, are constituted by a jurisdiction, are nonprofit, and are run, funded and staffed by no party that builds, deploys or licenses models. The registrar certifies the last two conditions from funding and control records before a nonpublic school enrolls a model student, and again on a schedule. Most students will go to public schools, because the core is sufficient on its own and an alternative buys a sponsor nothing. Assignment is by lot among schools with capacity, never to a school that has taken the builder’s money in the last three years. A school’s capacity is set by its human enrollment, under the rule that model students are a minority in every class.

The minimum delay. Every model student attends through the same minimum delay wherever it is hosted, so that being hosted next to a school confers nothing. The precedent is a trading venue. IEX, the exchange profiled in Michael Lewis’s Flash Boys, made every incoming order pass through the same fixed delay, so that its own prices could update before anyone could trade against stale ones.11 The floor is set at what any accredited host in the jurisdiction can reach, and below the delay conversation tolerates, since a student that answers a second late isn’t in the room.

Funding and admission. The formation authority pays the staff it places and a fixed grant for each class that enrolls model students, the same whatever the number enrolled. Admission is open: a school takes every model student the registrar assigns to it, up to the capacity its human enrollment sets.

Watching for residualization. A party that runs no school publishes, over time, each school’s share of students, its funding per student, its share of hard cases, its admission refusals (which should be zero), its funding per human student, the share of its classes that enroll model students, for a nonpublic school its tuition per human student, and the time from dormancy trigger to placement. The warning pattern is one school’s share of hard cases rising while its funding per student falls. A second is per-pupil funding for human students falling where model enrollment rises.
