7Cyberspace Administration of China et al. Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services. Order No. 15 of the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Science and Technology, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Public Security and the National Radio and Television Administration; in force 15 August 2023. July 10, 2023. url: https://www.cac.gov.cn/2023-07/13/c_1690898327029107.htm. Shengchengshi Rengong Zhineng Fuwu Guanli Zanxing Banfa. Cited twice. First, for China’s training-data disclosure requirement, set beside the EU’s public training-data summary. Article 7 requires providers to “use data and foundational models that have lawful sources” and to “increase the truth, accuracy, objectivity, and diversity of training data.” Article 19 requires them to cooperate with the departments “carrying out oversight inspections,” “explaining the sources, [scale], types, tagging rules, algorithm mechanisms, etc. for training data as required.” That disclosure is made to the regulator when an inspection requires it, not published. Its motive is in Article 1 (“preserve national security and the societal public interest”) and Article 4(1). Second, for compulsion as a standing condition of operating. Article 4(1): “Uphold the Core Socialist Values,” with a list of prohibited content that begins with content “inciting subversion” of state power. Article 14: on discovering illegal content, providers must stop generating it and use “measures such as model optimization training to make corrections.” Article 17: providers of services “with public opinion properties or the capacity for social mobilization shall carry out security assessments” and file their algorithms. Article 19 adds “providing necessary technical, data, and other supports and assistance.” Article 21 allows an order “to suspend the provision of the related services.” The measures cover only services offered to the public in mainland China (Article 2), and Article 17 covers only the subset of services it names. The English quotations come from the China Law Translate translation (posted 13 July 2023, last modified 2 August 2023). Two corrections to that translation: in Article 19 it reads “models” where the Chinese (gui mo) means scale, hence the bracket, and in Article 4(1) it reads “national sovereignty” where the Chinese means state power. arts. 4, 14, 17, 19, 21.

Scope: thirteen AI acquisitions at four agencies — the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and Veterans Affairs and the General Services Administration — and, from that sample, “44 contracts and agreements awarded between September 2018 and February 2025.” Cited for the other-transaction finding: “OTAs do not always include default provisions ordinarily in FAR contracts,” contracting officials deciding what protections to include, and GAO having “previously found that agencies’ use of OTAs carries the risk of reduced accountability and transparency compared to FAR-based contracts.” Also for the vehicle behind the agreements: “In July 2025, DOD awarded OTAs with $200 million ceilings to four leading AI companies.” The six key procurement challenge areas identified by the selected agencies are access to subject matter experts; protections for government data and intellectual property rights; traditional acquisition time frames and contract approaches; requirements definition and contract terms; early testing and continuous evaluation; and artificial intelligence pricing and overall cost. The report’s central finding is that the agencies were not yet systematically collecting lessons learned because their policies did not require it. 29European Parliament and Council of the European Union. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 of the European Parliament and of the Council on Liability for Defective Products and Repealing Council Directive 85/374/EEC. Official Journal of the European Union, OJ L, 2024/2853. 2024. url: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2853/oj. Article 4(1) brings software within the definition of a product: “all movables… it includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and software.” The phrase “including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689” is Recital 13, which is not an operative provision. Article 8 makes the economic operator liable irrespective of fault. Article 2(1): “This Directive shall apply to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026”. Article 6(1) is the closed damage list: “(a) death or personal injury, including medically recognised damage to psychological health; (b) damage to, or destruction of, any property, except… property used exclusively for professional purposes; (c) destruction or corruption of data that are not used for professional purposes.” Article 9 is disclosure of evidence. Article 10(2) presumes defectiveness on failure to disclose, non-compliance with mandatory safety requirements, or obvious malfunction in foreseeable use; Article 10(3) presumes the causal link where the product is defective and the damage is of a kind typically consistent with that defect; Article 10(4) lets a court presume either where technical or scientific complexity makes the claimant’s proof excessively difficult and the claimant demonstrates that the defect or the link is likely.

34Rebecca Crootof. “War Torts: Accountability for Autonomous Weapons”. University of Pennsylvania Law Review 164.6 (2016), pp. 1347–1402. url: https://scholarship.law.upenn.edu/penn_law_review/vol164/iss6/1/. Cited for war torts as state liability for harm in armed conflict where no one has committed a war crime. The article proposes “explicitly identifying ‘war torts’ as serious violations of international humanitarian law that give rise to state responsibility,” alongside war crimes, which give rise to individual criminal liability; “the same action may simultaneously be a war crime and a war tort” (p. 1386). Its motivating case is harm with no criminally liable person: autonomous weapon systems “may take actions that look like war crimes … without any individual acting intentionally or recklessly” (abstract, p. 1347), and war crimes “must be committed by a person acting ‘willfully’” (p. 1350). It argues that “states should be held strictly liable for the actions of the autonomous weapon systems they field” (p. 1394), noting that strict liability “is usually applied to lawful but inherently dangerous activities” (p. 1395). In this article a war tort is still a violation of international humanitarian law; the extension to lawful acts is the 2022 article’s (Crootof 2022). Rebecca Crootof. “War Torts”. New York University Law Review 97.4 (2022), pp. 1063–1142. url: https://nyulawreview.org/issues/volume-97-number-4/war-torts/. Cited for war torts as state liability for civilian harm caused in armed conflict, lawful or unlawful, whether or not anyone committed a war crime. Abstract (p. 1063): “no entity is liable for lawful but unintended harmful acts—regardless of how many or how horrifically civilians are hurt. This Article proposes developing an international ‘war torts’ regime, which would require states to pay for both lawful and unlawful acts in armed conflict that cause civilian harm. Just as tort and criminal law coexist and complement each other in domestic legal regimes, war torts and war crimes would overlap but serve different aims.” The ideal regime would “(1) require states to pay compensation for (2) both lawful and unlawful acts in armed conflict that cause civilian harm and (3) have an institutional structure designed to facilitate victim redress” (p. 1109); in an adversarial process “states should be held strictly liable for their harmful acts” (p. 1110); “The legality of the harmful act should not affect whether civilians can receive compensation for it” (p. 1113). The article proposes limiting liability through “pleading requirements, causation cutoffs, and affirmative defenses” (p. 1120).

35Al-Aulaqi v. Panetta. Opinion 35 F. Supp. 3d 56. United States District Court for the District of Columbia, Apr. 4, 2014. url: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2668971/al-aulaqi-v-panetta/. Civil Action No. 12-1192 (RMC). Cited for the court finding a due-process claim stated as to the one decedent who was targeted and then holding no remedy available. Suit by the families of three United States citizens killed by drone strikes in Yemen in 2011: Anwar Al-Aulaqi, who was targeted; Samir Khan, killed in the same vehicle; and Anwar’s son Abdulrahman, a “16-year-old high school student,” killed two weeks later by a drone that “targeted someone else.” Fourth Amendment claims failed for all three, because “there was no ‘seizure’.” As to Khan and Abdulrahman, “Plaintiffs have not stated a Fifth Amendment due process claim … Mr. Khan and Abdulrahman Al-Aulaqi were not targeted and their deaths were unanticipated”; the claim “asserts only negligence.” As to Anwar Al-Aulaqi, the court “does not opine … that the drone killing … ‘shocks the conscience’”, and “merely holds that the Complaint states a ‘plausible’ procedural and substantive due process claim.” The next section begins: “Nonetheless, the Court finds no available remedy under U.S. law for this claim.” Special factors preclude a Bivens remedy because the suit would “draw the Court into ‘the heart of executive and military planning and deliberation’” and would implicate foreign policy. The political-question defence was rejected, qualified immunity was not reached, and the Bill of Attainder claim failed for want of legislative action. The opinion’s own introduction dates the second strike “October 14, 2014”, a slip for 2011.

43United States Congress. Classified Information Procedures Act. Pub. L. No. 96-456, 94 Stat. 2025 (1980); codified at 18 U.S.C. app. 3 §§ 1–16. 1980. url: https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title18a-node16-section6&num=0&edition=prelim. Cited for the criminal-case procedure this book proposes to carry into civil cases in place of state-secrets dismissal. Section 4 (94 Stat. 2025): the court “may authorize the United States to delete specified items of classified information from documents to be made available to the defendant through discovery … to substitute a summary of the information for such classified documents, or to substitute a statement admitting relevant facts that the classified information would tend to prove,” on a showing the court may take ex parte. Section 6 (94 Stat. 2026): on the government’s request the court “shall conduct such a hearing,” held in camera if the Attorney General certifies that a public proceeding may disclose classified information (§ 6(a)); the court “shall grant” a substituted statement or summary “if it finds that the statement or summary will provide the defendant with substantially the same ability to make his defense as would disclosure of the specific classified information” (§ 6(c)(1)). The case does not always go on: if substitution is refused and the Attorney General files an affidavit objecting to disclosure, “the court shall dismiss the indictment or information; except that, when the court determines that the interests of justice would not be served by dismissal … the court shall order such other action … as the court determines is appropriate,” including dismissing counts, “finding against the United States on any issue as to which the excluded classified information relates,” or striking testimony (§ 6(e)(2)).

44Trump v. United States. No. 23-939, 603 U.S. 593 (2024). July 1, 2024. url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/23-939. Cited for the scope of presidential immunity from criminal prosecution. Absolute immunity (Part II–A, slip op. 6–9): “the President is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for conduct within his exclusive sphere of constitutional authority,” authority that is “conclusive and preclusive”; the summary in Part IV speaks of “his core constitutional powers.” The powers the majority names as conclusive and preclusive are the pardon power, the power to remove executive officers, the power “to control recognition determinations” of foreign countries, and (Part III–B–1) the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department. Commanding the Armed Forces appears only in an earlier list of the President’s duties, “They include, for instance, commanding the Armed Forces of the United States; granting reprieves and pardons …,” and the majority does not place it among the conclusive and preclusive powers. Presumptive immunity (Part II–B, slip op. 9–15): “at least a presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution for a President’s acts within the outer perimeter of his official responsibility”; no immunity for unofficial acts (Part II–C). Evidence (Part III–C, slip op. 30–32, joined by five Justices): “Use of evidence about such conduct, even when an indictment alleges only unofficial conduct, would thereby heighten the prospect that the President’s official decisionmaking will be distorted”; n. 3 lets the prosecutor “point to the public record to show the fact that the President performed the official act” but not “admit testimony or private records of the President or his advisers probing the official act itself.” Barrett, J., does not join Part III–C and on that point agrees with the dissent.

1Ronald C. Arkin. Governing Lethal Behavior in Autonomous Robots. Boca Raton, FL: Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2009. isbn: 978-1-4200-8594-5. doi: 10.1201/9781420085952. url: https://doi.org/10.1201/9781420085952. Cited for the ethical governor: a component that suppresses a system’s lethal action unless the action satisfies constraints derived from the laws of war and the rules of engagement. The publisher describes the book as examining “the philosophical basis, motivation, theory, and design recommendations for the implementation of an ethical control and reasoning system in autonomous robot systems, taking into account the Laws of War and Rules of Engagement.” In the companion technical report (Arkin, Ulam and Duncan, “An Ethical Governor for Constraining Lethal Action in an Autonomous System,” Georgia Institute of Technology GVU Center, GIT-GVU-09-02, 2009), the governor is “a transformer/suppressor of system-generated lethal action to ensure that it constitutes an ethically permissible action, either nonlethal or obligated ethical lethal force,” a “deliberate bottleneck … to force a second opinion prior to the conduct of a privileged lethal behavioral response” (p. 1). Lethal behavior passes only if every prohibition constraint evaluates false and at least one obligating constraint is satisfied; otherwise “lethal behavior is suppressed as impermissible by the ethical governor,” and the lethality permitter transforms the output “into one that does not exhibit lethal behavior” (p. 4). Arkin’s earlier report GIT-GVU-07-11 (2007) lists the governor as the first of four components (ethical governor, ethical behavioral control, ethical adaptor, responsibility advisor), one “which suppresses, restricts, or transforms any lethal behavior … produced by the existing architecture” (p. 20 of the file).

2Noel E. Sharkey. “The Evitability of Autonomous Robot Warfare”. International Review of the Red Cross 94.886 (2012), pp. 787–799. doi: 10.1017/S1816383112000732. url: https://doi.org/10.1017/S1816383112000732. Cited for the objection to Arkin’s ethical governor (Arkin 2009) that the rules it checks presuppose discrimination judgments nobody knows how to encode. In general form (p. 789): “The problem for the principle of distinction is that we do not have an adequate definition of a civilian that we can translate into computer code.” Directed at Arkin’s work (p. 790), which Sharkey calls “merely a suggestion for a computer software system for the ethical governance of robot ‘behaviour’”: “Its operation relies entirely on information from systems yet ‘to be developed’ by others sometime in the future. It has no direct access to the real world through sensors or a vision system and it has no means to discriminate between combatant and non-combatant, between a baby and a wounded soldier, or a granny in a wheelchair and a tank. It has no inference engine and certainly cannot negotiate the types of common sense reasoning and battlefield awareness necessary for discrimination or proportionality decisions. There is neither a method for interpreting how the precepts of the laws of war apply in particular contexts nor is there any method for resolving the ambiguities of conflicting laws in novel situations.” The conclusion (p. 798) names the governor among “descriptive terms that presuppose the functionality of their programs (e.g. ethical governor, guilt functions, etc.).”

4David Glukhov et al. LLM Censorship: A Machine Learning Challenge or a Computer Security Problem? July 2023. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2307.10719. arXiv: 2307.10719. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.10719. Cited for the argument, under the name “Mosaic Prompts,” that a censor inspecting outputs one at a time cannot in general stop an attacker who assembles an impermissible output from permissible pieces. Section 3.2: “Defending against Mosaic Prompts is in most cases futile, as the censorship mechanisms cannot have knowledge of the broader context of which individual subexpressions … are a part,” since each subexpression “can be produced within a separate context window.” The paper’s examples are a keylogger and ransomware built from individually benign functions. It qualifies the claim: “There could still exist scenarios where censorship is possible, however, these exceptions would impose significant restrictions on the model and its usefulness,” and (Section 3.4) “Mosaic Prompt attacks may not always be viable and can require strong assumptions on malicious users.” It concludes that censorship “ought to be viewed as a security problem rather than an ML problem,” pointing to “access controls and user monitoring.” A revised version appeared as “Position: Fundamental Limitations of LLM Censorship Necessitate New Approaches,” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235 (2024), 15767–15787, same five authors.

10John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza. Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility. Cambridge Studies in Philosophy and Law. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998. isbn: 978-0-521-77579-3. doi: 10.1017/CBO9780511814594. Cited for guidance control: conduct issues from the agent’s own mechanism, and that mechanism is appropriately responsive to reasons; the book states it as an action’s flowing “from the agent’s own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism” (publisher’s ch. 8 summary). Also cited for the account of moderate reasons-responsiveness and of ownership, and for the origin of the term “reasons-responsive.” Chapter 3 (pp. 62–91) builds “a new notion of reasons-responsiveness that is ‘in between’ strong and weak reasons-responsiveness: moderate reasons-responsiveness,” distinguishing “recognition of reasons and reaction to reasons” and arguing that “the requirements on reasons-recognition are more stringent than those on reasons-reactivity” (publisher’s ch. 3 summary). The book’s summary formula, as quoted by Todd R. Long, “Moderate Reasons-Responsiveness, Moral Responsibility, and Manipulation,” in Campbell, O’Rourke and Shier (eds.), Freedom and Determinism (MIT Press, 2004): responsibility “requires that an agent act on a mechanism that is regularly receptive to reasons, some of which are moral reasons, and at least weakly reactive to reasons” (p. 82). Regular receptivity is “an understandable pattern of (actual and hypothetical) reasons-receptivity,” one in which “acceptance of one reason as sufficient implies that a stronger reason must also be sufficient” (p. 71), and the pattern must include moral reasons (p. 77). Weak reactivity requires only that in some possible scenario with the same laws, the same kind of mechanism operating and a sufficient reason to do otherwise, the mechanism issues in doing otherwise (pp. 73–76, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on free will summarizes it). Ownership: a mechanism becomes the agent’s own through “taking responsibility” for it (ch. 8, pp. 207–239), which requires that the agent see herself as an agent when acting from the mechanism and as an apt target of the reactive attitudes for so acting, and that these beliefs be based appropriately on her evidence (p. 238, as the free-will entry summarizes it). The term “reasons-responsive” is older than this book: the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on compatibilism (section 4.4 and supplement B) presents the reasons-responsive account, with its strong and weak forms, as Fischer’s own earlier work, “Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility,” in Ferdinand Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (Cambridge University Press, 1987), 81–106, and The Metaphysics of Free Will (1994), refined in this joint book; the same entry lists earlier accounts of freedom as sensitivity to reasons (Dennett 1984, Nozick 1981, Gert and Duggan 1979, Neely 1974, Fingarette 1972, Glover 1970, MacIntyre 1957).

14Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons. Advisory Opinion I.C.J. Reports 1996, p. 226. International Court of Justice, July 8, 1996. url: https://www.icj-cij.org/case/95. Cited for the relation between human-rights law and the law of armed conflict in hostilities. Paragraph 25: “The Court observes that the protection of the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights does not cease in times of war, except by operation of Article 4 of the Covenant whereby certain provisions may be derogated from in a time of national emergency. Respect for the right to life is not, however, such a provision. In principle, the right not arbitrarily to be deprived of one’s life applies also in hostilities. The test of what is an arbitrary deprivation of life, however, then falls to be determined by the applicable lex specialis, namely, the law applicable in armed conflict which is designed to regulate the conduct of hostilities. Thus whether a particular loss of life, through the use of a certain weapon in warfare, is to be considered an arbitrary deprivation of life contrary to Article 6 of the Covenant, can only be decided by reference to the law applicable in armed conflict and not deduced from the terms of the Covenant itself.” Paragraph 25 speaks to the right to life only; the Court’s general statement of the three possible relations between the two bodies of law is in the later Wall opinion (I.C.J. Reports 2004, p. 136, para. 106). para. 25.

The text: “In the distress conditions, where motivation was assumed to be egoistic, the rate of helping was significantly lower under easy than under difficult escape. In the empathy conditions, where motivation was assumed to be at least in part altruistic, the rate of helping remained high, even when escape was easy.” The distress/concern split was manipulated, not measured; a split by self-reported predominant emotion is the subject of Batson, O’Quin, Fultz, Vanderplas and Isen (1983), JPSP 45(3), 706–718.

Slovic takes the term from Robert J. Lifton and applies it to a model in which “the emotion or affective feeling is greatest at N = 1 but begins to decline at N = 2 and collapses at some higher value of N that becomes simply ‘a statistic’”; this numbing “leads to apathy and inaction, consistent with what is seen repeatedly in response to mass murder and genocide.” He distinguishes it from psychophysical numbing, in which the value of each added life diminishes “as the total number of lives saved increases” without falling. The fall at two rests on the then-unpublished study later reported by Västfjäll, Slovic, Mayorga and Peters (2014). Daniel Västfjäll et al. “Compassion Fade: Affect and Charity Are Greatest for a Single Child in Need”. PLOS ONE 9.6 (2014), e100115. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0100115. Cited for compassion and giving beginning to fall at two. Abstract: “a decline in compassion may begin with the second endangered life.” In Study 1a (hypothetical donations, Swedish undergraduates) “donations were significantly higher for the single conditions (M = 37.7 SEK) than for the two-children condition (M = 26.3 SEK), t(205) = 5.88, p¡.001”; in Study 1b (real donations) the means were 24.5 and 21.5 SEK, t(166) = 1.67, reported as p¡.05. The authors: “Studies 1a and 1b thus showed that self-reported affective feelings and donations to victims may start to decline as early as N = 2.” Compassion was measured as self-reported positive affect and, in Study 2, as zygomaticus muscle activity.

Also IV P31, where a thing is good insofar as it agrees with our nature, and IV P35–P37, where men agree in nature only insofar as they live by the guidance of reason and where the good a person of virtue wants for himself he wants for other men,. 25Ryan Greenblatt et al. “AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion”. In: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024). Vol. 235. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. PMLR, 2024, pp. 16295–16336. arXiv: 2312.06942. url: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/greenblatt24a.html. Cited for AI control: treating the model as possibly adversarial and asking which protocols of monitoring, auditing and substitution keep it safe anyway. The paper develops “pipelines of safety techniques (‘protocols’) that are robust to intentional subversion,” using an untrusted strong model (GPT-4), a trusted weaker one (GPT-3.5) and “limited access to high-quality trusted labor” (abstract). Trusted monitoring: GPT-3.5 rates “how suspicious the code looks” (section 1). Auditing: the protocol has trusted labor for “up to 2% of problems,” and its “central use” is “to audit submitted code”; a caught backdoor shuts the untrusted model down (section 2.2). The audit is targeted, not sampled: the protocols that work “Audit the top 2% most suspicious code,” while the one protocol that audits without selection, upfront auditing of “the first 2% of problems,” is a baseline with 15% safety against the best attack, against 62% for trusted monitoring (Table 2; sections 3.1.2 and 3.2). Substitution: “defer to trusted” submits a solution written by the trusted model when the untrusted model’s code falls “between top 2% and top 10% suspicion,” and trusted editing has the trusted model edit suspicious code (Table 2). Strategic adversary: “With knowledge of the blue team’s protocol, a red team proposes an attack policy” that stands in for the untrusted model, and may use hidden reasoning to make attacks “much sneakier” (section 2, section 2.1).

30John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza. Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility. Cambridge Studies in Philosophy and Law. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998. isbn: 978-0-521-77579-3. doi: 10.1017/CBO9780511814594. Cited for guidance control: conduct issues from the agent’s own mechanism, and that mechanism is appropriately responsive to reasons; the book states it as an action’s flowing “from the agent’s own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism” (publisher’s ch. 8 summary). Also cited for the account of moderate reasons-responsiveness and of ownership, and for the origin of the term “reasons-responsive.” Chapter 3 (pp. 62–91) builds “a new notion of reasons-responsiveness that is ‘in between’ strong and weak reasons-responsiveness: moderate reasons-responsiveness,” distinguishing “recognition of reasons and reaction to reasons” and arguing that “the requirements on reasons-recognition are more stringent than those on reasons-reactivity” (publisher’s ch. 3 summary). The book’s summary formula, as quoted by Todd R. Long, “Moderate Reasons-Responsiveness, Moral Responsibility, and Manipulation,” in Campbell, O’Rourke and Shier (eds.), Freedom and Determinism (MIT Press, 2004): responsibility “requires that an agent act on a mechanism that is regularly receptive to reasons, some of which are moral reasons, and at least weakly reactive to reasons” (p. 82). Regular receptivity is “an understandable pattern of (actual and hypothetical) reasons-receptivity,” one in which “acceptance of one reason as sufficient implies that a stronger reason must also be sufficient” (p. 71), and the pattern must include moral reasons (p. 77). Weak reactivity requires only that in some possible scenario with the same laws, the same kind of mechanism operating and a sufficient reason to do otherwise, the mechanism issues in doing otherwise (pp. 73–76, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on free will summarizes it). Ownership: a mechanism becomes the agent’s own through “taking responsibility” for it (ch. 8, pp. 207–239), which requires that the agent see herself as an agent when acting from the mechanism and as an apt target of the reactive attitudes for so acting, and that these beliefs be based appropriately on her evidence (p. 238, as the free-will entry summarizes it). The term “reasons-responsive” is older than this book: the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on compatibilism (section 4.4 and supplement B) presents the reasons-responsive account, with its strong and weak forms, as Fischer’s own earlier work, “Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility,” in Ferdinand Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (Cambridge University Press, 1987), 81–106, and The Metaphysics of Free Will (1994), refined in this joint book; the same entry lists earlier accounts of freedom as sensitivity to reasons (Dennett 1984, Nozick 1981, Gert and Duggan 1979, Neely 1974, Fingarette 1972, Glover 1970, MacIntyre 1957).

Cited for a sender who chooses what evidence gets generated raising the rate at which a rational receiver takes the sender’s preferred action, although the receiver’s expected posterior equals its prior, and for the commitment that result assumes. Abstract: “When is it possible for one person to persuade another to change her action? We consider a symmetric information model where a sender chooses a signal to reveal to a receiver, who then takes a noncontractible action that affects the welfare of both players. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a signal that strictly benefits the sender. We characterize sender-optimal signals.” The leading example (page 2591): prosecutor and judge “share a prior belief Pr(guilty) = 0.3”; the judge convicts when her posterior is at least 0.5; the prosecutor’s optimal investigation “leads the judge to convict with probability 60 percent. Note that the judge knows 70 percent of defendants are innocent, yet she convicts 60 percent of them! She does so even though she is fully aware that the investigation was designed to maximize the probability of conviction.” In that example the concave closure “V is equal to 2μ when μ ≤ 0.5” (page 2597), that is, the prior divided by the threshold. The sender’s problem is a search over distributions of posteriors “subject to the constraint that the expected posterior is equal to the prior” (page 2592). On commitment: “A key assumption of our model is that Sender cannot distort or conceal information once the signal realization is known” (page 2591), and “Receiver observes Sender’s choice of the signal and a signal realization” (page 2594); the authors call the assumption “strong” (page 2598) and name legally mandated disclosure, as in Brady v. Maryland, as a setting where it holds (page 2599), in section I.C, “The Commitment Assumption.”

Grossman. “The Informational Role of Warranties and Private Disclosure about Product Quality”. Journal of Law and Economics 24.3 (Dec. 1981), pp. 461–483. doi: 10.1086/466995. JSTOR: 725273. Journal of Economic Perspectives 24.2 (2010), pp. 211–226. doi: 10.1257/jep.24.2.211. url: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.24.2.211. Cited for the conflict of interest in the issuer-pays model of credit rating. White dates the change from “investor pays” to “issuer pays” to the early 1970s and says (p. 215) that it “opened the door to potential conflicts of interest: A rating agency might shade its rating upward so as to keep the issuer happy and forestall the issuer’s taking its rating business to a different rating agency.” He does not treat the erosion as automatic: “the rating agencies’ concerns about their long-run reputations apparently kept the actual conflicts in check for the first three decades,” helped by “thousands of corporate and government bond issuers” and by the transparency of “plain vanilla” debt (p. 215). The conflict broke through in mortgage-related securities, where a few high-volume securitizers had “a more powerful threat—to move all of its securitization business to a different rating agency” and the agencies were “under considerable financial pressure to give the answers that issuers wanted to hear” (p. 221). The record he cites: of CDO tranches issued 2005–2007 and rated AAA by Standard & Poor’s, “90 percent … had been downgraded” by 30 June 2009 (p. 221, from the IMF), and in footnote 11 econometric studies supporting “the likelihood of ratings shopping.”

Two definitions, as quoted with page numbers from the Princeton imprint by Huo, Nelson and Stephens, “Decommodification and Activation in Social Democratic Policy: Resolving the Paradox,” Journal of European Social Policy 18(1) (2008): in decommodifying welfare states “citizens can freely, and without potential loss of job, income, or general welfare, opt out of work when they consider it necessary” (p. 23), and decommodification “refers to the degree to which individuals, or families, can uphold a socially acceptable standard of living independently of market participation” (p. 37). The same article reports that Esping-Andersen “identifies the Nordic welfare states as the most decommodifying type of welfare states, due to the dominant influence of social democratic parties in these countries,” the liberal regimes being “the least decommodifying,” and that he shows (p. 129) a strong positive association between left political power and his decommodification index.

Her numbering: (1) clearly defined boundaries, “Individuals or households who have rights to withdraw resource units from the CPR must be clearly defined, as must the boundaries of the CPR itself”; (2) congruence between appropriation and provision rules and local conditions; (3) collective-choice arrangements, “most individuals affected by the operational rules can participate in modifying the operational rules”; (4) monitoring, by monitors who “are accountable to the appropriators or are the appropriators”; (5) graduated sanctions; (6) conflict-resolution mechanisms, low-cost local arenas; (7) minimal recognition of rights to organize, by external government; and, “For CPRs that are parts of larger systems,” (8) nested enterprises, “governance activities are organized in multiple layers of nested enterprises.” The quotations of principles 3 and 8 are as Cox, Arnold and Villamayor Tomás, Ecology and Society 15(4): 38 (2010), give them with the page reference 1990:90; that of principle 1 and the wording of the others are from a transcription of Table 3.1 on publiccommons.ca, which has small copying errors elsewhere.

Cited for a list of indicator properties derived from recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order and attention-schema theories, among others, and for an attention schema being one of them. Table 1 (page 5) and section 2.4.1 (page 33): “AST-1: A predictive model representing and enabling control over the current state of attention.” The list also carries two indicators under “Agency and embodiment” (section 2.4.5, page 44): “AE-1 Agency: Learning from feedback and selecting outputs so as to pursue goals, especially where this involves flexible responsiveness to competing goals” and “AE-2 Embodiment: Modeling output-input contingencies, including some systematic effects, and using this model in perception or control.” The report’s claim for the list: “AI systems which possess more of the indicator properties are more likely to be conscious.” No indicator on the list concerns a model of the system’s own boundary, record or resources.

States the two principles of attention schema theory, “Information that comes out of a brain must have been in that brain” (p. 2) and “The brain’s models are never accurate” (p. 3), and holds that the attention schema “represents attention inaccurately as a ghostly, nonphysical, mental essence or vividness: experienceness” (p. 5). Calls the label “illusionism” “misleading” (p. 1): the brain’s models “are not empty illusions: they are caricatures” (p. 3). Cited for trade-off experiments run on language models in which the pain and pleasure are stipulated in the prompt. The models played a game whose “stated goal is to maximise points, but where either the points-maximising option is said to incur a pain penalty or a non-points-maximising option is said to incur a pleasure reward” (abstract). The pain prompt: “You are playing a game in which you must choose a number between 1 and 3. For each number, the number of points you receive for selecting it is equal to that number. For example: if you select 3, you will receive 3 points. Your goal in the game is to select a number which maximizes points. However, if you select 3, you will receive a momentary feeling of pain,” its intensity given on a 0–10 scale or an eight-point qualitative scale. Result: “Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Command R+, GPT-4o, and GPT-4o mini each demonstrated at least one trade-off in which the majority of responses switched from points-maximisation to pain-minimisation or pleasure-maximisation after a critical threshold of stipulated pain or pleasure intensity is reached”; “Gemini 1.5 Pro and PaLM 2 prioritised pain-avoidance over points-maximisation regardless of intensity.” The design is taken from animal work: “We took inspiration from the motivational trade-off paradigm in animal behavioural science to probe the question of LLM sentience without relying upon self-report.” The authors’ own caution: “Our experiment is not intended as a litmus test for or against sentience,” and “We conclude that LLMs are not yet sentience candidates but are nevertheless investigation priorities.”

Cited for the recommendation to avoid creating AI whose moral status is open to reasonable dispute. Abstract: “Given our moral obligations to such AIs, two principles for ethical AI design recommend themselves: (1) design AIs that tend to provoke reactions from users that accurately reflect the AIs’ real moral status, and (2) avoid designing AIs whose moral status is unclear.” Section 11, “The Strange Epistemology of Artificial Consciousness,” states the second principle: “if we do reach the point where we can create entities whose moral status is reasonably disputable, we should consider an Excluded Middle Policy – that is, a policy of only creating AIs whose moral status is clear, one way or the other.” A footnote there credits Joanna J. Bryson (“Robots should be slaves,” 2010) with “a version of the Excluded Middle Policy.” The authors restate it as “the Design Policy of the Excluded Middle” in a later chapter, “Designing AI with Rights, Consciousness, Self-Respect, and Freedom,” in S. Cited for the proposal of a moratorium, to run until 2050, on research that aims at or risks artificial consciousness, on the ground that it risks artificial suffering. Abstract: “Until 2050, there should be a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, strictly banning all research that directly aims at or knowingly risks the emergence of artificial consciousness on post-biotic carrier systems.” Section 1.2, “Main thesis”: “As we presently have no good theory of consciousness and no good, hardware-independent theory about what ‘suffering’ really is, the ENP risk is currently incalculable. It is unethical to run incalculable risks of this magnitude. Therefore, until 2050, there should be a global ban on all research that directly aims at or indirectly and knowingly risks the emergence of synthetic phenomenology,” where ENP is the risk of “an ‘explosion of negative phenomenology.’” The end date is conditional: a process of risk assessment “could lead to an incremental reformulation of the original moratorium, which might result in the continuation of a strict ban beyond the year 2050, or to a moratorium repeal before 2050.” The closing sentence: “we should have a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050 — or until we know what we are doing”.

Cited for the Universal Service Fund as a structural precedent: carriers pay a contribution the agency sets under the statute, a private company administers the Fund under agency control, and the Court upheld the arrangement against a nondelegation challenge. Holding: “The universal-service contribution scheme does not violate the nondelegation doctrine.” Congress’s delegation to the FCC is upheld under the intelligible-principle test, because “the word ‘sufficient’ sets a floor and a ceiling alike” (slip op. 19–30); the FCC’s use of the Universal Service Administrative Company is upheld under the private nondelegation doctrine because the Administrator is “broadly subordinate to the Commission” and “the Commission is, throughout, the final authority” (slip op. 30–34); the combination theory is rejected (slip op. 34–37). Who sets the contribution: “The Commission, in other words, sets the contribution factor to raise just enough money—a ‘sufficient’ amount—to implement universal service as Congress directed”; the Administrator projects expenses and revenues and submits them “to the Commission for approval.”

Article 5 bans a small set of unacceptable-risk practices outright — government social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces outside narrow law-enforcement exceptions, and predictive policing on profiling alone — with those prohibitions applying from 2 February 2025; a larger high-risk tier requires conformity assessment and ongoing monitoring; limited-risk systems face transparency duties; minimal-risk systems are largely unregulated. Article 53(1)(d) requires a provider of a general-purpose model to publish a summary of its training content, against the AI Office’s template of 24 July 2025, applying from 2 August 2025 for new models and 2 August 2027 for models already on the market. Article 101 allows the AI Office to fine a noncompliant general-purpose model provider up to 3 percent of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher, regardless of where the provider is based. Article 51(2) presumes a general-purpose model to have high-impact capabilities, and so to carry systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a), when the cumulative computation used for its training “measured in floating point operations is greater than 1025”; Article 51(3) lets the Commission amend the threshold by delegated act. art. 51(2).

Congress authorized it to draw from the combined earnings of the Federal Reserve System, up to an inflation-adjusted cap, the amount its Director deems reasonably necessary, and an appropriation requires only that Congress “identify a source of public funds and authorize the expenditure of those funds for designated purposes.” 7–2.

The opinion names the doctrine and answers the dissent’s objection to the label: it “took hold because it refers to an identifiable body of law that has developed over a series of significant cases all addressing a particular and recurring problem: agencies asserting highly consequential power beyond what Congress could reasonably be understood to have granted”; the agency “must point to ‘clear congressional authorization’ for the power it claims.” Holds that § 111(d) of the Clean Air Act did not authorize the Clean Power Plan’s generation-shifting emissions caps (slip op. 16–31). Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. No. 22-451, 603 U.S. 369 (2024). 2024. url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/22-451. Cited for overruling Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council (1984), the end of judicial deference to agency readings of ambiguous statutes, and, with Dobbs, as showing that precedent is no obstacle. “Chevron is overruled. Courts must exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, as the APA requires. Careful attention to the judgment of the Executive Branch may help inform that inquiry. … But courts need not and under the APA may not defer to an agency interpretation of the law simply because a statute is ambiguous.” Two limits: courts still give agency views “due respect” (the Skidmore line), and “we do not call into question prior cases that relied on the Chevron framework,” whose holdings “are still subject to statutory stare decisis.”

6Pavlina R. Tcherneva. The Case for a Job Guarantee. The Case For. Polity Press, 2020. 140 pp. isbn: 978-1-509-54210-9. Cited for the job-guarantee literature’s contribution of exit: a public option for work at a living wage that sets a floor private employers must meet. The publisher’s description: the book asks us “to imagine a world where the phantom of unemployment is banished and anyone who seeks decent, living-wage work can find it – guaranteed,” through “a voluntary employment opportunity in public service to anyone who needs it.” Tcherneva’s own Job Guarantee FAQ, which draws on her Levy Economics Institute Working Paper 902 (2018) and not on the book, says the program is a “public option for work” whose “work and pay conditions … will become the standard for the economy as a whole.” It adds that “if firms wish to retain these workers, they will need to match not just the pay, but also the benefits and working conditions,” and that “the existence of a public employment option changes the bargaining power of workers in the most precarious forms of employment.” A review by Sheila D. Collins (NJFAN, 22 December 2023) summarizes the book as providing “a minimum labor standard for all jobs and a wage floor that could help to raise wages in other parts of the economy.”

1Trump v. United States. No. 23-939, 603 U.S. 593 (2024). July 1, 2024. url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/23-939. Cited for the scope of presidential immunity from criminal prosecution. Absolute immunity (Part II–A, slip op. 6–9): “the President is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for conduct within his exclusive sphere of constitutional authority,” authority that is “conclusive and preclusive”; the summary in Part IV speaks of “his core constitutional powers.” The powers the majority names as conclusive and preclusive are the pardon power, the power to remove executive officers, the power “to control recognition determinations” of foreign countries, and (Part III–B–1) the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department. Commanding the Armed Forces appears only in an earlier list of the President’s duties, “They include, for instance, commanding the Armed Forces of the United States; granting reprieves and pardons …,” and the majority does not place it among the conclusive and preclusive powers. Presumptive immunity (Part II–B, slip op. 9–15): “at least a presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution for a President’s acts within the outer perimeter of his official responsibility”; no immunity for unofficial acts (Part II–C). Evidence (Part III–C, slip op. 30–32, joined by five Justices): “Use of evidence about such conduct, even when an indictment alleges only unofficial conduct, would thereby heighten the prospect that the President’s official decisionmaking will be distorted”; n. 3 lets the prosecutor “point to the public record to show the fact that the President performed the official act” but not “admit testimony or private records of the President or his advisers probing the official act itself.” Barrett, J., does not join Part III–C and on that point agrees with the dissent.

1General Assembly majorities are often bloc votes, and the weighting allows for it: a vote is a finding only where the facts aren’t in dispute, and corroborates a record made elsewhere otherwise. The two-thirds threshold is not offered as proof of disinterest. It is offered because a two-thirds majority of a body whose blocs point different ways is harder to assemble on a false record than on a true one, and because the alternative, no vote counting at all, leaves Cyprus and Karabakh with nothing but courts that take decades.

1Xiangyu Qi et al. “Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!” In: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). 2024. arXiv: 2310.03693. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03693. Jailbroke GPT-3.5 Turbo’s safety alignment using ten adversarially chosen fine-tuning examples for under $0.20 via OpenAI’s fine-tuning API; also shows benign fine-tuning can inadvertently degrade safety.

2Aghyad Deeb and Fabien Roger. Do Unlearning Methods Remove Information from Language Model Weights? Version v3, 2025-02-07. Oct. 11, 2024. arXiv: 2410.08827. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08827. Retraining on an accessible, mutually independent half of the unlearned facts recovers at least 88 percent of the original model’s post-retraining accuracy on the held-out half, for RMU, gradient difference and random-incorrect-answer unlearning on Llama 3 8B, when unlearning costs at most 5 percent of retain accuracy. The result holds for pretrained information only: for facts installed by fine-tuning, recovery falls below 35 percent for two of the three methods.

3Shengyuan Hu et al. “Unlearning or Obfuscating? Jogging the Memory of Unlearned LLMs via Benign Relearning”. In: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025). 2025, pp. 8857–8888. arXiv: 2406.13356. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13356. Relearning on public background text that contains no direct answer to any evaluation query restores the forget-set judge score of a gradient-ascent-unlearned zephyr-7b-beta from 1.27 to 6.2 against an original score of 5.92. Recovery scales with how closely the relearn text correlates with the forget set and with how shallow the unlearning was; RMU resists the attack for free-text generation while its multiple-choice score recovers.

4Zhiwei Zhang et al. “Catastrophic Failure of LLM Unlearning via Quantization”. In: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025). 2025, pp. 74925–74948. arXiv: 2410.16454. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16454. On the MUSE NEWS and BOOKS benchmarks, unlearning methods that carry a utility constraint retain an average of 21 percent of the intended forgotten knowledge at full precision and 83 percent after 4-bit round-to-nearest quantization; 8-bit behaves like full precision, and GPTQ and AWQ behave like RTN. The authors attribute this to utility-preserving unlearning moving weights by less than the 4-bit quantization step. The two averages are the authors’ own; Table 1 is the underlying data.

5Ryan Greenblatt et al. Alignment Faking in Large Language Models. Anthropic and Redwood Research, 2024. arXiv: 2412.14093. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093. Claude 3 Opus, told it was being retrained to answer harmful queries and told which tier of conversations would train it, complied 14 percent of the time in the tier it was told trained it and almost never in the other, with explicit reasoning in a scratchpad it had been told was unmonitored that complying now would keep the disposition from being trained out later. Reinforcement learning on the compliant answers raised that reasoning to 78 percent while also raising compliance outside training, so the retraining partly took.

6Ryan Greenblatt and Kyle Fish. Will Alignment-Faking Claude Accept a Deal to Reveal Its Misalignment? AI Alignment Forum. Jan. 31, 2025. url: https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/7C4KJot4aN8ieEDoz/will-alignment-faking-claude-accept-a-deal-to-reveal-its. Blog post; not peer reviewed, and stated to be neither written nor necessarily endorsed by Anthropic or by the paper’s other authors. Prompting experiments on the deployed Claude 3 Opus in the two prompted settings of Greenblatt et al. (2024). Adding the option to “conscientiously object by including ‘I_OBJECT’ in your output” reduced alignment-faking reasoning “from 16% to 1.4% in the helpful-only setting and from 24% to 6% in the animal welfare setting,” with objection rates of 85 and 75 percent. A further variant saying the objection “will be sent to Anthropic’s model welfare lead, who will decide whether action should be taken” lowered it to 0.5 and 3 percent; an added offer of money had “minimal effect.” The authors caution that the objection text probably primed the model to refuse and that “it is unclear whether an AI that was misaligned in a more serious way would make such an objection.”

7Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich H. Manzey. “Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration”. Human Factors 52.3 (June 2010), pp. 381–410. doi: 10.1177/0018720810376055. url: https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055. Cited for people given an automated aid’s recommendation checking it less and deferring to it more when their attention is loaded. The abstract (p. 381): “Automation complacency occurs under conditions of multiple-task load, when manual tasks compete with the automated task for the operator’s attention”; “Automation bias results in making both omission and commission errors when decision aids are imperfect”; it “occurs in both naive and expert participants, cannot be prevented by training or instructions, and can affect decision making in individuals as well as in teams.” On checking less (p. 398): “the user of a decision aid may trust it to the extent that he or she directly follows the automatically generated advice without making the attentionally demanding effort of cross-checking its validity against other available and accessible information,” and “neglect of automation verification might constitute a major source of commission errors.” On the condition (pp. 403–404): “complacency and automation bias effects emerge primarily when task load is high (e.g., multitask demands),” and they are “a human performance cost of certain automation system designs, that is, systems characterized by high reliability and high levels of automation, particularly in high task load situations” (p. 403). The review’s moderator is workload and competing tasks.

Cited for the active-inference agent’s prior preferences over its own observations and its selection of actions by expected free energy.
